#9975. Multi-Vector (Late Interaction) Embedding Models with Sentence Transformers

Sentence Transformers is a Python library for using and training embedding and reranker models for applications like retrieval augmented generation, semantic search, and more. With the v6.0 update, it gains a fourth model type: MultiVectorEncoder, for ColBERT-style late interaction retrieval. Any PyLate checkpoint and any Stanford-NLP ColBERT checkpoint loads straight into it, and colpali-engine models for visual document retrieval can be used too, through the same familiar API you already use for dense, sparse, and reranker models.

Where a regular embedding model compresses a whole text into one vector, a multi-vector model keeps one vector per token and scores query against document with the MaxSim operator. That preserves token-level matching information that a single vector has to average away, which usually means stronger retrieval at the cost of a bigger index. It's also the state of the art for visual document retrieval, where a text query is matched against page images directly, with no OCR step in between.

In this blogpost, we'll show you how to use these models: loading the various checkpoint formats, encoding and scoring, plugging them into a search stack, running them on page images, and keeping the index affordable. Everything below runs on a plain pip install -U sentence-transformers.

This blog is about using multi-vector models. If you want to learn how to train them, see the companion Training and Finetuning Multi-Vector Embedding Models with Sentence Transformers blogpost.

A dense embedding model reads a text and returns a single fixed-size vector. Everything the model noticed has to fit in those 384, 768, or 1024 numbers, and similarity is one dot product between two such summaries. This works remarkably well, but the compression is lossy in a specific way: a rare entity, an exact identifier, or one crucial clause in a long passage all have to compete for room in the same vector. A query with several requirements at once runs into the same wall. For "green sofa with wooden legs and rounded cushions", a single vector has to blend all four into one point, so a green sofa with the wrong legs ends up sitting close to the one you actually asked for.

A multi-vector model (also called a late-interaction or ColBERT-style model, after the ColBERT paper) skips that compression. It runs the same transformer, but instead of pooling the token embeddings into one vector, it projects each token embedding down to a small dimension (classically 128) and keeps all of them. A 9-token document becomes a 9x128 matrix, not a 1x128 vector.

The interaction between query and document is then deferred until scoring time, which is where the name "late interaction" comes from. A cross-encoder interacts early, with both texts going through the model together, which is accurate but leaves nothing to precompute, since every document has to be re-encoded for each new query. A bi-encoder, which is what the dense embedding model above is, barely interacts at all (one dot product between two finished summaries), and that is exactly what lets you encode a collection once and query it fast. Late interaction sits in between. Documents are still encoded independently and can be indexed offline, but scoring compares every query token against every document token, which leaves far more room for the two to interact.

Scoring uses MaxSim: for each query token, take its highest similarity against any document token, then sum those maxima across the query.

MaxSim(Q,D)=∑Qi∈Qmax⁡Dj∈DQi⋅Dj\text{MaxSim}(Q, D) = \sum_{Q_i \in Q} \max_{D_j \in D} Q_i \cdot D_jMaxSim(Q,D)=Qi​∈Q∑​Dj​∈Dmax​Qi​⋅Dj​

Because the token embeddings are L2-normalized, each of those dot products is a cosine similarity in [-1, 1], so the whole sum lands within [-num_query_tokens, num_query_tokens].

You can read the operator as a soft alignment, where every query token points at the one document token that best explains it, and the score is how well the document supports the query overall.

The alignment doesn't have to be lexical, since the token embeddings are contextualized. Encode "Where do penguins live?" against "Penguins inhabit Antarctica." with lightonai/mLateOn and the query token live finds its best match on inhabit at 0.94, a word it shares no characters with! That is the thing lexical retrieval cannot do, BM25 and its relatives need the term itself, so synonyms and paraphrases slip past them. Dense embedding models bridge that gap as well, of course. What late interaction adds is that it does so without giving up the other direction. When an exact match is what matters (a product code, a surname, a function name), MaxSim still has that token sitting there on its own, where a single-vector model had to average it in with everything else. It isn't one-to-one either, since several query tokens routinely settle on the same document token.

You gain retrieval quality, particularly on queries where one specific piece of a document is what makes it relevant, on multi-requirement queries like the sofa above where each requirement gets to find its own evidence, and on out-of-domain data where a dense model's compression was tuned for a different distribution. That compression is learned from the training queries, so the model learns to keep what they needed and drop everything else, which may include exactly what your production queries ask about. The effect grows with document length, since more text has to fit in the same fixed vector.

The cost is index size. One vector per token instead of one vector per document is a lot more vectors, only partly offset by the smaller dimension. Encoding 4,874 Natural Questions passages with lightonai/LateOn produced 608,414 token vectors, an average of 124.8 per passage:

That's about 42x the storage of the MiniLM index, or 62 KiB per passage. However, indexes are often compressed, e.g. the same 608,414 vectors take 92 MB as a fast-plaid index, since PLAID stores a centroid id plus a quantized residual per vector rather than the vector itself. For scale, a 4096-dimensional dense model like Qwen3-Embedding-8B would need about 80 MB for these same 4,874 passages, so a compressed multi-vector index sits in the same territory as the dense indexes people already run. Token Pooling cuts the vector count before any of that, and Retrieve and Rerank avoids building an index at all.

PyLate comes up throughout this post, so here is the short version. Sentence Transformers handled dense and sparse models but not late interaction, so LightOn built PyLate on top of it to close that gap, adding the training, inference, and retrieval pieces these models need. Much of what you'll load below was trained with it, and LightOn built an ecosystem around it too, including fast-plaid, the late-interaction index that turns up in Indexing. With v6.0 those capabilities live in Sentence Transformers itself.

With the tradeoff in mind, let's get a model running.

Multi-vector models work with a plain install:

For ColPali-style visual document retrieval, you also need the image dependencies (see Installation for all extras, and Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models for multimodal support in general):

Sentence Transformers v6.0 requires transformers v5.x, torch 2.2+, and huggingface-hub v1.x. If you pin any of those lower, plan the upgrade first. See the Migration Guide for the full list of breaking changes.

Loading a multi-vector model looks exactly like loading any other Sentence Transformers model:

To find models that work, look for the multi-vector and sentence-transformers tags on the Hub. Any model with those tags loads with the line above, whether it started life as a PyLate checkpoint, a Stanford-NLP ColBERT checkpoint, or a ColPali-family model for visual document retrieval. We're working through the ecosystem to get that tag onto every model that works, so the list keeps growing.

Underneath, MultiVectorEncoder reads each of the formats these checkpoints have been published in over the years, so PyLate and Stanford-NLP checkpoints load directly even where the tag hasn't been added yet:

Visual document retrieval models are the exception. ColPali-family checkpoints ship in colpali-engine's own format, which carries no information Sentence Transformers can use, so each one needs a small configuration added to its repository before it loads. Most of that work is done and waiting to be merged. See Supported Models for the current state and how to load them today.

Multi-vector models carry a handful of recipe knobs that differ per checkpoint: marker prefixes for queries and documents, length caps, whether queries are padded out with [MASK] tokens, and which tokens are skipped when scoring documents. All of them live in the module configs, so print(model) shows you exactly what you loaded. Here's the original ColBERTv2 checkpoint, which pads every query to exactly 32 tokens and truncates documents at 180:

That's the classic ColBERT pipeline: a Transformer producing contextualized token embeddings, a token-level Dense projecting each of them to 128 dimensions, a MultiVectorMask deciding which tokens count during scoring, and a token-level Normalize. Other checkpoints fill in different values. lightonai/GTE-ModernColBERT-v1 uses the same four modules with [Q] and [D] prompts, no query expansion, and caps of 48 and 300.

You rarely need to touch any of this, since every released checkpoint configures its own. It matters when you build a model from a bare backbone, which is covered in Creating Custom Models.

One value is worth checking against your own data, though. document_length truncates, so anything past it never reaches the index. For example, a 662-token passage through LateOn's cap of 300 comes back as 273 vectors, with the rest of the passage simply gone. Most of these checkpoints were trained on short passages, so if your chunks are longer than the cap, you can lift it for a single call with encode_document(..., processing_kwargs={"text": {"max_length": 512}}), keeping in mind that you would be running the model past the length it was trained on and that the index grows roughly in proportion. Multi-vector models tend to tolerate that well. On MLDR, a long-document retrieval benchmark, the multilingual siblings of the pair above show the gap clearly: mLateOn scores 77.92 against mDenseOn's 51.59.

Multi-vector models are asymmetric, so queries and documents go through different prefixes, different length caps, and different scoring masks. Unlike many dense models, where the two are interchangeable, encode_query() and encode_document() are required to get correct embeddings:

What you get back is a list of 2D tensors, one per input, each of shape (num_tokens, embedding_dim). Unlike dense embeddings, you can't stack these into one rectangular tensor, because every input has its own token count. The second document is longer than the first, so it comes back as a taller matrix.

Each call applies the model's own recipe for you. encode_query prepends the query marker, expands the query to a fixed length if the checkpoint asks for it, and caps it at the query length. encode_document prepends the document marker, caps at the document length, and drops any skiplisted tokens (punctuation, for most checkpoints) from the scoring mask.

The usual encode() arguments all still apply, so batch_size, show_progress_bar, convert_to_numpy, device, and multi-process pools work the way you'd expect:

model.similarity() computes the full all-pairs MaxSim matrix:

Mars wins, as it should, though the runners-up are close behind. Saturn also contains the literal phrase "the Red Planet", and Jupiter is a planet with a red spot, so a token-level operator has plenty to latch onto in all three. The ordering is what matters.

Scores often sit this close together, as GLInt shows by measuring the spread across a full candidate pool. MaxSim takes a maximum per query token, so a document will usually give every query token some decent best match, and scores start from a floor. Contextualized token embeddings are also anisotropic, clustering in a narrow cone rather than spreading out, so even arbitrary token pairs tend to score high.

There is also model.similarity_pairwise(), for when you already have matched pairs and just want the pair scores instead of the full similarity matrix:

MaxSim sums over query tokens, so its magnitude scales with how many query tokens there are, which means you can't compare scores across models with different query recipes. LateOn encodes the Red Planet query above as 12 tokens. Run that same query and those same documents through ColBERTv2, which pads and truncates every query to exactly 32 tokens, and the scores land in a completely different range:

Within one model the ordering is all you need, but if you want scores on a bounded scale, switch the model's similarity function to MeanMaxSim, which divides by the query token count. Back on LateOn:

Now every score is an average cosine similarity in [-1, 1], although you'll only see [0, 1] in practice.

If your corpus is small, exhaustive MaxSim over all of it is the simplest thing that works. Encode the corpus once, then score each query against everything:

Those 4,874 passages encoded in 20 seconds on an RTX 3090, and each search takes about 120ms end to end, most of that the MaxSim scoring against all 608,414 token vectors. This is exact, but it scales linearly in total corpus tokens and keeps every token vector in memory, so reach for it when you have a few thousand documents rather than a few million. The runnable version of this script is semantic_search.py.

Past that size you want a real late-interaction index, which Sentence Transformers doesn't ship. It doesn't need to, because these indexes store whatever encode_document produced, so you encode here and hand the token embeddings to something built for them. Indexing has working snippets for four of the options, and the section directly below covers how to skip the index entirely.

You can also get late-interaction quality without maintaining a late-interaction index, by using a multi-vector model as your reranker. A fast bi-encoder narrows a large corpus to a handful of candidates, then the multi-vector model rescores only those:

Only the 50 candidates are ever encoded as multi-vectors, so your index stays a normal dense index and the token vectors are transient. This is the same role a cross-encoder plays in a retrieve-and-rerank stack, but a multi-vector model is considerably cheaper per candidate. You encode the documents in one batch and score them with a matrix multiplication, instead of one forward pass per query-document pair. The runnable script is retrieve_rerank.py, which prints the timings of both stages.

Several vector databases index and score multi-vectors natively: Qdrant since v1.10, Weaviate since v1.29, Vespa for years now, LanceDB since v0.15.0, and VectorChord, which adds a MaxSim operator to Postgres that plain pgvector doesn't have. Milvus joined them in v2.6.4, under array-of-structs rather than the unrelated feature it calls multi-vector search. If you would rather not run a server at all, LightOn's fast-plaid is a pip install away and implements PLAID directly, and PyLate wraps it in a fuller retrieval stack.

A few others get you partway. OpenSearch and Elasticsearch can rescore candidates with MaxSim but not retrieve on it, and the Elasticsearch field is additionally in technical preview and Enterprise-tier. turbopuffer has late-interaction indexing in private beta.

The snippets below index text, but nothing in them is text-specific. encode_document hands back the same list of token-vector matrices whether the document was a passage, a page image, an audio clip, or a video, so the ColPali-style models from Visual Document Retrieval go into any of these unchanged. There are simply more vectors per document, which is what makes Token Pooling worth reaching for sooner there.

fast-plaid, Qdrant, Weaviate, and Vespa all take exactly what encode_document returns, so the code is the same up to the client library. Here's a working snippet for each, run against the 4,874 passages and 608,414 token vectors from the Semantic Search example. Each one carries the ingestion and query times it produced on one machine (RTX 3090, i7-13700K), with no tuning beyond what the code shows, to give a sense of the shape of the work. All four answer the query faster than the 98ms model.similarity took in that section, and three of them do it on the CPU, since fast-plaid is the only one here using the GPU.

All four returned the same three passages in the same order as the exhaustive PyTorch MaxSim earlier in this post, and the three databases reproduce its scores to four decimals! That is because their snippets score every document, which is affordable at this size and removes approximation as a variable. fast-plaid is approximate by design, so its scores differ slightly. The notes under each one say what changes when you switch to an approximate index, which is where rankings start to drift.

fast-plaid is LightOn's Rust implementation of PLAID, the index ColBERT was originally built around. There's no server to start, and it reads the tensors encode_document hands back without any conversion.

The index argument is a directory, not just a label, so the index is written to disk as it is built. Pointing a new FastPlaid at the same path reopens it for searching or for adding more documents, instead of rebuilding from the embeddings each time. On this corpus it occupies 92 MB, against 311.5 MB for the raw float32 vectors.

This is the only one of the four that is approximate, and it is the one place in this section where the scores do not match the exhaustive MaxSim. PLAID prunes with centroids and stores quantized residuals, so the three scores drift by a few hundredths in both directions against the 11.9192 / 11.7591 / 11.6710 computed earlier. The ranking is unaffected here, and that is the trade PLAID is making. It was designed for corpora far larger than this one, where scanning everything is not an option.

Qdrant needs a server: docker run -p 6333:6333 qdrant/qdrant. The client also has a local mode (QdrantClient(":memory:")) that needs no server, but it's a pure-Python reimplementation, so use it for trying things out rather than for timing them.

MAX_SIM is the only comparator Qdrant offers, and hnsw_config=HnswConfigDiff(m=0) is their recommendation for late-interaction fields, since the vectors are used for rescoring rather than graph traversal. Note that Qdrant themselves suggest reserving late interaction for reranking a few hundred candidates rather than scanning a whole collection, which is the Retrieve and Rerank pattern. At 4,874 documents the full scan costs 18ms and is exact, but that doesn't extrapolate.

Weaviate needs a server too: docker run -p 8080:8080 -p 50051:50051 cr.weaviate.io/semitechnologies/weaviate:1.34.0. Multi-vector support needs 1.29 or newer, and the embedded mode isn't available on Windows.

Defaults are enough here. Weaviate's dynamic ef resolves to 100 for a top-3 query, and this ranking is already exact from about 32 upward. That margin is a property of the embeddings rather than of Weaviate, so it's worth confirming on your own model instead of assuming the defaults hold.

Weaviate also supports MUVERA encoding, which made ingestion 3x faster and queries 1.8x faster in our test. It cost far more accuracy than that speed is worth at this size though, since the correct third passage didn't appear even in its top 50.

Vespa also runs in a container, but pyvespa starts it for you, so there's no separate docker run.

Vespa asks for the most upfront structure of the four, because you're declaring a ranking pipeline rather than just an index. In exchange you get to write MaxSim out as a tensor expression and see exactly what it computes. This version puts MaxSim in first-phase over where true, which scores all 4,874 documents and is why the output matches exhaustive MaxSim exactly. It's deliberately not what Vespa recommends at scale. Their ColBERT sample app stores int8-binarized vectors and moves MaxSim into second-phase to rerank a cheaper first stage.

Moving to that phased setup needs care, because second-phase rescores only the best 100 candidates by default, and here that window left two of the three correct passages unscored entirely. Raising rerank-count to cover your candidate set fixes that, though at this size the phased version still came out slower than simply scanning everything.

Late interaction is the state of the art for visual document retrieval, matching a text query against page images, with charts, tables, and layout intact, and no OCR step. This is what the ColPali family of models does, and those checkpoints load and run through the same API, with the revision pinning the open pull request that adds this one's Sentence Transformers configuration (Supported Models has the full list). Image documents are passed as URLs, local paths, or PIL images:

Each query retrieves its own page (the diagonal), and the second query separates much more cleanly than the first, since only one of the four pages is about outlay over time.

The code is unchanged. Underneath, the processor handles the visual prompt and the image patches, and MaxSim scores query text tokens against document image patches. A page holds many separate regions, which is exactly what makes late interaction a natural fit here, since a single vector would have to average a chart, a table, and three paragraphs into one summary. That fidelity costs index space, though. The shapes above are 755 token vectors for one page against 25 for the query, where a Natural Questions passage from earlier averaged about 125, so token pooling is worth reaching for earlier here than it is for text.

These are VLMs, so plan for the memory they need. The table in Supported Models runs from 252M to 8.8B parameters, and the small end of it stays practical on CPU where the multi-billion ones don't.

Page images are the common case, but they're not the only non-text modality. Sentence Transformers accepts text, images, audio, and video, and a checkpoint supports whichever of those its processor does, which model.modalities reports. A single document can combine modalities too, by passing a dict like {"text": ..., "image": ...} in place of a bare value. Multimodal Embedding & Reranker Models covers multimodal models in Sentence Transformers more broadly, and the Usage documentation lists exactly which input formats each modality accepts.

vidore/colqwen-omni-v0.1 is built on Qwen2.5-Omni and takes all four modalities. Retrieving a recorded conversation with it is the same two calls as retrieving a page:

ColQwen-Omni was trained purely on image-text pairs, so its audio retrieval is zero-shot. It never heard a training example, and there is no transcription step anywhere in the pipeline. The query says nausea where the recording says carsickness, and it still picks the pharmacy conversation out of twenty by a wide margin.

Video works the same way, but sample the frames or it will eat your VRAM. Its release blogpost is blunt about this, that video "is very memory-intensive, so it's best suited for short clips":

At 1 fps and full resolution the same pair of videos produces 8,426 and 5,137 token vectors and peaks at 20.8 GB of VRAM, against 4,240 and 2,446 vectors and 12.5 GB here, for a model that occupies 9.0 GB on its own. The ranking is identical either way. Long audio wants the same treatment, and the release blogpost recommends 30-second chunks, which come to roughly 800 tokens each.

Because MaxSim is a sum of per-query-token maxima, a ranking decomposes exactly, so every point of a document's score belongs to one query token and one document token. That lets you answer "why did this rank here?" precisely, rather than by eye.

For image documents, sentence_transformers.multi_vector_encoder.interpretability overlays that decomposition onto the page as the standard ColPali heatmap, either aggregated over the query or one map per query token. Asking "How much was spent on water resources and power?" against the outlays page from above, this is where the water token went:

heatmap.py is the runnable version, including the masking step that lines the document embedding up with the patch grid.

Text documents have no patch grid to overlay, but the same decomposition applies. text_similarity_map.py ranks a corpus and then attributes the top hit's score token by token, here on the Natural Questions corpus from earlier with the 32M-parameter mxbai-edge-colbert-v0-32m:

rich, mond, preliminary, and final matched themselves, while when settled on since and play on game. Three special tokens contribute 22.7% of the score while carrying none of the query's content. Below this table the script prints the passage itself, with the winning tokens highlighted in place.

If the index footprint worries you, the most effective knob is to store fewer token vectors. HierarchicalTokenPooling implements the token pooling technique from Clavié, Chaffin, and Adams by clustering each document's token vectors with Ward linkage on cosine distance and replacing each cluster with its mean, keeping roughly 1 / pool_factor of the tokens. Within one document a lot of token vectors end up close to each other, so much of what you drop is redundancy rather than signal:

There are three places to apply it, depending on when you want to pay for it:

By default, pooling applies to documents only, since queries are short and are the side you can't afford to distort. On the Natural Questions corpus from earlier, the reduction tracks pool_factor closely, and pooling all 608k token vectors took about 6 seconds:

A cluster mean is a worse match for a query token than the best of its members was, and the coarser the clusters, the more that shows. The original experiments measured that cost on BEIR and found very little of it, at 100.6% of the unpooled retrieval performance on average at pool_factor=2, and 99.0% at pool_factor=3. Halving your index for free is a good deal, so 2 is a reasonable place to start. How much it costs on your data is corpus-specific though, so measure it with an evaluator before you settle on a factor. The runnable comparison is token_pooling.py.

How far you can push pool_factor is also partly a property of the model. LightOn's hierarchical pooling regularization trains for exactly that, shaping the embedding space so pooling costs less and reporting 99.4% retention at 5x compression. Training with that regularizer isn't in Sentence Transformers yet, but the resulting checkpoints are ordinary PyLate models, so lightonai/LateOn-hpool-regularized loads and pools like any other.

Multi-vector models run through the same backend machinery as the rest of Sentence Transformers, so you get torch (default), onnx, and openvino, alongside half precision, Flash Attention, and torch.compile.

On GPU, fp16 with Flash Attention is the best configuration we measured, at 2.44x the throughput of fp32 with no measurable retrieval quality loss. Flash Attention helps multi-vector models more than most, because documents are only truncated and never padded to a shared length, so your batches have widely varying sequence lengths that unpadding can exploit:

Models with non-attend query expansion (attend=False, which covers the Stanford-NLP checkpoints like colbert-ir/colbertv2.0 and answerdotai/answerai-colbert-small-v1) reject Flash Attention at load time. Flash Attention strips attention_mask=0 positions, so the [MASK] expansion tokens that MaxSim scores would never receive an attention update. Use "sdpa" for those models.

On CPU, OpenVINO is your better bet where the architecture is supported, and int8 quantization buys a further speedup at a cost of about 0.4% accuracy. See Speeding up Inference for the full benchmark details, the export and quantization helpers, and a flowchart for picking a backend.

MultiVectorNanoBEIREvaluator runs the NanoBEIR suite of 13 small BEIR subsets with MaxSim scoring, and needs no data preparation on your side:

This also makes it easy to check the claim from the top of this post. lightonai/LateOn and lightonai/DenseOn were trained by LightOn on the same data with the same ModernBERT backbone and the same 149M parameters, differing only in whether they keep one vector per token or pool down to one per document. Running both over all 13 NanoBEIR datasets isolates what that choice buys:

Late interaction wins on 9 of the 13 datasets and on the mean, by roughly one NDCG point. The four it loses (ArguAna, FiQA2018, SCIDOCS, and SciFact) are the shape of the tradeoff you should expect, a real gain in retrieval quality at the same model size, paid for in index footprint, rather than a universal win on every dataset. The same pair scores 57.22 against 56.20 on the full 15-dataset BEIR, a comparable gap, so the margin is not an artifact of the small benchmark.

Alongside NanoBEIR, MultiVectorInformationRetrievalEvaluator, MultiVectorRerankingEvaluator, MultiVectorTripletEvaluator, and MultiVectorDistillationEvaluator cover the usual evaluation setups on your own data. They're documented in the Evaluation API Reference.

MultiVectorEncoder absorbs the modeling, inference, training, and evaluation of both libraries. Every PyLate checkpoint loads directly, and Supported Models lists the colpali-engine checkpoints along with the revision to pass where one is still needed. If you're migrating, these are the calls that change:

The difference worth knowing about is on bare (non-ColBERT) checkpoints, where PyLate's ColBERT("bert-base-uncased") applies the classic recipe by default while MultiVectorEncoder("bert-base-uncased") builds a plain stack, leaving the prefixes, query expansion, and skiplist as explicit choices. The training loss and evaluator equivalents, and the data-handling differences, are in the Migration Guide.

Save compatibility is one-way in every case. PyLate, Stanford-NLP ColBERT, and colpali-engine checkpoints all load into MultiVectorEncoder, but MultiVectorEncoder.save_pretrained output isn't loadable by any of them.

Models carrying the multi-vector and sentence-transformers tags on the Hub are the list that stays current, and we're working to get those tags onto every model that works. The tables below are what we test against directly, so treat them as a starting point rather than the full set. For text retrieval in particular, any PyLate or Stanford-NLP ColBERT checkpoint loads whether or not it carries the tag yet.

Some entries need a small Sentence Transformers configuration added to their repository first, and several of those are still open pull requests at the time of writing. Where a revision is listed below, pass it until that pull request is merged, after which the plain model name is enough:

These load with their trained prefix tokens, query expansion, and punctuation skiplist recovered from the saved configuration.

The NanoBEIR column reports the mean NDCG@10 (higher is better) across the 13 NanoBEIR datasets, each a 50-query subsample of a BEIR dataset, as a fast proxy for English text retrieval quality. We used the MultiVectorNanoBEIREvaluator to compute the scores for the primarily-English models. A - means the model was not evaluated on it. Note that NanoBEIR is a small benchmark, and its scores aren't a substitute for evaluating on your own data, which is always the right way to pick a model.

ColPali-style models embed page images as documents and text as queries.

The NanoViDoRe column reports the mean NDCG@10 (higher is better) across NanoViDoRe v3, a compact visual document retrieval benchmark spanning 8 subsets (computer science, energy, finance in English and French, HR, industrial, pharmaceuticals, and physics). Like with NanoBEIR, NanoViDoRe is a small benchmark which shouldn't replace evaluation on your own data.

Most of these are LoRA adapter repositories, with the adapter applied directly onto its base at load time. Some also have a -merged sibling on the Hub (e.g. vidore/colpali-v1.3-merged) with the adapter already folded into the weights.

The three -hf entries are the transformers-native *ForRetrieval ports. They load without any configuration, but use more modeling from transformers and less from sentence_transformers. Generally, it's preferable to use the original models instead, as the ports score approximately the same.

Late interaction in Sentence Transformers rests on a lot of earlier work. Thanks to Omar Khattab and Matei Zaharia for ColBERT, which everything here descends from, and to the LightOn team (Antoine Chaffin, Raphael Sourty, Paulo Moura, and Amélie Chatelain) for PyLate and fast-plaid, which carried late interaction for years and shaped a good deal of the API described above.

Thanks to the ColPali team (Manuel Faysse, Hugues Sibille, Tony Wu, Bilel Omrani, Gautier Viaud, Céline Hudelot, and Pierre Colombo) for ColPali and colpali-engine, which brought late interaction to page images, and to Benjamin Clavié, Antoine Chaffin, and Griffin Adams for token pooling.

Thanks as well to the core MTEB team, Kenneth Enevoldsen and Roman Solomatin among many others, for MTEB and for the kind of hidden work that keeps information retrieval research running.

And thanks to everyone who trained and released the checkpoints in Supported Models. Without them this post would have had nothing to measure.

To learn how to train or finetune these models on your own data:

See the companion blogpost: Training and Finetuning Multi-Vector Embedding Models with Sentence Transformers.

#9974. A Decade of Kill Bugs

On the morning of September 24th 2026, Endcrawl had a brief outage. I'd just typed:

Right away I blamed myself. Maybe I mistyped that number! Maybe my code had a signal handling bug. Maybe I don't understand Unix as well as I think I do. Maybe I'm an idiot!

As it turned out, the outage was caused by a bug in kill(1).

This is really surprising. The kill program is 50 years old. Its spec is simple and stable. It's probably exercised a billion times a day.

A bug in kill was so surprising that, once I'd found it, I couldn't stop there. I needed to know how this bug came to be, and what had led the programmers so badly astray. When I eventually found the root cause, there was an even bigger surprise. It had led to not just one bug, but a whole series of kill bugs that shipped in Ubuntu 14, 16, 18, 22 and 24 LTS.

This post documents a decade of kill bugs, then makes some recommendations.

Back to the outage. I scrambled to put the fire out. After that came a surprise second fire. By the end of all this I was pretty demoralized. I was ready to accept that I'd made a dumb mistake and ready to get on with the work day. There was this nagging feeling thoughâ¦

Remember that final scene in Burn After Reading?

"I don't f**king know either. I guess we learned not to do it again."

"Although I'm f**ked if I know what we did..."

What had just happened? Was I about to be hit with a third outage? How could I be sure?

An outage not understood is an outage that happens again. That nagging feeling I had was a call to understand. With a sigh, I put all my other work on hold and started a proper post mortem.

Let's examine the command that caused the outage:

The negative number here is a process group identifier, or pgid for short. A pgid is like a pid, but identifies a group of related processes. By convention, killing a positive number sends a signal to a single process, while killing a negative number signals all processes in that process group.

I was attempting to cancel a big Endcrawl 7k test render. A normal person would have killed one of the processes involved and let failures cascade to the others. But killing the whole group simultaneously strikes me as cleaner.

Process group signaling isn't some exotic operation. You use it all the time. Every time you ^C a command, the tty sends SIGINT to the foreground process group. Interactive shells run all but the simplest commands in a new process group, which among other things makes job control possible.

Process group signaling is in fact an awesome Unix innovation. I love it so much I added it to daemontools, where svc -+h now avoids orphans in a multiprocess service bounce.

At any rate, imagine my surprise when the command didn't just kill those render processes, but killed all processes on the machine save one!

Here's the relevant snippet from procps 4.0.4, the provider of /bin/kill in Ubuntu 24.04 LTS. Can you spot the bug?

My initial guess was wrong. There's no underflow or overflow bug with -1490947.

Notice we're in the unrecognized option switch case. Here's what getopt(3) says about unrecognized options:

By default, getopt() prints an error message on standard error, places the erroneous option character in optopt, and returns '?' as the function result.

Aha. The optopt variable only holds the first character after the dash, not the whole negative pid. When character 1 is subtracted from character 0 we get a pid of -1. What happens when you kill pid -1? Bad things:

If pid equals -1, then sig is sent to every process for which the calling process has permission to send signals, except for process 1 (init).

This ran as root, so the misparsing of -1490947 as -1 killed every process but init. Bug found, mystery solved.

Except for me this just raised more questions. Why is the code assuming the unrecognized option is a "signal [sic] digit negative PID"? Why is the single digit negative pid case special, and what handles the general case of a multidigit negative pid?

Moreover, how could a bug like this exist in 2026, and in a Ubuntu LTS release no less? Has it always been there?

No, that couldn't be. I've killed process groups in the past. And the kill -TERM -12345 thing is an ancient Unix incantation. This used to work dammit!

Thinking back, I could vaguely remember some negative pid kills gone awry. Never in an "oops this killed everything in sight" way. More in a "weird, nothing happened" way, or a "poof there goes my shell" way. Minor ways more easily shrugged off as user error.

It turns out I wasn't imagining these. The last decade has been a rough one for negative pid killers. There have been no less than FOUR distinct bugs around negative pids. And they all shipped in Ubuntu LTS versions.

Before I tell the tale of four bugs, let's go even farther back in Unix history.

In the beginning Unix had processes. By 1973 it had the kill(1) program. But it took a decade to evolve process groups as we now know them. It wasn't until Unix V9 in 1986 that you could kill a process group via negative pid. Near as I can tell, negative pid killing has worked fine in the BSDs all these years.

In the early 90s this thing called Linux came along. Although Linux initially borrowed a lot of BSD code for its userland, by the late 90s this approach was in legal jeopardy. Everything had to be rewritten, every wheel reinvented. And quickly. It was an exciting time to be a unix programmer.

And so it came to pass that Linux's kill was reinvented written by Albert Calahan. After Albert DoSed himself by forking 5 children, Debian downstream maintainer Craig Small took over poor old neglected procps.

Negative pid killing seems to have worked fine until 2013. Then the trouble began.

Ubuntu 14.04 LTS included procps 3.3.9. Prior to this, the kill code did what the BSDs do and used pointer arithmetic to walk and parse argv.

Personally I'm fond of that approach. Stallman isn't so fond of it though. In GNU world, you're supposed to standardize command line parsing via getopt. This is probably a good idea in the general case, but as we'll see, it was probably the wrong choice in the specific case of kill(1).

Here's the relevant code after the conversion to getopt:

The code worked fine for multidigit negative pids. However, if you were one of those freaks creative sysadmins who delighted in a kill -HUP -1 now and again to restart all your services, you noticed a bug: nothing happened.

Multidigit case: With kill -HUP -123, getopt acts as if -1, -2, and -3 were all separately passed. The unrecognized option case will be hit three times, and only at -3 will the -123 argument be consumed by incrementing optind. Because the code breaks out of the getopt loop early at -1, an unconsumed -123 argument correctly makes it to the pid killer.

Single digit case: With kill -HUP -1, however, getopt has fully consumed that argument and incremented optind before we break out of the loop. The pid killer sees no arguments and nothing happens.

A cure was in order. Unfortunately it was worse than the disease.

Ubuntu 16.04 LTS shipped with procps 3.3.10. The kill -HUP -1 bug was fixed at the expense of multidigit negative pid kills: a kill -TERM -12345 now killed everything.

This is the same bug that caused the outage under Ubuntu 24. We reviewed this above. The only mystery here is why procps circa Ubuntu 24 resurrected the known-buggy code circa Ubuntu 16. My best guess is that the following bugs were deemed even worse.

Ubuntu 18.04 LTS shipped with procps 3.3.12.

This attempted to fix multidigit negative pid killing. Instead of parsing optopt, which only corresponds to a single bundled character like -1 when -123 is passed, the new code stops and tries to parse the whole argument:

This works correctly for multidigit negative pids. But if you passed a single digit negative pid, as in a kill -TERM -1, the pid argument was fully consumed, and optind would run off the end of argv[]. Segfault!

Ubuntu 22.04 LTS shipped with procps 3.3.17.

This fixed the segfault by ensuring optind never ran off the end of argv[]:

Once again, it seems the contributor didn't understood how getopt option bundling interacts with optind, and hopefully by this point you're developing some sympathy for them. With this patch a kill -TERM -1 works correctly and no longer segfaults. But multidigit negative pid killing was broken for a second time, in a brand new way.

Suppose we try to kill -TERM -123. Thanks to option bundling, optind isn't incremented yet when we hit the unrecognized option case. Per some quirky behavior noted below, argv[optind-1] is now the string kill.

How does atoi(3) handle a non-numeric string like "kill"? It returns 0.

And what does the kill system call do with zero?

If pid equals 0, then sig is sent to every process in the process group of the calling process.

Because it's a simple command, your shell won't isolate kill -TERM -123 in a new process group. So this bug will unexpectedly kill your shell. Poof!

For one, the way getopt only advances optind with the final bundled option is deeply non-obvious. I didn't find evidence that any contributor understood this. I didn't understand it myself at first. That took careful study.

It's a real surprise. Surprising behavior like this should be avoided.

I feel this learning is too myopic though. Can one even avoid this surprising getopt behavior? You can't disable option bundling.

Well okay, at least in this specific case. The kill(1) program is just an unusual beast. It accepts options that are actually signal names, like -KILL. You can also specify that same signal by number, like -9. And pgids are negative numbers that look deceptively like options.

How should a command line like kill -1 -9 be interpreted?

All of these interpretations are potentially valid if any argv element can be an option or a pid.

The solution is to instead parse argv positionally. Don't use getopt here. Abandon capabilities like option bundling and option reordering that are more footgun than feature in this context. The POSIX spec says that only argv[1] can specify the signal to send, and arguments beyond that are pids and pgids. These are nice simplifying assumptions.

I think the old-school Unix and BSD approach is the right one. Have a look at FreeBSD's kill.c. Like ancestral Unix did back in the 70s, it parses argv positionally. The approach is simple and the code is simple. By contrast with Linux's kill, FreeBSD's kill has had no command line parsing bugs.

I do regard getopt dogma as the real root cause of the outage.

If abandoning getopt for "primitive" argv parsing still feels sinful, just look at what procps does before even calling getopt_long:

It scans argv looking for the first signal spec. If it finds a -KILL, a -9, or similar, it modifies argv in place (!) so getopt doesn't have to deal with that.

This is already "primitive" argv parsing! We're halfway there.

The previous takeaways were aimed at software developers. For users of kill, I'd recommend the following.

First, use -- to separate options from pids and pgids:

The second form is parsed correctly even by the buggy procps versions listed above.

Second, kill with least privilege. If I'd done a sudo -u render kill instead of a sudo kill, it would have only killed in-flight renders instead of all processes on the box. I feel a little insane recommending this kind of defensive tool usage â let's be clear, we're defending against bugs in kill, a small, mature, widely-used and very important tool â but here we are.

Finally, the good news is that a bugfix for Ubuntu 24 is already on its way at the time of publication. I still favor a simplifying rewrite of procps's kill though.

#9973. Third Serengeti Sweep Tops 1,400 Arrests as Investigations Mature

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Interpol's annual Operation Serengeti, now in its third iteration, led to 1,462 arrests across 20 African countries and the US, recovering $105 million in stolen funds.

A two-month operation in Africa led to the arrests of nearly 1,500 cybercrime suspects across 20 African countries and the US, the recovery of $105 million in stolen funds, and the shutdown of nearly 11,000 malicious networks.

The third annual roundup of cybercriminals and financial scammers, dubbed Operation Serengeti III, aimed to take down groups responsible for ransomware, phishing, and cyber-enabled fraud, Interpol stated. The operation expanded the impact of cyber-focused investigations from previous law enforcement efforts in 2024 and 2025, which netted 1,006 suspects in the original Operation Serengeti and 1,209 suspects in last year's effort, dubbed Operation Serengeti 2.0.

The increasing arrests show that the national law enforcement partners are becoming more mature in their investigative practices and collaboration across jurisdictions, says Neal Jetton, director for cybercrime at Interpol.

Related:UAE Transitions 50% of Government Services to Agentic AI

"Rising arrest figures reflect stronger enforcement activity, not a change in the scale of offending," he says. "The success of law enforcement efforts should be judged by whether fewer people are victimized over time and not by the number of suspects arrested or victims identified during a specific operation."

The crackdown came as cybercriminals in the region continue to develop more sophistication in their operations, with a survey of African members finding that 72% of the 36 African countries have discovered a criminally operated scam center and more than half of cybercrime cases involved the use of AI — 8% frequently and 47% occasionally, according to Interpol's "African Cyberthreat Assessment Report 2026."

The data highlights the rapid improvements in cybercriminal infrastructure, says Jacomo Piccolini, vice president of global data partnerships at Team Cymru.

"Scams that once looked like individual schemes now run like businesses, with recruitment pipelines, international staff, and, increasingly, trafficked workers," he says.

In Uganda, for example, two transnational criminal organizations (TCOs) used a rotating call-center model with scripted communications, fraudulent websites, and fake trading platforms to convince elderly victims in Asia to invest in their financial scams, Interpol said in a statement on Operation Serengeti III's impact. Ugandan law enforcement authorities successfully dismantled the fraud rings, arresting 365 foreign nationals, consisting almost entirely of citizens from various Asian nations, Interpol's Jetton says.

Related:Australian Gov't Weighs Mandatory AI Incident Reporting

In another arm of the operation, national police arrested nine suspects in Angola, dismantling two illegal cryptocurrency mining sites and seizing more than 2,000 devices used to mine crypto along with six illegal power transformers valued at more than US $1 million. Cybercriminal mining operations are a common way to generate cryptocurrency, the favored method of cashing out on illegal schemes, Jetton says.

"Cryptocurrency played a significant role in moving the proceeds," Jetton says. "It is now the principal rail for this type of fraud."

In Nigeria, police shuttered two fraud operations: One using 2.1 million email addresses to create a large-scale phishing and business email compromise (BEC) operation, while another scheme focused on international investment fraud and garnered at least US $2.4 million in profits, Interpol stated.

The schemes showed off the role that AI is taking in enabling cybercriminal campaigns. The phishing and BEC campaigns used email addresses and AI agents to scrape information from LinkedIn and other social media to identify high-value targets, Jetton says.

"AI enabled the threat actor to create highly personalized phishing emails by mimicking the writing style of executives, colleagues, and suppliers," he says, adding that "AI helped criminals manage and prioritize millions of email addresses for large-scale campaigns and, in some cases, combined with voice cloning, deepfake videos, and AI chatbots to make social engineering attacks even more convincing."

Related:EU Cyber Resilience Act to Enforce New Reporting Requirements

Law enforcement collaboration is making the individual nations more effective in tackling transnational cybercrime. With international partners, the individual countries are able to gain intelligence on signs of cybercriminal activities in their country, says Team Cymru's Piccolini.

"The biggest change is timing. Since Serengeti 2.0, investigators have gone in with intelligence on suspicious IP addresses, domains, and command-and-control servers before the operation begins, along with training in open source, crypto, and ransomware investigation."

Without such collaboration, TCOs could evade repercussions, especially if they limited their activities to impacting only citizens of other nations, as in the case of the Asian investment fraud ring.

"Actors targeting victims in Europe and North America use infrastructure spread across multiple jurisdictions, which makes it harder to pursue through any single country," Piccolini says. "That’s a big part of why international operations like Serengeti, with partners who can see across borders, matter so much."

Both Interpol and Team Cyrmu stressed that several operations are ongoing, with investigators continuing to use seized data and other information to pursue suspected cybercriminals.

Rob is an award-winning, veteran technology journalist of more than 30 years, reporting on global cybersecurity issues, the latest offensive and defensive technologies, malware incidents, cyber conflict, and AI's impact on software and cybersecurity.

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. Recent reports include analyses of the shortage in cybersecurity workers, annual vulnerability trends, and annual threat reports.

Rob holds degrees from Cornell University in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (double major).

The Autonomous Endpoint Management Advantage

2026 State of Cybersecurity Report: Bridging the Divide

#9972. kitty 0.50.0

kitty is a feature-rich, cross-platform, fast, GPU based terminal. To update kitty, follow the instructions.

kitty windows can now be docked to an edge of another window or of the tab. Docked windows are placed outside the layout, making them perfect for status bars, file trees or a shell kept next to your editor. A dock attached to a window follows it around, moving with it to other tabs and closing when it closes. Create docks with launch --type=window-dock or launch --type=tab-dock. Docks are saved in sessions too.

Like other applications, kitty can now save its state when you log out, restart or shut down your computer, and restore it the next time it starts. Simply set restore_session_after_logout and every kitty instance comes back with all its OS Windows, tabs and windows in place, including their scrollback. On macOS, the saved state is encrypted using a key stored in your keychain. See Restoring kitty after logging out for details.

kitty now has official support for Custom Shaders. These can be used for all manner of graphical effects, from animated backgrounds to focus highlighting to animations that change how cursor movements or mouse clicks are visualised.

See the documentation for a video gallery showcasing various custom shaders that ship with kitty.

This release saw tons of performance work focused on improving throughput making kitty even faster than it already is. Real world effective throughput should see a 15-35% improvement depending on workload. Some details:

Improve throughput when processing large amounts of text with a scrollback buffer much larger than the CPU cache by ~35% by prefetching scrollback memory before it is written to

Improve throughput when processing large amounts of text by ~50% for ASCII and ~15% for Unicode by writing runs of plain ASCII chars to the screen in batches and skipping unnecessary bookkeeping in the scrolling and tab handling hot paths

Speed up SIMD UTF-8 decoding: ~20% faster for ASCII and ~50% faster for multi-byte text on both x86 and ARM, by processing pairs of vectors of plain ASCII text at a time and compacting decoded codepoints within 128-bit lanes, avoiding expensive cross-lane operations. Also add an AVX-512 based decoder, another ~75% faster for multi-byte text, used automatically on CPUs that support it (Intel Ice Lake+, AMD Zen 4+).

Improve throughput when processing escape code heavy input by ~30% by taking the input buffer lock once per buffer of input rather than once per escape code and using cheaper arithmetic to parse CSI parameters

Improve throughput when processing large amounts of plain text by another ~10% by finding runs of printable ASCII chars with SIMD, filling cells using wide stores and skipping unnecessary work in the scrolling hot path when there are no images

Speed up pixel compositing with SIMD vectorization: alpha blending of graphics protocol images and animation frames is 2-3.5x faster and glyph alpha masks are composited onto canvases using the same vectorized primitives.

Cache HarfBuzz results for repeated short runs (≤32 cells) so redraws of the same on-screen text are not reshaped

kitty now has support for vertical tabs along the left or right edge of the OS Window. Useful for people that have wide aspect ratio windows.

kitty now has a new Drag and Drop kitten that allows you to seamlessly drag and drop files between kitty and any GUI program like the OS file manager or a webapp. It even works over SSH! It is powered by a new protocol allowing the use of drag and drop from any TUI program.

kitty already had excellent mouse support, but now it is taking it to the next level. The kitty scrollback buffer grew support for smooth scrolling and momentum based scrolling for a natural, smooth and kinetic scrolling experience.

Additionally, you can now drag kitty tabs around with the mouse to re-order them, move them to another kitty OS Window or even detach them into their own OS Window.

Finally, a long requested feature, the ability to resize kitty windows (aka splits) with the mouse was implemented.

A new kitten to select files at the speed of thought with a keyboard first interface and support for content previews of text files with syntax highlighting, images, videos, e-books and more. Allows you to select files for use at the shell prompt or other terminal workflows with just a few keystrokes, similar to how fuzzy finders like fzf operate, but designed for files in particular, leveraging the various innovations of kitty such as image display and variable sized text.

On Linux, it can even be used as a drop in replacement for the File Open/Save dialog boxes in GUI programs.

kitty has long had support for Sessions, aka simple text files where you can define what tabs, windows and programs you wish to run in kitty. Now in addition to that kitty has the ability to create and switch between sessions with a single keypress and also to manually setup some tabs/windows in kitty and save it as a session file, for seamless and intuitive session file creation.

A long requested feature, kitty has finally gotten a scrollbar that can be used with the mouse for browsing its scrollback. The bar appear automatically when you start scrolling backwards and is extensively configurable in kitty.conf. Note that the old scrollback_indicator_opacity option is deprecated.

kitty has pioneered a new escape code protocol that allows terminal applications to use multiple cursors, rendered natively. These are typically used in editors to make the same edit at multiple locations. Now terminal based editors can use properly rendered native cursors, just like their GUI cousins, at last.

kitty now has a Quake like floating, translucent terminal window, so you can access all that kitty goodness instantly with a single keypress.

See the screenshots on the side and head over to the kitten page for details on how to set it up.

kitty is the first major terminal to introduce the concept of multiple sized text. Terminal programs running in kitty can now opt-in to use and display text in multiple font sizes both larger and smaller than the base font size. This is done in a backwards compatible, opt-in way that does not affect how traditional terminal programs work at all. For details on the new feature and how to use it, see The text sizing protocol.

Show an animated trail when the text cursor makes large jumps making it easy to follow cursor movements. Inspired by the similar feature in neovide, but works with terminal multiplexers and kitty windows as well. See the pull request for a demonstration video. This feature is optional and must be turned on by the cursor_trail option in kitty.conf.

Terminal aficionados spend all day staring at text, so getting text rendering just right is very important. In that spirit, kitty now supports OpenType Variable fonts. These allow precise customisation of font characteristics, such as weight and spacing. Not only that, kitty now has a new choose-fonts kitten that provides a UI for choosing fonts with support for font features, variable fonts and previews of how the font will look. This is in addition to its existing best-in-class font customization abilities, such as: symbol_map, text_composition_strategy, font_features and modify_font. kitty knows text rendering is important, and goes the extra mile for it.

kitty now has a notify kitten that can be used to display desktop notifications from the command line, even over SSH. It has support for icons, buttons, updating notifications, waiting till the notification is closed, etc. The underlying Desktop notifications protocol has been expanded to support all these features.

Wayland users should rejoice as kitty now comes with major Wayland quality-of-life improvements:

Draw GPU accelerated desktop panels and background running arbitrary terminal programs. For example, run btop as your desktop background

Background blur for transparent windows is now supported under KDE using a custom KDE specific protocol

The kitty window decorations in GNOME are now fully functional with buttons and they follow system dark/light mode automatically

kitty now supports fractional scaling in Wayland which means pixel perfect rendering when you use a fractional scale with no wasted performance on resizing an overdrawn pixmap in the compositor

With this release kitty’s Wayland support is now on par with X11, provided you use a decent Wayland compositor.

Allow docking kitty windows to the edges of other windows or of the tab, for status bars, file trees, etc. Create them with launch --type=window-dock or launch --type=tab-dock, see Docked windows

A new option restore_session_after_logout to save the state of every kitty instance, including scrollback, when logging out, restarting or shutting down and restore it the next time kitty starts. On macOS, the state is encrypted with a key in the keychain. On Linux, it requires the Inhibit desktop portal. See Restoring kitty after logging out (#1197, #10659)

Allow using tabs like named workspaces: A new launch --focus-existing option to focus an existing window or tab instead of creating a new one, a new by-title value for launch --location to keep tabs in alphabetical order and new options for kitten @ detach-window and the detach_window action to send windows to a named tab, creating it if needed (#10627)

Wayland: The client side window decorations used on compositors such as GNOME now look like native GNOME decorations and follow the desktop titlebar font, text scaling, button layout and titlebar click action settings (#10766)

Wayland: Support touchscreens. A tap is a click, a finger that moves scrolls with momentum, and a finger held still before it moves selects text (#5432, #10551)

Custom shaders: New cursor-trail-railgun, cursor-trail-torpedo and cursor-trail-pixiedust shaders that make particles fly off the cursor as it moves, in the style of neovide. Shaders can now be controlled with key presses via the new shader_event action (see Controlling shaders with key presses), can be faded in and out, reversed and looped with new animation_* pipeline directives and can define a pointer_map() function so that clicks and selections land on the text shown under the mouse, which the crt shader now uses, see Shaders that move content. Also fix animations becoming jerky after kitty has been running for a few hours, shaders specified by path not being found and various pipeline bugs (#10587, #10667, #10693, #10595, #10694, #10639)

Graphics protocol: Add two new indexed color image formats whose pixels are indices into the terminal color palette, so that images change color along with the color scheme, and allow clients to detect support for individual protocol features, such as animation and Unicode placeholders, via the new e query key, see Querying support for protocol features (#9379, #10732)

Support the Program Status Protocol (OSC 7501) that lets programs report whether they are working, finished, failed or blocked waiting on the user. Shown in the tab bar via a new tab.program_status field for tab_title_template, see Reporting the status of a program

Automatic color themes: When the system switches between light and dark, keep colors set by programs running in a window, by the ssh kitten, by launch --color or launch --copy-colors, and use the current theme colors when a program restores its saved colors. launch --color colors now also survive config reloads. The ssh kitten can use different color schemes for remote hosts in dark and light mode via the new kitten-ssh.color_scheme_dark, kitten-ssh.color_scheme_light and kitten-ssh.color_scheme_no_preference options (#10724)

Layouts: Align the borders of neighboring windows and keep the gaps between them uniform, and add a new option collapse_window_margins to have the margins of neighboring windows collapse into each other instead of adding up (#10508)

Window resizing: A new --strategy=edge mode to select and move a specific internal divider in the Splits layout, and hold Alt with a resize letter to take a fraction of the remaining resize steps, configurable with the new --fraction option

Scale the thickness of box drawing characters, cursors and the window title bar border with the font size, so they no longer look too thin when zoomed in or too thick when zoomed out. At the configured font_size nothing changes (#10362)

mouse_map can now map the scroll wheel, via the wheel_up, wheel_down, wheel_left and wheel_right buttons, for example, to change the font size with Ctrl+scroll

A new option hyperlink_target_position to control where the URL shown by show_hyperlink_targets is displayed, including as a browser style tooltip next to the mouse cursor (#10770)

Show the hand pointer and hover highlighting over links only when the pressed modifiers match a configured mouse action for opening the link with a single click, updating immediately when modifiers are pressed or released

quick-access-terminal kitten: New kitty +kitten quick_access_terminal --if-running, kitty +kitten quick_access_terminal --listen-on and kitty +kitten quick_access_terminal --hold options to run programs in an already running quick access terminal, use a fixed remote control socket and keep the terminal open after the program exits (#10603)

Sessions: A new os_window_position keyword and a new --os-window-geometry option for save_as_session to save the size, position and state of OS Windows in session files. Also fix the OS Window size and os_window_title in sessions sometimes being ignored (#10675)

Command palette: Show action and kitten aliases at the top when the search query is empty, so they can be used to pin frequently used actions (#10711)

Vertical tab bars: When tab_title_max_length is set, size the tab bar to fit the decorations of the current tab_bar_style, allowing much narrower tab bars (#10680)

Linux/BSD: Detect MIME types for open actions and kittens using the shared-mime-info cache, matching the rest of the desktop, including files without an extension, such as Makefile, and MIME type aliases (#3056)

IME: Keep the candidate window anchored at the start of the pre-edit text and at the cursor, so it no longer jumps around while composing text. On macOS, commit in-progress IME or dictation text instead of discarding it when the OS window loses focus (#10642, #10644)

Shell integration: Make the kitty terminfo files available in commands run via run0, similar to sudo (#10692)

kitty --config=NONE now also skips the automatic color theme files, open-actions.conf, launch-actions.conf, mime.types, paste-actions.py, notifications.py and the custom window icon in the kitty config directory

Processes kitty inserts to wrap the program it runs, such as /usr/bin/login on macOS or the wrapper for launch --hold, are now skipped when reporting the pid, working directory, command line and environment of a window in kitten @ ls and when matching windows. Also fix launch --cwd=root using the working directory of the foreground process instead of the root process while the shell is running a command

Nightly builds now show the date and hash of the commit they were built from in the output of kitty --version and kitten --version

Do not render between render frames to reduce flicker from programs that draw with many small partial updates (#10749)

Performance: Faster growing of the GPU sprite cache, particularly on macOS, less CPU usage with a non-zero input_delay and no continuous re-rendering when a selection is present and the window is scrolled back (#10714)

Remote control: Fix a crafted request being able to bypass password based remote control authentication by masquerading as a cancellation of an asynchronous request

Remote control: Fix many commands, including action, send-key, set-colors, set-background-opacity, set-font-size, ls, run and set-enabled-layouts, ignoring options, reporting false success or silently misinterpreting invalid input, particularly when used in remote_control mappings. set-colors now parses color files the same way as kitty.conf. Also fix a single unresponsive peer blocking all remote control communication and a crash when using damaged images with set-window-logo or set-background-image (#10672, #10632, #10688, #10690, #10715)

Fix various terminal emulation bugs, including in origin mode cursor position reports, erasing multicell characters, the CHT escape code and copying text containing tabs, wide characters being drawn on the wrong row after colliding with scaled text, emoji sequences being split into multiple cells when wrapped, text typed into a new window before the program is ready sometimes being garbled, as well as a heap buffer overflow, an out of bounds write and a use-after-free when reloading the config (#10609, #10729, #10632, #10682, #10767)

Graphics protocol: Allow shared memory object names without a leading slash again, for sandboxed macOS applications, and fix various bugs with animation frames and Unicode placeholders (#10684, #10599, #10632)

Fix various window and tab management bugs, with focus moving to the wrong window on close, drag and drop onto title bars, visual window selection, Grid layout placement, title bar padding and tab titles being truncated too early. detach_tab now shows custom titles in the OS Window chooser (#10640)

Fix render jitter when scrolled back with a partial line and the client is using the synchronised rendering escape code (#10794)

Fix bold or italic Nerd Font icons sometimes being rendered using glyphs from an unrelated font, the cursor trail not always being shown when focus moves to a different window, watcher entries not being removed on config reload and changing text marker colors at runtime, for example with kitten @ set-colors or automatic theme switching, applying the colors of each marker to the next one (#10591)

ssh kitten: Preserve the permissions of copied directories, fix copying files outside HOME whose paths share its prefix and files in HOME being copied to an absolute path with --symlink-strategy=resolve when HOME is a symlink, fix hanging when re-using a shared connection that has silently died and fix colors 16-255 being set to white with themes that do not define them (#10691, #10661, #10727, #10737)

Desktop UI kitten: Fix D-Bus activation when kitten is installed in a path containing spaces or quoting characters (#10784)

Automatic color themes: Stop using cached colors and background images after the corresponding theme file has been deleted and apply theme files created after kitty was started when reloading the config (#10786)

Themes kitten: Fix overwriting the Unicode input kitten’s recent entries and input mode, and vice versa, by using separate caches (#10780)

Remote file kitten: Preserve the local edited copy and show its recovery path when the final upload fails, including when the SSH connection has died (#10789)

Transfer kitten: When receiving files, replace existing symbolic and hard links at the destination instead of overwriting the files they point to, and write to a temporary file that is renamed into place, so an interrupted transfer no longer leaves a truncated file behind (#10713)

Drag and drop kitten: Reject copying or moving a directory into itself or one of its subdirectories, and moving a directory into a symlink that points inside it, which would delete the moved files. When moving, do not delete sources that were replaced during the drop, for example by files merged through a symlink in the destination. Respect overwrite confirmation for case and Unicode equivalent names on filesystems that treat them as aliases, list the existing files that will be overwritten under their actual names, including inside symlinked directories, and fix dropping a directory over an existing file. No longer rename remotely dropped files whose names differ only in case on case sensitive filesystems (#10769, #10772)

Drag and drop protocol: Fix base64 data with padding at the end being rejected, as allowed by the protocol (#10777)

Clipboard kitten: Fix only the last of several outputs that use the same MIME type being saved, for example with kitten clipboard -g picture.png picture.jpg, the data is now downloaded and decoded only once for all such outputs. Reject duplicate output files, including ones that differ only in case on case-insensitive filesystems or whose paths contain a symlink followed by ... Fix a race when replacing an existing output file, losing the original file if writing it fails and kitten clipboard -g -m . formats.txt silently doing nothing. Also preserve the permissions of and follow symlinks at existing output files (#10738, #10744)

Kittens: When saving files, such as themes, config files or clipboard output, write to the target of a symlink even when the target does not yet exist, instead of replacing the symlink with a regular file (#10740)

Kittens: Fix laggy mouse selection and failures comparing remote directories in the diff kitten, Unicode quotes not being removed from around paths and URLs in the hints kitten, the order of styles with negative or closely spaced fractional axis values in the choose-fonts kitten, various bugs in the choose-files, quick-access-terminal and other kittens and reject command-line options missing their required value (#10634, #10641, #10676, #10687, #10730)

Wayland: Fix a crash on compositors without cursor-shape support, kitty being disconnected by GNOME when showing a long covered window, the app_id being lost when hiding and showing windows, kitty --os-window-tag not setting the window tag and various drag and drop bugs (#10597, #10602, #10604, #10759, #10632)

Linux: Fix momentum scrolling up or left, X11 wheel events from sources without smooth scrolling being ignored and various desktop notification bugs. Notifications now identify kitty’s desktop file, so desktops such as KDE can group them (#10625, #10695, #10610, #10721)

macOS: Fix padding rendering black after sleep, OS windows not staying on all spaces, a duplicate path when dropping items from Apple Mail, emoji from a monochrome emoji font such as Noto Emoji not using the foreground color, a memory leak, reloading config causing Apple injected shortcuts to not work and kitty freezing when opening a new window while another entry in /dev is stuck (#10708, #10581, #10628, #10673, #10741, #10757, #10793)

zsh: Respect the user’s descriptions format style for completion group headings, fixing literal %B markers appearing with fzf-tab, and fix a “maximum nested function level reached” error at every prompt after interrupting a command run at shell startup, for example via a session file (#10748, #10768)

Fix reverse-video extra cursors to use the color type encoded by the multiple-cursors protocol.

Make reverse-video cursors follow dimmed text colors while keeping text under block cursors legible.

A new option detect_url_regex to detect arbitrary text, such as file references in compiler output, as clickable URLs under the mouse (#10407)

Reduce input latency by processing small amounts of program output, such as the echo of typed characters, immediately instead of waiting for input_delay (#10560)

Drag and drop: Restore the previously active tab after dropping a dragged tab on the same OS window’s tab bar, even if it was reordered after a hover switch

Drag and drop: Fix an out of bounds memory access when parsing a URI list sent by a remote client that does not end with a newline (#10618)

Sessions: Expand launch option variables when an option value matches the command name

Preserve transparent background colors when applying unrelated launch color overrides

ssh kitten: Preserve SSH option values following a spaced --kitten option

Fix a memory leak when loading a corrupt PNG image that has an embedded ICC color profile

Custom shaders: The builtin dim-inactive-windows shader no longer dims the tab bar and the padding, border and margin around the active window (#10524)

Custom shaders: The builtin northern-lights shader is now about twice as fast. Its MARCH_STEPS setting can now be lowered to trade a little quality for even more speed on slower GPUs

Custom shaders: A new cursor-trail-motion-blur shader that makes the cursor trail glide smoothly during fast cursor movements

Vertical tabs: Improve rendering of tabs when using the powerline tab_bar_style

Graphics: Fix images briefly disappearing for one frame the first time an image is replaced during a synchronized update (#10538)

X11: Fix copy and paste targeting the wrong OS window when the keyboard focus is set to PointerRoot or None

diff kitten: Fix freezes and very high memory use when a very long line, such as in a minified file, is changed

themes and choose fonts kittens: Fix search freezing for many seconds when typing a long query, such as the full name of a theme

macOS: Fix a custom dock icon reverting to the stock icon after a progress bar is cleared (#10545)

macOS: Fix a regression in the previous release causing background_opacity less than one with no background_blur making the titlebar transparent (#10540)

macOS: Fix regression in 0.49 that caused rounded rect shader to not work on ancient macs with AMD GPUs (#10549)

diff kitten: Fix search not finding matches at the end of a line

hints kitten: Fix delays of many seconds when selecting paths or line numbers on a screen with long lines that contain no spaces

File transfer: Fix a security issue where a malicious program on the remote machine could bypass the transfer confirmation prompt when no file_transfer_confirmation_bypass password is set

Fix an out-of-bounds memory access when drawing a multi-line text sized character with the cursor below the bottom margin of the scroll region

Fix a heap buffer underflow when parsing ANSI-C quoted strings in the command line sent by shell integration via the OSC 133 escape code

macOS: Fix a regression in 0.49 that caused rendering issues after wake from sleep or display re configuration under memory pressure due to a bug in Apple’s OpenGL drivers (#10571)

Drag and drop: Hover over a tab while dragging a window or a single window tab to switch to it and choose a split position. Drop a window at a tab edge or gap to put it into a new tab at that position. Dragging tabs now shows an insertion marker rather than moving the other tabs during the drag. See Overview for details.

Splits layout: Dragging a divider now resizes only its adjacent regions, consistently after rearranging windows. Fix nested dividers not tracking mouse movement correctly, including when returning from a minimum size.

Splits layout: Fix windows in a nested split overlapping their neighbour by a couple of pixels when the split is resized down to its minimum size.

Splits layout: Fix the next split collapsing to a single line after equalizing a tab with only one window, or closing a window with equalize_on_window_close enabled (#10522)

icat: Fix a regression in 0.49.0 --transfer-mode=memory not displaying anything and --detect-support reporting files, because the names of the POSIX shared memory objects it created were missing the leading slash mandated by the graphics protocol (#10517)

Fix a packaging bug that could cause pipeline files to be omitted from some kitty builds

save_as_session: Show an error instead of saving next to the directory when the specified path is an existing directory (#10520)
