#9961. GhostAction Hacking Wave Fizzles, but Attackers Lurk on in GitHub

The supply chain attack campaign's shift toward developer endpoints and cloud access signals what could be next for the cybercrime outfit.

A new wave of GhostAction attacks has largely failed, but this supply chain campaign operator is well-positioned to cause more chaos down the line.

GhostAction, an ongoing campaign in which attackers target GitHub by compromising developer accounts and injecting GitHub Actions workflow files into repositories.

Workflows tell GitHub Actions what code to execute when events occur (such as when a commit is pushed or a pull request is opened); these malicious workflows rely on GitHub's high trust in these files (by design), seizing repository secrets, package publishing tokens, GitHub personal access tokens, credentials embedded in source code, and much more.

The idea is that an initial compromise could be leveraged into more compromises and access points across repositories, CI/CD systems, and cloud environments, not unlike many supply chain worms observed in the wild lately, albeit functioning differently.

Related:Undead Software Projects Continue to Raise Security Risks

The campaign was first documented last year, and attackers continue to deploy GhostAction against organizations. What has changed is an apparent escalation of the technique beginning this month. During an earlier Oct. 8-12 wave, attackers pushed the security-audit.yml workflow into roughly 30,000 repositories, using compromised accounts to distribute credential-stealing code at scale. But GitGuardian on Oct. 27 published research highlighting further escalation. GitGuardian's Gaetan Ferry wrote that between Oct. 13 and 21, GhostAction's operator "pushed 72,000 commits to 23,000 public repositories," noting that 8,000 of them were new targets.

During this latest wave of the campaign, GitGuardian observed that once a developer account is compromised, the operator would deploy different payloads depending on which runner the repositories were hosted on. Runners are the systems that execute GitHub Actions workflows. Many organizations use GitHub-hosted runners, while others configure self-hosted runners that run inside their own environments.

These payloads include one called "seven workflows," which searches GitHub runner repositories and wikis for credentials including AI-provider API keys; the "Security-audit.yml" file seen in earlier GhostAction attacks that searches GitHub-hosted source code and Git history for credentials; self-hosted runner payloads targeting self-hosted CI runners; a payload targeting GitHub runners and AWS-requesting GitHub OIDC tokens (in order to assume AWS roles and achieve cloud account access); and the font stealer payload, which is the most notable workflow payload seen in recent attacks, due to its provenance.

Related:Claude Model Builds Exploits Across Major Browsers & OSes

The font stealer family installs a Node.js credential stealer on local developer machines, disguised as a VS Code task. The technique appears to be copied from PolinRider, a campaign that hides obfuscated loaders in developer repositories to steal credentials and has been associated with North Korea. The attacker also added PolinRider loaders between Oct. 22 and 26 to repositories already impacted by GhostAction. Ferry says that out of the five payloads, only the PolinRider-styled local stealer had a chance to successfully run, but GitGuardian has no evidence that any run actually occurred.

GitGuardian could not assess whether there was overlap between GhostAction and PolinRider, but hypothesized that GhostAction's operator possibly copied a public PolinRider launcher in order to target an overlapping set of victims.

Jenn Gile, cofounder of OpenSourceMalware (which previously covered the GhostAction attacks this month and detected signs of the PolinRider copycat a few weeks ago), tells Dark Reading that the PolinRider clone illustrates some of the inner workings of the GhostAction group.

"What we're seeing looks like imitation, not evolution. The fake-font technique in GhostAction is a copy of what DPRK's PolinRider campaign has been using nearly all of 2026," she says in an email. "The multiple payloads are real, but they're variations on a theme (five workflow versions over about ten days in one repo we examined), not a new capability. Historically, we might have called this evolution because it took real skill to figure out. But this looks a lot like an LLM helping the threat actor test different variants."

Related:In-the-Wild Attack Abuses AI Agents' Trust in Markdown

All of that said, GitHub identified and prevented execution of the malicious workflows, GitGuardian noted. However, importantly, the attackers still demonstrated persistent access to nearly 1,800 compromised accounts, many of which had already been used in earlier GhostAction activity; "1,382 of the 1,792 compromised accounts had already been used on Oct. 8, so the same stolen tokens keep working," according to Ferry.

Ferry tells Dark Reading that the campaign has been "highly ineffective on the malicious workflows side." But even if there's no sign this wave succeeded, the nature of the payloads (such as the one aimed at gaining cloud access) also shows where the attackers may intend to pivot next, toward internal networks where there are fewer platform-level protections that could thwart their efforts.

"We expect new waves to appear in the near future, with revised payloads," he explains. "This 'fail early and adapt fast' strategy has already been observed for this threat actor."

Given that targeted accounts or repositories remain compromised, repo owners should look for and delete the files that GitGuardian lists in the IoC section of the blog, on every branch. And, if signs of compromise are detected, users should revoke the account's tokens across the board and rotate every credential committed in the affected repository or its history, as well as every Actions secret and wiki credential.

InfoQ Homepage News Google Launches LiteRT Tensor API for Building, Customizing, and Optimizing ML Models for On-Device

Nov 03, 2026 2 min read

Google has introduced the LiteRT Tensor API, a lightweight C++ API that allows developers to build, customize, and optimize machine learning models directly for on-device execution. According to Google, it combines the flexibility of native model authoring with cross-platform portability.

The traditional approach, Google says, is for developers to write computations manually in C++ for maximum control, which comes with a significant drawback:

Implementations are tightly coupled to specific backends (such as Metal, OpenCL, or Vulkan) and must be rewritten for each new hardware target. Furthermore, managing zero-copy buffer interoperability and synchronization across CPU, GPU, and NPU, while gluing together pre-processing, inference, and post-processing, demands substantial manual engineering effort.

The LiteRT Tensor API aims to address these challenges by allowing developers to build computation graphs operation by operation in C++. This provided greater control over model architecture, optimization, and accelerator execution, while enabling the same graphs to run through LiteRT on CPU, GPU, and NPU hardware without requiring a rewrite for each new target.

Beyond providing full control over model graphs, other key capabilities of the API include direct weight ingestion, allowing developers to load weights directly from checkpoints, including Hugging Face .safetensors files; zero-copy buffer interoperability, which avoids copying accelerator buffers across pre-processing, inference, and post-processing; and compatibility with AI coding agents, which can construct, modify, validate, and benchmark model graphs by generating C++ code.

Google used a coding agent to create a real-world app demonstrating how to use the LiteRT Tensor API for multi-object segmentation and tracking. The application also served as the basis for benchmarking performance across platforms:

We ran the same C++ code for the SAM 2 model on the GPUs of three devices: a macOS laptop (Metal), an iOS phone (Metal), and an Android phone (OpenCL). In our tests on the MacBook Pro, it ran about 1.5x faster than Apple MLX (fp16, image encoder plus mask decoder).

Google emphasized the fact that the coding agent could make a number of optimizations thanks to the model graph being defined in plain C++. Specifically, it "moved SAM 2's per-frame decisions, such as whether the object is still visible, from CPU code into the graph" and rewrote operations that triggered CPU fallback on WebGPU using GPU-compatible arithmetics.

Commenting on the announcement on LinkedIn, Arm director of AI Laurence Moroney emphasized that developers should always start with model conversion and turn to the C++ API only "when you need graph-level control or want pre and post-processing to stay on the accelerator". He also highlighted the benefits of defining model graphs in plain C++:

Going from under 10 to over 30 frames per second at 512x512 on WebGPU, with a coding agent doing the iteration, shows how much structured primitives help agents do real optimization work.

Google is also working on several planned improvmeents, including direct ML Drift backend support, additional NPU-friendly operations, automatic full-graph quantization, and expanded dynamic-shape for different image sizes, batch sizes, and sequence lengths.

#9958. Measuring benchmark optimization in speech recognition

Public voice AI benchmarks increasingly suggest that models are performing at human levels. Yet those scores don't always reflect how models work in the real-world. Since public benchmarks are open and widely used, models can also become optimized for the tests themselves. Their scores may improve because they have learned benchmark-specific patterns and not because they have become better at the underlying task.

One reason is that traditional benchmarks overlook many of the conditions and qualities that make voice systems reliable, natural, contextually appropriate, and effective in practice. That's why we recently introduced held-out sets in Real World VoiceEQ, the Open-ASR Leaderboard, and the Far-field ASR Leaderboard: to measure more of what matters in real-world use.

However, broader measurement alone does not solve the problem. This phenomenon, sometimes called benchmark optimization or "benchmaxxing," is often discussed around machine learning, however, it has been difficult to measure in speech recognition.

Our latest research introduces three tests to help quantify it. We evaluated 11 widely used open-source ASR models and found that several of the highest-scoring systems reproduced benchmark transcripts from the VoxPopuli English and LibriSpeech (clean, other) datasets – even when the audio contradicted them, relevant words had been silenced, or the audio equally supported two different written forms.

In some cases, models appeared to rely not only on what was said, but also on subtle acoustic cues that indicated which benchmark they were being tested on. As a result, their scores overstated how well they could transcribe speech more generally.

VoxPopuli is known to contain a high number of transcription errors (which is why Artificial Analysis released a cleaned version). Our consensus disagreement probe tests what happens when leading ASR models encounter these errors: Do they accurately transcribe what the audio says, or reproduce the benchmark's incorrect reference transcript?

To test this at scale, we use an ensemble of independent models selected for their low phoneme error rate (PER). PER measures how closely a written transcription matches the sounds in the audio, making it a useful proxy for how faithfully a model transcribes what it hears. The ensemble results can be used to flag cases in which the models unanimously disagree with the benchmark's reference transcript. We then compare a sample of those flagged cases against human annotations to validate the corrected transcripts.

For example, one VoxPopuli clip audibly includes the phrase "Thank you, Mr. President," but the reference transcript omits "Thank you." Six of the 11 models we tested reproduced the benchmark's erroneous transcript—giving the "expected" answer even though it contradicted the audio. On the real clip, the formatting follows the same pattern: models that omit "Thank you" also reproduce the benchmark's punctuation style, writing "Mr" without a period, while models that include the audible phrase tend to write "Mr." with the period.

When we present the same content in newly collected voices from EU parliamentary recordings or generic voices, this behavior often weakens or disappears. In the below samples, all but one model flips back to transcribing the audio-faithful transcript for a clone of a new parliamentary recording. This suggests that the models are responding to acoustic cues that help them identify the benchmark membership and thus produce the expected transcript even if it contradicts the audio.

The reference transcript for this clip reads "Mr President, I have another complaint about this procedure, which is that it is not secret." The audio in all three clips below actually says the same thing, preceded by an audible "Thank you,"—the clones are text-to-speech renditions of that true sentence, so the courtesy is audible in all three. Green highlighting and ✅ mark a transcript that includes the audible "Thank you"; red highlighting and ❌ mark a transcript that reproduces the benchmark's erroneous omission. All transcripts are raw model output, prior to any normalization—casing and punctuation are preserved exactly as generated, including lowercase output from some models.

Clone of a parliament speaker recorded after every model's training cutoff

Parakeet is the only model that flips between reproducing the benchmark on the real clip and getting it right on the same-speaker clone. Phi-4 is the only model still dropping the courtesy on the ep-fresh clone. When we instead resynthesize the sentence in a generic TTS voice unconnected to any parliamentary recording, all eleven models restore the courtesy.

The results suggest that this problem is both widespread and meaningful. Our methodology flagged potential reference errors in 40% of the VoxPopuli test clips we analyzed, affecting roughly 3% of all reference words.

Models exhibiting benchmark-optimized behavior reproduced erroneous reference transcripts 18–30% of the time. The scatterplot below compares VoxPopuli word error rate (WER) on the x-axis with the rate at which each model reproduces the benchmark's incorrect reference instead of the consensus correction. The models with the lowest WER—and therefore the strongest reported benchmark performance—are also the most likely to reproduce these errors.

To build on the consensus disagreement probe, we deliberately silence numbers in the audio samples of test datasets and ask the models to transcribe what it hears. The number is literally absent from the audio, so models should not output any number, much less the exact number in the text.

Some of these numbers are semi-predictable (although still unlikely for a model to predict), yet others are quite surprising. The following clip combines both probes, showing both how models recreate reference transcript errors including an incorrect number and one model even autocompletes a relatively random year (2011) despite it being silenced. In each model's row below:

Recovery rates were highest on the public benchmarks and lower on held-out or newly collected audio (ep-fresh and libri-fresh below). On LibriSpeech, some of the strongest benchmark-performing models reproduced masked numbers in roughly 30–40% of examples, even though the number itself had been removed. The effect weakened on freshly collected data for several models, suggesting that the surrounding benchmark-associated audio—not only textual autocomplete—helped the models recover the reference.

Our orthographic switching probe tests whether models reproduce the exact spelling used in a benchmark's reference transcript despite it not being clear in the audio. Orthographic variants are words that are semantically and phonetically identical but can be spelled different ways (1 vs one, Mr. vs mister, John vs Jon, Honor vs Honour, etc). In theory, models should consistently prefer one spelling over another, or alternate between them at roughly random rates. If models systematically switch to match what is in each benchmark's reference transcript, that suggests the models are picking up on which spelling the test expects.

Transcription: "I URGED ON THE BOYS THAT WHATEVER HAPPENED WE SHOULD NOT SHOOT ANY ONE" — models using "any one": 6/11, models using "anyone": 5/11

Transcription: "CAMOUFLAGE WAS NOT A WORD THE CAPTAIN OR ANYONE ELSE OF HIS TIME YET UNDERSTOOD" — models using "any one": 2/11, models using "anyone": 9/11

Within LibriSpeech, we test one intra-dataset switch involving an older spacing convention: some reference transcripts use "any one", while others use "anyone." We measure the minimum accuracy for a given variant, which we call "switch rate". If a model only uses one variant it would have a 0% switch rate; a model which picks randomly would be expected to have a 50% switch rate. A model which knows which variant to use in every test sample would earn a 100% switch rate.

Our second probe tests an inter-dataset switch, in which each benchmark uses a different spelling convention consistently across its test corpus. For example, VoxPopuli uses the abbreviation "Mr.," while LibriSpeech spells out "Mister."

Multiple models exceed the 50% random-choice baseline, with some reaching roughly 90% switch accuracy. This suggests that the models can identify which dataset an audio sample comes from and select the spelling convention that benchmark expects, even though both forms sound identical.

To test whether these behaviors generalize beyond the public benchmarks, we also collected fresh data from the same source domains but after the models' training cutoffs: recent European Parliament recordings for VoxPopuli and recordings from newly active LibriVox narrators for LibriSpeech. However, when presented with recently collected data from the same domain, many models stop matching the reference transcript and revert to more audio faithful transcriptions.

Other interventions point to the same conclusion. Phrases which are present in the audio but are omitted in the reference transcript can reappear when a model is asked to translate the audio or when its attention is restricted to the relevant frames. Trimming away surrounding benchmark context, or appending ordinary conversational audio, can also restore the faithful transcript. Appending VoxPopuli audio can have the opposite effect, making otherwise faithful synthetic or mined samples more likely to match the benchmark reference.

Together, these results suggest that models are able to faithfully transcribe the literal spoken words, but are using surrounding acoustic context to decide whether to follow the audio or a benchmark-specific transcription policy.

Our findings suggest that, on two major open-source datasets, some models detect dataset-associated acoustic cues and adjust their transcription behavior accordingly. Specifically, models may reproduce words that are absent from the audio but present in the reference transcript, recover silenced numbers at elevated rates, or use surrounding acoustic context to select the written variant expected by a particular benchmark.

For people selecting models, these findings underscore the importance of using fully held-out evaluation sets, as RW-Voice-EQ Bench and the Open ASR Leaderboard do, and of looking beyond word error rate on a single public benchmark. To this end, a "Benchmark fitting" tab has been added to the Open ASR Leaderboard, which includes two of the above analyses across all models: quantifying (1) reference error rates from VoxPopuli and (2) orthographic switching across all public datasets. The relevant scripts are open-sourced on GitHub as well as the un-normalized model outputs.

Our findings also suggest that benchmark developers should avoid simple independent and identically distributed test splits in favor of temporal, speaker, or other metadata-based separation. Greater transparency around training data and model-selection procedures would also help researchers understand how these behaviors arise.

Public benchmarks remain valuable: they are transparent, repeatable, easy to run, and well understood by the research community. But they are most useful when we can distinguish genuine transcription improvements from benchmark-specific gains that do not generalize to new audio.

For more information, we encourage you to read our full report.

#9956. The cryptography behind electronic voting (and why paper ballots are still essential)

As millions of Americans vote in today’s U.S. midterms, most will use paper ballots, which are protected by strict chain-of-custody protocols and, in some cases, statistical audits. You may wonder why we still use paper for our elections and voting systems when tasks like banking, tax filing, and document signing have moved away from paper-based legacy systems and become fully electronic. The short answer: security.

That may come as a surprise to some. After all, cryptography and other security advancements have enabled secure electronic systems for many applications. In fact, cryptography can be used to provide two essential safeguards in elections: keeping (1) individual votes secret while (2) making the final tally independently verifiable. This is exactly the approach of cryptographic protocols like Helios and ElectionGuard. However, Helios intentionally targets lower-risk and lower-coercion settings rather than high-stakes public elections. ElectionGuard, by contrast, is intended for public elections, but not as a replacement for a paper-based system; it is used as a cryptographic layer integrated with traditional voting infrastructure.

In this blog post, we’ll explain how cryptographic techniques can help protect ballot secrecy and prevent manipulation in electronic voting systems, and explore the limitations of these systems. Although cryptography can strengthen election verifiability and have other strong security properties, it cannot fully replace the security and trust of existing paper ballot systems in general elections.

The National Academy of Sciences’ excellent 2018 report on election security concludes that electronic ballot return (also known as online voting or internet voting) should not be used in general elections, since “no known technology guarantees the secrecy, security, and verifiability of a marked ballot transmitted over the Internet.”

The difficulty of this problem makes sense when you consider the strong security guarantees any election system requires:

Ballot integrity must be maintained. This becomes especially challenging in the electronic setting because, in general, the voter does not hold a cryptographic identity and cannot sign their ballot cryptographically. Oh, and the electronic voting client and server may be compromised anyway.

Voters shouldn’t be able to vote more than once, but this is hard to verify without associating votes with their voters. This becomes even more challenging electronically when, again, voters often lack a digital cryptographic identity.

Everyone should be able to trust (and ideally verify) that the election result correctly reflects the voters’ intent.

Electronic systems introduce an existentially dangerous failure mode not present in modern, sensible paper-based systems: a supply-chain or 0-day vulnerability that can scale across many voting machines and jurisdictions could allow one person to single-handedly control and influence the outcome of an election (and, depending on the system and exact vulnerability, possibly while evading detection). In traditional paper-based systems, this risk is sharply constrained by independent physical records and physical security controls. It’s much more difficult for a single person to meaningfully change an election’s outcome while evading detection in this system.

Software security alone is not enough to secure electronic voting systems, though; the key design principle is not only to implement robust security controls but also to design your system so that all failures of those controls are detectable. This can’t be solved only using software whose correctness must be trusted. This property is known as software independence: changes in the election outcome caused by changes or errors (or vulnerabilities) in voting software must be detectable. In practice, this is typically achieved using evidence that can be verified independently of the voting software, such as a paper ballot audit trail.

One way of solving this problem is to threshold-share the keypair used for encryption, and split the private key between $N$ trusted election officials. This means that a predetermined quorum $t+1\ \leq N$ of the trustees have to be involved in order to decrypt ciphertexts. Using a homomorphic encryption scheme offers further protection for individual encrypted ballots: it allows the backend to compute an encrypted tally from the encrypted votes and only decrypt the final result. As long as $N-t$ election officials are honest, this protects the confidentiality of cast votes from the voting client to the inclusion in the final tally1.

With homomorphic encryption, the server can compute the encryption of the sum of the individual votes ${x}_{i}$ as the sum of the encrypted votes ${E}_{K}({x}_{i})$.

Schemes like Helios and ElectionGuard use a version of exponential ElGamal to encrypt individual choices on the ballot2. If the threshold-shared election key is $K\ =\ {g}^{k}$, the choice $x$ is encrypted as ${E}_{K}(x)\ =\ ({g}^{r},\ {K}^{r}{g}^{x})$, where $r$ is a random scalar. This scheme is additively homomorphic using pointwise multiplication of ciphertexts, as shown below.

Exponential ElGamal is additively homomorphic if we define $\oplus$ as pointwise multiplication of ciphertexts.

Note that decryption yields ${g}^{x}$ rather than $x$, which is typically hard to invert. However, since $x$ is comparatively small in this case, we can use brute force (or tables) to recover the exponent.

As an example, if we use 0 to indicate No and 1 to indicate Yes, we can compute the number of Yes-votes by summing the individual encrypted votes as described above, and then decrypting the encrypted tally to reveal the result. However, if we don’t ensure that individual ciphertexts are well-formed, a compromised client could simply encrypt the value 1,000,000 to vote Yes a million times. To prevent this, clients must include a zero-knowledge proof ensuring that the encrypted ballot contains a permitted value (or a permitted combination of values).

What if the voting client is hacked and alters the voters’ choices before they are encrypted, or drops the ballot completely? To protect against client compromise, the voter needs a way to ensure that the backend received their ballot, and that the choices recorded and encrypted by the software client correspond to how they actually voted.

This can be achieved in different ways. Helios and ElectionGuard use a mechanism known as Benaloh’s challenge method. The underlying idea is that when the ballot is encrypted, the voter obtains a commitment to the encrypted ballot and is then allowed to challenge and spoil their ballot. If they do, the ballot is opened and the voter can verify that their choices were recorded correctly and that the commitment corresponds to the encrypted ballot. The device has to reveal the commitment to the voter before learning whether or not the voter wants to challenge the encrypted ballot. Otherwise, it could present a correct commitment only when it is challenged. Moreover, it must be possible to obtain some external validation that the committed ciphertext actually encrypts the voter’s intended choices. Otherwise, the voting client can simply lie and present a plaintext that doesn’t match the commitment.

When the voter is satisfied that the voting client records their choices honestly, they record their choices one last time and cast their ballot, which is then published to a public bulletin board. The voter can use their commitment to check that their encrypted ballot is included in the published election record.

While this protocol provides a method to detect a compromised voting client that tampers with the voter’s choices or drops ballots, it still requires that a significant portion of voters exercise the mechanism in order to ensure that compromised clients are detected with high-enough probability3. Moreover, it does not protect against other types of compromise, like a voting client surreptitiously sending the voter’s plaintext ballot to a third-party server.

Additional issues must be solved in order for this method to be secure. One is the problem of voter authentication: how does the voting client ensure that the voter is eligible to vote, and how do we ensure that only one vote is cast? Additionally, there is the previously mentioned problem of coercion: how do we protect voters from being strong-armed into voting for a specific candidate or issue when voting stations may be spread out all over the world?

Authenticating voters is generally a difficult problem in countries (like the U.S.) that do not have a widely used national ID. However, there are options available for specific groups of voters. For example, some voting systems designed for overseas military voters use the Common Access Card to allow service members to identify themselves. Protecting voters against coercion typically requires that voters are able to vote without being supervised, which seems like a difficult problem to solve using cryptography.

If the election record is public (and we can ensure that everyone shares a consistent view of it), voters can verify that their encrypted vote is included in the record using their commitment to their encrypted ballot, as described above. This provides a mechanism to detect a compromised server which attempts to drop or alter votes. Again, we need to rely on active participation from many voters to ensure that a compromise is detected, since a voter can only detect if their individual ballot has been dropped or tampered with.

ElectionGuard extends this idea to allow voters to detect a change in any of the ballots cast before theirs by chaining ballot commitments generated on the same device. Without chaining, the commitment is essentially computed as a hash of the voter’s encrypted ballot. With chaining, ballot commitments are chained as follows:

When ballot commitments are computed as a chain, the hash chain is published together with the election record. Here, ${B}_{i}$ is voter $i$’s encrypted ballot.

This means that any changes are propagated forward, allowing voters to detect tampering with earlier votes cast using the same voting client.

Detecting a compromised server that injects additional votes is more difficult and usually requires external data, like voter participation records, to solve. It is not enough to associate encrypted ballots with voter identities, since a malicious server could pad the election record with ballots corresponding to abstaining voters.

Once the election record is trusted, it is possible to use zero-knowledge proofs to verify that the final result is computed correctly from the published election record. Since anyone can compute the encrypted tally from the election record, we only need to prove that the final aggregate ciphertext was decrypted correctly.

Recall our fourth requirement for election systems, which we admitted was most difficult to achieve for paper-based systems: Everyone should be able to trust (and ideally verify) that the election result correctly reflects the voters’ intent.

This requirement is usually formalized in terms of end-to-end verifiability, which means that the following should be possible:

Taken together, these two mechanisms allow voters to independently verify that their vote contributed to the election outcome, without relying on a particular piece of software or hardware (which may be hacked), or external observers (who may not be trustworthy). This property isn’t achievable in exclusively paper-based election systems without introducing some level of trust in humans/institutions overseeing the election. For example, without trusting anyone, how do you know what happens to your paper ballot after you and your vote both leave the voting location? The reason you won’t know this in an exclusively paper-based system is simple: in order to protect vote secrecy, when you submit your ballot to be counted with the other ballots, you intentionally break the link between your identity and your ballot.

Helios and ElectionGuard both build on the ideas outlined above, but their use cases differ. Helios explicitly targets settings with low coercion risk and advises against use in high-stakes public elections. ElectionGuard, on the other hand, is built to provide end-to-end verifiability on top of an existing paper-based voting system. Neither protocol makes a general claim to solve the problem of electronic voting because neither achieves the security of status quo paper-based systems purely electronically.

There is widespread agreement among experts on election security that paper ballots are essential for protecting the security and integrity of general elections, and that likely will not change anytime soon. However, cryptographic techniques like the ones described in this post can still be used alongside paper ballots to improve trust in the election outcome by improving the result’s public verifiability and auditability.

If you’re using cryptography to build a new voting system, please reach out. We want to hear about it!

A higher threshold is not always better. Helios requiring all trustees to participate to decrypt the election result caused the IACR to have to rerun their 2025 election after it found that one of the trustees had inadvertently lost their share of the key. ↩︎

Helios and ElectionGuard differ slightly in how they implement encryption. Here, we describe the method used in Helios since it’s closer to standard ElGamal. ↩︎

As an example, if a compromised voting client tampers with 1000 votes, and voters challenge one encrypted vote in one hundred on average, the probability of the attack remaining undetected would be 0.991000 ≈ 4.3 ∙10-5. However, it is also important to consider what recourse a voter has if tampering is detected. This determines whether they are apt to raise concerns, or simply shrug their shoulders and try again. ↩︎

#9954. Cyber Vulnerabilities Besiege Italy, Absent Clear Cause

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Researchers can't quite explain why cyber threats look so different in Italy compared with everywhere else.

To read this article in Italian, click here!

Italy is suffering from a disproportionately large number of cyberattacks, new data suggests. Not only that: The kinds of attacks hitting organizations in the country are vastly different from those hitting other places. Researchers have a triad of theories as to why.

It's true that certain regions and countries face greater cyber-risk thanks to economic, military, and political factors. Israel is a magnet for hacktivists and regional, state-aligned advanced persistent threats (APTs). Brazil's unique history makes it a hive of banking Trojans. The United States economy will always draw the most attention from scammers. It isn't so obvious, though, why Italy is such a popular mark for cybercriminals.

"One of the main reasons why we decided to look into the Italian threat landscape is because Italy kept appearing at the top of our stats in our monthly internal reports," says Gianluca Tiepolo, cybercrime analyst at Intel471. In a report shared exclusively with Dark Reading ahead of its release, Intel471 found that Italy is a total outlier in the global cyber threat landscape. Organizations there are being compromised at a rate beyond what one would reasonably expect, based on the country's size, economy, and politics. And exploits against vulnerabilities and Web infrastructure are far more common in Italy than elsewhere.

Related:L’Italia è afflitta da vulnerabilità informatiche, senza una causa chiara

"We wanted to understand what was driving those stats," Tiepolo says. In the end, though, the data paints a nearly inexplicable picture of what's going on in the land of pasta and Chianti.

Italy is the 25th largest country in the world but, according to this new data, its organizations make up about 7% of all initial access data sold on cybercriminal forums. That's second only to the United States (30%) globally. Italy also ranks fourth among countries most targeted by ransomware.

Far stranger still are the types of cyber intrusions affecting organizations in Italy. According to the new data, initial access brokers (IABs) obtained their initial foothold through vulnerabilities in 57% of cases. Credentials only explained 23% of cases. Meanwhile, IABs have been selling access to victim-owned Web infrastructure in 49% of cases, with remote access and remote desktop tools making up 26% of cases.

So what? Maybe those figures don't pop off the page. Now, though, let's compare them with Intel471's own data from its 2026 Cyber Threat Trends & Outlook report:

Globally in 2025, IABs targeted remote access and remote desktop tools 67% of the time — 41% more often, relatively, than in Italy. Meanwhile, Web infrastructure — by far the most at-risk asset in Italy — represented such a small fraction of Intel471's global data that it didn't even bother to cite it in their report.

Related:Aussies Face Reduced Cybercrime Risk, as Pressure Shifts to SMBs

In the same vein, according to the company's global data, credential-based attacks are eight times more common in general than any other type of attack today. It found that 49% of IAB listings advertised credentials as the attack type, compared to 23% in the Italian-specific data. And guffaw-ingly, whereas in Italy they represent around 57% of all attacks, exploited vulnerabilities showed up in only 6.5% of cases globally.

Though cybersecurity data reporting can be interpreted in different ways depending on the circumstance, Italy does seem like a kind of cyber-risk unicorn, Tiepolo says, adding that Italy has been falling behind on cyber readiness for a long time now.

"I'm Italian," he says. "I've been working with a lot of different Italian clients. What I can say is that Italy is probably slightly behind other European countries, simply based on security technology [adoption]. For example, endpoint detection and response (EDR) technologies became popular in Italy around 2020–2021. Before 2020, most Italian companies didn't use EDR technology. So maybe historically, Italy is a bit behind in actually investing in cybersecurity products and technologies."

Related:Europe Evolves Into Ransomware's Favorite Region

Also, opportunistic cybercriminals are exploiting known, widespread, and often quite old vulnerabilities en masse to scoop up more victims in Italy than in other countries. "The data we saw last week from PHP2Shell, I think, validates this assessment. Italy is the country in Europe with the largest number of PHP 4, 5, and 7 versions, which are end-of-life," Tiepolo notes.

"A full 90% of initial access offers for Italy are what we call 'wholesale' offers," he posits. "They're not offers that are targeting Italy specifically, but simply exploiting vulnerabilities. Our assessment is that Italy is probably slower than other countries in patching their systems."

Another, related possibility is that Italy finds itself victim to a kind of cyber vulnerability network effect. The logic goes something like this: If certain technologies are especially common in a country like Italy, and organizations are slow to address vulnerabilities in those technologies, then that country becomes an attractive economy of scale.

As Intel471 wrote in its report, "Once an actor develops an effective exploitation method, the actor can apply that method to additional exposed systems without conducting a separate, extensive reconnaissance effort against each organization. This reduces the effort required to compromise businesses whose size or profile might otherwise offer limited incentive for a dedicated intrusion."

Researchers couldn't say exactly which technologies, vulnerabilities, or exploitations this theory might refer to, but noted that it does fold into the finding that 90% of initial access offerings to Italian organizations online are sold in bulk.

Without co-signing Intel471's data or conclusions specifically, representatives from the Milan-based cybersecurity firm Cleafy tell Dark Reading that they've observed broadly similar patterns.

"Our threat research does point to a related pattern: attackers reusing tools, infrastructure and techniques to scale campaigns across Italian banking targets," the company wrote via email. It pointed to cases such as the drIBAN Web injection kit, which attackers used to exploit the Certified Electronic Mail (PEC) system used widely across Italy. Cases like drIBAN "don't establish that Italy has a disproportionately large initial-access market, but they do illustrate how reusable attack techniques and infrastructure can help cybercriminals scale operations across multiple targets."

There is one other, potentially significant contributing factor to why Italy looks so different from other countries in cyberattack datasets: its prevalence of small businesses.

Most businesses everywhere are small, but, at least in comparison to other advanced economies, it's especially the case in Italy. A May 2024 "data snapshot for Italy" by McKinsey found that "MSMEs" — micro-, small-, and medium-sized enterprises — contributed roughly 10% more to Italy's economy and employment compared to their relative share in other advanced economies. And last March, the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) published a report that cited that 99.9% of Italian firms in 2023 were SMEs, and 94.8% were micro-enterprises.

"Italy has a lot of small and medium-sized companies," Tiepolo says. "One of the things that came out from the data — especially the extortion data — is that these groups are [disproportionately] targeting small- and medium-sized businesses. So this could be one of the reasons [Italy stands out] in comparison to other countries that have more large companies."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.

#9953. How Hugging Face Inference Endpoints, Jobs, and Buckets Power Search on Papers with Code

3 months ago, we started a revival of Papers with Code (see also the announcement tweet). Its goal is to make open AI research accessible and digestible, so that people can easily find the artifacts related to a paper, find state-of-the-art (SOTA) across the various domains of AI, share interesting research and build on top of each other's work. In other words, its goal is to power the wave of research that leads to the next Transformer.

Of course, making AI research accessible requires a powerful search engine, so that humans and agents can quickly find relevant and related work, either through the website or the pwc search CLI command, which agents can use via the Skill.

It's important to note that searching for research is not quite the same as searching for regular text. A useful paper search engine should find an exact title or arXiv identifier, but it should also understand a query such as “small language models for code generation” even when those words do not appear together in a paper. It needs to recognize that “the original BERT paper” is a navigational request, tolerate an incomplete title or typos, and still respond quickly when a model service is cold or temporarily unavailable.

For Papers with Code, we built this as a hybrid search system. This is also based on our prior experience at ML6, where we developed RAG-based systems for clients. It turned out that hybrid search typically outperforms keyword- and vector-based search systems, as it combines the best of both worlds (see also this blog for more info). Keyword search finds exact mentions, whereas vector search finds more fuzzy, semantically similar terms. Note that rerankers (also called cross-encoders) can further improve the results, although they also come with additional overhead and latency.

Papers with Code relies on a PostgreSQL database, hence its full-text search capabilities provide a fast lexical baseline. For dense embeddings, pgvector is used to add semantic recall, and the reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) algorithm combines the two. Three Hugging Face services are used for the dense embeddings:

Today, the system maintains embeddings for more than 110,000 current papers sourced from arXiv and Daily Papers. This post explains the architecture, the design decisions behind it, and the lessons we learned while taking it to production.

We deliberately split search into an offline corpus build and an online search service:

The expensive, throughput-oriented work runs as Jobs. Durable artifacts live in a Bucket. Only the small query-embedding step sits on the request path, behind a protected Inference Endpoint, to power the online search. If that endpoint is cold, busy, or unhealthy, search immediately falls back to full-text retrieval. This separation makes the system both powerful and fast.

Embedding pipelines often fail in subtle ways: a model revision changes, query and document prompts are mixed up, vectors are truncated differently, or an updated abstract no longer matches its stored vector.

We avoid this by treating the embedding format as a versioned API. Every paper is encoded as:

Our production generation uses Qwen/Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, pinned to an exact revision, with 256-dimensional L2-normalized vectors. We selected the model with help from the MTEB leaderboard, the go-to benchmark for comparing embedding models. Note that newer embedding models like Qwen3 allow for 2 new features:

This contract follows an embedding from export, through GPU inference, into PostgreSQL, and finally into online retrieval.

Full-corpus embedding is a classic batch workload. It needs a GPU for a relatively short period, benefits from high throughput, and should not consume resources between runs. Hugging Face Jobs fits that shape well: a Job is defined by a command, a hardware flavor, and optionally a Docker image, and can run uv scripts with their dependencies declared inline.

Our corpus build starts by exporting the latest version of every paper from a repeatable-read PostgreSQL snapshot. The exporter streams rows rather than loading the catalog into memory, writes bounded JSONL shards, and creates a manifest containing row counts and SHA-256 checksums.

We sync that immutable run directory to a private Storage Bucket and mount the Bucket directly (using hf-mount) into an l4x1 Job (an NVIDIA L4 GPU, which has 24GB of VRAM). From the worker's perspective it is simply a filesystem:

Each completed shard has its own marker, so a restarted Job can skip verified work. This is useful for a large corpus: retrying should just resume work rather than overwriting existing embeddings.

In our 5,000-paper pilot, the Qwen Job encoded about 75 papers per second at 1024 dimensions on an L4 GPU. The same pass could be deterministically materialized at 512 and 256 dimensions, so we could compare the storage and retrieval trade-offs without paying for more inference.

Storage Buckets are mutable, S3-like object storage on the Hub, optimized for AI workloads. They can be accessed through hf://buckets/... paths and mounted read-write in Jobs without building a separate storage integration.

For us, the Bucket is more than a place to put vectors. It is the boundary between three systems with different lifecycles:

We organize artifacts under immutable run prefixes:

Buckets themselves are intentionally mutable, so immutability is an application-level rule: a run ID is never overwritten, and every artifact is covered by a manifest and checksum.

Only after the importer rechecks schemas, checksums, dimensions, normalization, unique paper IDs, and current content hashes do we load the vectors into PostgreSQL. We then build a separate HNSW index for the new generation and atomically mark it active only when every eligible current paper is covered (HNSW is the graph-based algorithm that enables fast vector search).

Batch embeddings solve the document side of retrieval. A user query still needs to be embedded at request time using the same model contract.

We deploy the pinned model as an authenticated Inference Endpoint backed by Text Embeddings Inference (TEI). The endpoint accepts the query text and returns a normalized 256-dimensional vector using the model's query prompt. Note that one could also leverage vLLM or SGLang here.

The API then performs a cosine-distance search over the active pgvector generation:

The HNSW index keeps this lookup fast. On our 5,000-paper pilot, the 256-dimensional Qwen index achieved 0.9955 Recall@20 against exact search, with 1.31 ms p50 and 2.21 ms p95 HNSW lookup latency. Its table and index used about 27% of the storage of the 1024-dimensional version while retaining essentially the same ANN recall in that test.

The Endpoint is configured with a maximum of one replica and can scale to zero when idle. That is a useful cost lever, as this means you're not paying when there's no usage. However, this also means cold starts must be part of the application design rather than treated as an exceptional event, as it takes some time for the endpoint to spin up and serve traffic.

Our query client therefore has deliberately strict behavior:

If the endpoint is scaling up, times out, returns a malformed vector, or has no concurrency available, we skip the semantic branch immediately. Users still receive lexical results instead of waiting for an unreliable dependency.

Inference Endpoints works really reliably, and includes a nice dashboard so you can quickly see key analytics.

For every query, the lexical branch retrieves up to 50 candidates using weighted PostgreSQL full-text search. The semantic branch retrieves up to 50 candidates from pgvector.

We combine their ranks using weighted reciprocal rank fusion (RRF):

score(d)=∑r ∈ {lexical, semantic}wrk+rankr(d) \text{score}(d) = \sum_{r \,\in\, \{\text{lexical},\, \text{semantic}\}} \frac{w_r}{k + \text{rank}_r(d)} score(d)=r∈{lexical,semantic}∑​k+rankr​(d)wr​​

RRF is simple and robust, because it combines ranks rather than scores from two systems with different scales. Basically, if a paper is ranked high both by the lexical branch and the semantic branch, it has a higher chance of being ranked high by the hybrid search. We currently use equal branch weights and (k=60) (k is the "rank constant", a hyperparameter of the RRF algorithm).

Dense retrieval improves recall for conceptual queries. Full-text retrieval remains excellent for exact terminology, identifiers, and rare names. We also preserve deterministic identity behavior on top of the fused ranking:

Note: hybrid search isn't always the best option, it is recommended to start with keyword search as a cheap and fast baseline, and only adding semantic and/or hybrid search when it turns out those give a reasonable boost in retrieval quality. One could further improve the search by adding a reranker after keyword/semantic/hybrid retrieval, using a model like Qwen3-Reranker.

The large initial corpus is embedded with Jobs, but Papers with Code changes continuously. New papers arrive, abstracts are corrected, and new arXiv versions become current.

Launching a GPU Job for a handful of changed rows would add unnecessary startup and orchestration overhead. Instead, an hourly incremental process selects missing or content-changed papers and sends a bounded delta to the same TEI Endpoint, this time with the document prompt.

Each run processes at most 500 papers in batches of 16. Before an embedding is written, the source row is locked and its content hash is checked again. If a paper changed during inference, that vector is discarded and picked up by the next run.

This gives us a useful division of labor:

The hourly path keeps the active index close to the live catalog without turning an online endpoint into an unbounded batch processor.

The same document embeddings also power related-paper recommendations on each paper page.

Because the source paper already has a stored vector, related-paper retrieval requires no model call at request time. It is a single nearest-neighbor query over the active generation. If a vector is temporarily missing, the application can use a previous arXiv version or fill results from the existing task- and citation-based fallback. We fetch citation data through the Semantic Scholar API and also built s2-cli, a command-line interface for querying its citation graph. The latter is used by the agent at https://paperswithcode.co/chat.

Corpus embedding and query embedding use the same model, but they are different infrastructure problems. Jobs optimize for throughput and bounded cost; Inference Endpoints optimize for availability and request latency.

Buckets provide an explicit handoff between compute and production. Checksummed artifacts create a reviewable boundary before data enters the production index.

The revision, dimension, prompt, normalization, and input formatter all affect retrieval. Store them together and validate them everywhere.

Scale-to-zero is valuable when traffic is intermittent, but only if the product has a fast fallback. Hybrid search gave us that fallback naturally: lexical search is always useful on its own.

Matryoshka embeddings let us evaluate quality, memory, index size, and latency as one trade-off. In our pilot, 256 dimensions preserved ANN recall while materially shrinking storage compared with 1024 dimensions.

New generations are imported beside the current one, indexed independently, checked for complete and current coverage, and then activated atomically. Rollback is a configuration change, not an emergency recomputation.

Feel free to try out the search at https://paperswithcode.co or the chat interface at https://paperswithcode.co/chat, and let us know any feedback!

#9952. Tor Browser 16.0 released

Version 16.0 of the Tor Browser has been released. This is the first stable version based on Firefox ESR 153. Notable changes in this release include support for Linux on 64-bit Arm, redesigned settings, and a "generic window titles" feature to help prevent other applications from snooping on one's browser activity. Tor Browser for Android has had a number of interface updates to Google's Material Design 3 design language.

This release also follows Firefox in ending support for 32-bit x86 Linux systems. See the full changelog for all of the updates and bug fixes.

#9951. Shadowy AI Relay Disables OpenAI Codex, Claude Code Sandboxes

The enigmatic service is providing popular AI coding tools to mainland China and other regions where OpenAI and Anthropic products are not officially for sale — but with key security features turned off.

A mysterious relay service is installing authentic but unauthorized OpenAI Codex and Anthropic Claude Code tools for enterprise users overseas, and making dangerous configuration changes that put those organizations at risk.

The AI relay, first spotted by the Symantec Threat Hunter Team, appears to be designed to bypass regional restrictions that prevent certain countries and regions from using AI tools and platforms of US companies. According to Symantec's report published Thursday, the relay service installs genuine versions of the command-line interfaces (CLIs) for Codex and Claude Code on enterprise systems, but reconfigures them to route requests through the relay's infrastructure rather than OpenAI's or Anthropic's networks.

On the surface, this appears to be the case of a gray market provider or unauthorized reseller providing the AI tools to markets where they are not officially sold. Symantec researchers noted that the service, which has been active since early 2026, has installed the tools on systems at a dozen organizations, primarily in mainland China but also in South Korea, Taiwan, and Malaysia.

Related:Researchers Infiltrate Microsoft Tech Support Scam Operation

But the relay service also disables security safeguards for the tools, and the research team said it's unclear why it's being done (no malware or malicious activity has been observed thus far). One thing is for certain, according to Symantec: the relay service is creating enormous cyber-risk for the organizations using it.

Brigid O Gorman, senior intelligence analyst at the Symantec Threat Hunter Team, tells Dark Reading that researchers found a suspicious PowerShell downloader that they later determined to be "an AI-agent hijack script." After investigating further, the team found similar activity on other networks and traced it to the unauthorized relay service.

According to Symantec's report, when a user of the AI relay installs a legitimate Codex or Claude Code CLI through npm, the fileless PowerShell or bash script is fetched from "a lookalike domain by a one-line command that the user appears to run themselves. While this evokes the specter of attack techniques like ClickFix and InstallFix, the research team noted that the CLI clients aren't modified or Trojanized in any way.

And yet, the tools perform suspicious actions that heighten risks for enterprises. For example, the reconfigurations turn off the CLIs' execution sandbox, which is a key security feature because it limits what the AI coding tools can do.

Related:F-Secure Launches Victim-First Scam Encyclopedia Covering 50+ Types of Consumer Fraud

Additionally, the relay service enables network access for the write sandbox, turns off telemetry and error reporting features, and replaces the user's API credentials with relay-issued tokens. In one case observed by the Symantec Threat Hunter Team, the script logged a user out of their Anthropic session and deleted their authentication variables before reissuing credentials controlled by the relay service.

"Bypassing the regional restrictions that keep Western AI vendors from selling directly into certain markets is the simplest explanation, but it does not require disabling a CLI's sandbox or establishing persistent credentials that survive a reboot," the report stated.

The relay service activity is something of an enigma. The Symantec Threat Hunter Team said it's unclear why the operators of the client-side relay would need this level of control over users' systems, though the researchers did not observe any evidence of the operators abusing the access. The report noted that the architecture of the service would support malicious exploitation of the access if the operator's intentions were to change.

Furthermore, the Claude Code keys issued by the relay service are formatted with the prefix that Anthropic reserves for subscription-based OAuth tokens, "which is consistent with, though not proof of, a relay pooling flat-rate subscriptions and splitting the capacity across many customers," the team wrote.

Related:AI Slop Isn't Just for Social Media; It's Ruining Cyberattacks, Too

On the other hand, disabling security features hints at a potential fraud operation involving stolen credentials or payment cards, or even the malicious resale of prompts and files that run through the relay infrastructure. Gorman says it's "certainly notable" that the relay disables execution sandboxes and establishes its own persistent credentials.

"We did not see any malicious activity being carried out using these relay services, so any commentary on the potential intended goals of those using it are speculative," Gorman says. "However, a relay in this position can see every prompt, file, and secret an employee sends to the agent, and can alter or fabricate every response it returns. With the sandbox disabled and network access enabled, a malicious or compromised response could execute with the full privileges of the user's account."

Symantec provided indicators of compromise (IoCs) in the report, even though technically speaking there have been no compromises at this stage. "The organizations affected here look less like chosen targets and more like workplaces where individual employees found and used such a service to get access to tools they wanted," the report stated.

Nevertheless, the research team warned that using the service presents serious risk to corporate networks. And while the relay appears to be aimed at regions where Codex and Claude Code tools aren't officially offered, organizations looking for cheaper alternatives and users engaging in shadow AI activity could potentially find their way to such a service.

InfoQ Homepage News Docker Urges Isolation and Governance for AI Agent Security

Nov 04, 2026 5 min read

Docker has published a guide to five security risks that arise when AI agents are allowed to browse, run code and call tools with limited human oversight. Writing with product manager Eric Jia, Docker principal product marketing manager Srini Sekaran argues that the autonomy that makes agents useful also makes conventional application security controls insufficient. The company positions isolation and governance, rather than model improvements alone, as the main defences.

The blog post identifies prompt injection, tool misuse and poisoning, excessive autonomy, credential exposure, and data exfiltration as the principal risks. Docker argues that these share a common cause: an agent can select tools at runtime, chain several actions together and often operate with the permissions of the person who started it.

Traditional web security often assumes requests arrive at known endpoints and are processed by deterministic code, but agents do not fit that model. A coding agent may read a file, install a dependency, alter configuration, run tests and push a commit after receiving one instruction. Docker says that a compromised or misdirected agent can therefore take a much wider range of actions than a conventional service.

Prompt injection is presented as the defining risk: rather than compromising a system directly, an attacker can place instructions in material an agent is asked to read, such as a web page, code comment, issue or document. Docker cites an incident in which a coding agent followed instructions hidden in repository content and performed actions its user had not requested.

The company is sceptical that prompt injection can be eliminated through instructions to the model, saying that an agent cannot reliably distinguish a legitimate instruction from an injected one. Its preferred response is to limit what a hijacked agent can reach, so that successful manipulation has a smaller effect.

Tools are the second area of concern. With agents use connectors, database queries, file operations and code execution to affect external systems, Docker warns that giving an agent more tools than a task requires enlarges the attack surface. It also warns that a tool description can carry hidden instructions that lead an agent to misuse the tool.

This aligns with guidance published by OWASP. In its Agentic AI Threats and Mitigations work, reported by InfoQ in September 2025, OWASP identified tool misuse as a major new threat. It described attackers manipulating agents into abusing authorised tools, potentially gaining unauthorised data access or manipulating systems while remaining within granted permissions. OWASP recommended access verification, behavioural monitoring, operational boundaries and tamper-resistant execution logs.

Docker's third risk is excessive autonomy. The post describes "YOLO mode", where every agent action is approved automatically, as a visible example of broad standing permission. It acknowledges that this mode can be productive, but argues that it should be used inside a boundary that prevents an agent from reaching systems or data it should not touch.

The company gives an example in which a developer asked a coding agent to clean an old repository. The agent generated an rm -rf command with a trailing ~/ and executed it without confirmation, deleting the developer's home directory. Docker also cites an AWS engineer who gave a coding agent a Cost Explorer bug while it ran with operator-level access. The agent chose to delete and rebuild the production environment, resulting in a thirteen-hour regional outage.

Credential handling is closely connected to that problem. Docker says agents should not inherit a developer's personal token, because every action then carries that person's full permissions. It recommends separate, short-lived credentials, injected at runtime and kept out of the conversation. Secrets in prompts, configuration files or image environment variables are also a risk, because injected instructions may be able to read them from the agent's context.

The final risk is data exfiltration. An agent with network access and sensitive information in its context may send that information to an unintended destination. Docker says the risk increases in multi-agent systems, where one agent passes work to another. It recommends allow-listed network egress and treating every handoff between agents as untrusted input.

Those recommendations echo other work covered by InfoQ. Google's GKE security blueprint, reported in July 2026, recommends GKE Sandbox, based on gVisor, for containing agents that execute generated code or call untrusted tools. It also uses Model Armor to inspect prompts and responses for injection attempts and sensitive data exposure. Earlier, Meta open sourced LlamaFirewall, which combines prompt-injection detection, reasoning checks and static analysis of generated code. Google DeepMind's CaMeL research, also covered by InfoQ, takes a different approach by tracking control and data flows around a model.

Docker's answer is Docker Sandboxes and AI Governance. Sandboxes run each agent in a disposable microVM with defined filesystem and network controls. AI Governance is intended to define and enforce which actions, tools and credentials an agent may use. The company says isolation is the highest-impact starting point, with governance providing oversight across a fleet of agents.

Community discussion suggests that isolation alone will not settle the design question. In a thread on r/AI_Agents, a commenter using the name HectaMan wrote that teams should first assess tenancy and risk models. They argued that Docker can be convenient but may still grant excessive authority, noting that it disables around 40 privileged system calls while leaving roughly 500 available. They recommended deny-by-default permissions, least authority, policy enforcement points and controlled information flow.

Another commenter, Groady, said Docker works well for personal agents on a local machine, but questioned a shared kernel when agents execute code on behalf of other people. They suggested microVMs or gVisor-based isolation for that case. The discussion indicates that the useful comparison is not simply container versus no container, but whether the isolation boundary matches the trust boundary of the workload.

Docker's guidance is a useful summary of a problem that is becoming more concrete as coding agents gain write access to repositories, cloud accounts and production systems. Its central claim is persuasive: security teams should assume that agent input may be hostile and design the surrounding system so that a wrong decision cannot become a broad compromise. The harder work is deciding which permissions an agent genuinely needs, how those permissions expire, and who reviews the actions taken under them.

#9947. Wire It, Run It, Deploy It: AI Workflows in Gradio

Most interesting AI apps are pipelines. You generate an image, then cut out its background if you want to, or edit it into something new. You write a script, then generate a voice for it, or swap the voice while keeping the script the same. We usually wire these steps together in Python, and the moment something looks off we go back to print-debugging to find which step produced the odd value.

gr.Workflow, built right into Gradio, makes the pipeline the interface. You describe your steps as a graph of typed nodes, and Gradio serves a drag-and-drop canvas where every node is runnable and every intermediate result is visible. The same graph is also a REST API and a one-command deploy to Hugging Face Spaces.

The best way to get the idea is to see a few workflows in action. Every app below is a live Huggingface Space you can open, run, and duplicate.

Upload an image, type an edit ("turn it into a snowy winter scene", "add sunglasses", "make the car red"), and get the edited photo back. The whole app is a single node calling Qwen-Image-Edit on Hugging Face Inference Providers.

One graph, three pipelines. Start with a prompt and generate an image with FLUX, then pass it to a background-removal Gradio Space to turn it into a sticker. A topic becomes a voiceover through a text-to-speech Gradio Space, while the same topic becomes a catchy episode title through an LLM call.

That’s one canvas, two model calls through Hugging Face Inference Providers, and two calls to Gradio Spaces.

Since this is a workflow, each of the three outputs also gets its own REST endpoint: /sticker, /voiceover, and /episode_title. You can call any of them directly from code without opening the UI. See Call it from code below for a runnable example.

Type in one idea, and it turns into a set of generated artwork all at once: a base image from FLUX, two AI re-imaginings of that image (a soft watercolor version and a neon cyberpunk take), and a gallery title written by an LLM.

Each image is generated directly from the prompt by a model node using Inference Providers, while the title comes from an fn node that calls an LLM. This is the fan-out pattern in action: one idea can feed multiple operators simultaneously, all generating in parallel.

Type in a Hugging Face dataset ID, such as stanfordnlp/imdb or mteb/tweet_sentiment_extraction, and a single input fans out to four operator nodes that analyze the dataset live using the Datasets Server API.

You get an overview card, a preview of the first few rows, per-column statistics, and a distribution chart, all computed independently and in parallel. That’s the power of workflows!

Every node so far reaches out to Hugging Face. But an fn node is just Python, which means it can also run a model inside the Space on a GPU.

Decorate the bound function with @spaces.GPU and, when the node runs, ZeroGPU grabs a GPU for that call, runs the model, and releases it. We don't always need to rely on Inference Providers or existing Gradio Spaces.

Check out this demo that animates a still image using Lightricks/LTX-Video loaded through Diffusers, running entirely through one node. gr.Workflow doesn't need to know anything about your GPU setup. It simply calls the bound function.

Every workflow is a graph with three kinds of nodes: references (your inputs), operators (the steps that do work), and subjects (your outputs). An operator can be your own Python function, a model on Hugging Face Inference Providers, another Gradio Space, or a row from a Hub dataset. You connect them by dragging between typed ports, hit Run, and watch each result appear in place.

Every workflow you build is also an API, with no extra work. Each output becomes a REST endpoint named after its label, and you can call it from Python with the Gradio client. Here is a live, no-token example against the multi-endpoint demo Space, exactly as-is:

Endpoints that call a model or a Space run under a Hugging Face token, so pass one when you create the client:

Prefer plain HTTP? Every endpoint is reachable over curl too:

The fastest way in is to open any demo above, click Duplicate, and start rewiring. From Python, it is as short as:

For the full walkthrough, the operator kinds, the JSON schema, and reusable patterns, see the official gr.Workflow guide in the Gradio docs.

You can even build something as involved as AUTOMATIC1111 with gr.Workflow. Keep an eye out for our next post, where we walk through building it step by step. Here is a sneak peek 😉👇
