#9866. My Claude Code Workflow: Lessons From Rebuilding a Website in Two Days

Hi there! 👋🏻 I'm a Senior Full-Stack Developer oriented on Javascript.

Hi there! 👋🏻 I'm a Senior Full-Stack Developer oriented on Javascript.

Hi there! 👋🏻 I'm a Senior Full-Stack Developer oriented on Javascript.

I shipped 32,784 lines of code in two days with Claude Code. I put that number in a LinkedIn post, and the first thing I wrote right after it was that lines of code is a weak metric. I meant it. The number is the least useful fact about the project, and this post is about the facts that matter more.

Here is what the two days covered: a full rebuild of this site on Next.js 16, 228 blog posts rewritten against real keyword data, 543 tests passing, and zero broken URLs. Two years ago a project like that would have taken me weeks. This time the typing was not the slow part. Neither was the writing.

The slow part was deciding what to build, and what to leave out. That is the real Claude Code workflow lesson, and it is the one I want to spend most of this post on.

With Claude Code, the cost of producing code dropped close to zero for me. The cost of deciding which code should exist did not move. That is the whole shift in one sentence.

In practice it meant my days looked different. Less time typing and debugging syntax. More time writing down constraints, reading diffs, saying no to features, and checking that the output matched what I actually wanted. I spent most of the two days acting as a reviewer and an editor, with the agent as a very fast and very literal builder.

If you only take three things from this post:

Here is the honest breakdown of what the work was, because "32,784 lines" tells you nothing.

A full rebuild on Next.js 16. The site started as an Astro project in December 2025. The new version runs on Next.js 16 with Cache Components, a light redesign, a shared breadcrumb component, new icons, and a rewritten set of main pages. Nearly every route had to be rebuilt, and every route that the old site served had to keep working.

228 posts rewritten against keyword data. The blog is the part of the site that earns search traffic, so each post's title, meta description, headings and intro got reworked against real query data instead of my gut. More on that below.

543 tests passing. The repo has tests for the metadata rules, the structured data, the sitemap, the llms.txt output, the tag pages, the proxy, the markdown negotiation and a lot more. They are what let me merge quickly without holding my breath.

Zero broken URLs. This one sounds boring and it was the hardest requirement. Every URL the live site serves has to keep returning a 200 with real content. Indexed pages are the asset. A pretty redesign that 404s half of them is a net loss.

All of that landed in roughly 100 commits and 11 merged pull requests. The first commit was late on October 21 and the last one was the morning of October 23.

Lines of code has been a bad measure of developer output for a long time. DX's write-up on the metric makes the old argument well: teams end up optimizing the number instead of the outcome. AI makes the problem worse, because generating lines is now nearly free. InfoWorld made a related point in its piece on AI agents and bad productivity metrics: the real bottleneck has moved to validation and integration, not writing.

My own number is a good example of why. Some of those 32,784 lines are:

That last category is the interesting one, and I will get to it. The point is that if I had been measured on lines, deleting code would have counted against me, and deleting code was one of the best decisions of the project.

The same gap shows up in the research. In the METR study I wrote about in the AI productivity paradox, experienced developers using AI tools took 19 percent longer on their own repositories while believing they were faster. Output feels like progress. It often is not. I did not escape that trap by being smarter. I escaped it by measuring things that are hard to fake.

I am not going to pretend there is a magic prompt. By "workflow" I mean my working habits, not Anthropic's dynamic workflows feature. What worked was a handful of Claude Code best practices, and most of them are about the work around the agent, not the agent itself. If you are new to the tool, start with my Claude Code tutorial and come back.

The most expensive mistakes with an agent are the ones where it does exactly what you asked and breaks something you never mentioned.

For this rebuild the constraints were mostly negative. Do not break any URL the live site serves. Keep the heading wrap on the homepage and page titles stable. Never use certain phrases in titles or metadata. Keep the page metadata rules enforced by tests. I kept them in the instructions and notes the agent reads at the start of a session, and I added to them every time I caught a violation.

This is the practical core of context engineering. The agent is only as good as what is in its context. A constraint that lives in my head does not exist as far as the agent is concerned.

When you generate code this fast, you cannot read every line with the same care. You need something that reads it for you.

Tests do that. The page metadata test fails if a title or description breaks the rules I agreed on. The structured data tests fail if the JSON-LD changes shape. The sitemap test fails if a route disappears. None of these are clever. They are cheap to write, and each one turns a rule I would otherwise have to remember into a failing build.

The rule I follow: when I catch the agent breaking something, I do not just fix it. I add the test that would have caught it, and then the next session cannot make the same mistake silently.

The 100 commits and 11 merged PRs were not an accident. Big diffs are where bugs hide, and an agent can produce a big diff in minutes. If I let one session run for hours and then opened a single pull request, I would be approving code I had not understood.

So I merged in slices: the redesign, the copy audits, the routing fixes, the review follow-ups. After one batch I ran a review pass and fixed the findings before moving on. This is the same problem I covered in AI code review is the new bottleneck. Generation speed is not the constraint. Your ability to review is, so size the work to fit it.

A lot of the project was a loop: have the agent audit the site against a checklist, read the findings, decide which ones are real, fix those, and run the audit again. Copy audits, metadata audits, project page audits.

The decision step is the important one. The audit produces a list, and agents are good at producing lists. They are not good at knowing which items are worth your time. If you accept everything an audit says, you have outsourced the judgment, not the typing.

Subagents and parallel sessions pay off when the tasks do not touch the same files. Rewriting the copy on one page and fixing the sitemap logic are separable. Changing the layout and the metadata helper at the same time is not. If you want the mechanics, I wrote guides on subagents and hooks. The catch is that parallelism multiplies your review load, so only split work when the review stays easy.

Here is the story I mentioned. On the morning of October 23 I had a public JSON API on the site. Posts, projects, an OpenAPI spec, the works. Hours earlier I had spent a commit versioning it under /api/v1 and adding deprecation headers to the old paths. It was clean, documented and tested.

The reason is in the commit message: the site is a portfolio, and the API added no SEO value and no value for AI discovery, while generating about 500 extra static pages. Agents that want to read the site are already served by llms.txt and Markdown content negotiation. Removing the API took the static page count from 1,093 down to 596.

Think about what that means. Claude Code built the versioning, the headers, the serializers and the tests in a very short time. It was easy. It was also pointless. The agent had no way to tell me that, because the question "should this exist?" is not a coding question. It is a product question, and it depends on what the site is for.

That is the pattern I keep seeing. When building was expensive, the cost forced a filter. You only built what you were sure about, because you could not afford otherwise. When building is nearly free, the filter is gone, and it is easy to ship a lot of well-made things nobody needs. Other people are noticing the same shift. A common theme across recent writing on this is that the question has moved from "can I build this?" to "should I build this?". I came to the same conclusion by deleting my own work.

If you are curious about the same dynamic at the startup level, my post on why AI wrapper startups are failing covers the market version of it. Cheap building makes weak ideas more visible, not less.

The 228-post rewrite is where I let data make the decisions I would normally make by feel.

I pulled keyword data from DataForSEO: volumes, difficulty scores, live search results and which domains were ranking. The whole research run was 313 API calls and cost $4.37. For that I got a map of which queries the blog could realistically win and which ones were a waste of time.

This is also where taste came in. The data showed one phrase with about 720 searches a month that fit my situation. I decided not to use it anywhere on the site, because I did not like how it sounded. A tool that optimizes only for volume would have used it. That decision cost me a bit of traffic and I would make it again.

The agent can run the analysis, cluster the posts and draft the rewrites. It cannot tell me which version of myself I want the site to present. That part is mine.

I do not want this to read like a victory lap, so here is what went wrong.

It broke URLs I told it to protect. Early in the rebuild, the new design did not need the paginated blog pages or a few hidden project pages. So the agent redirected the pagination and turned the hidden projects into 404s. From a design point of view that made sense. From an SEO point of view it was wrong, because both sets of pages are indexed on the live site. I caught it, and the fix became a commit titled "Keep every URL main serves." It became a standing rule, and I checked the old sitemap against the new routes after every routing change.

It followed its own logic over my intent. The agent kept optimizing for the cleanest structure. I kept needing the structure that preserved what already worked. Those are different goals, and it only knew about one until I wrote the other down.

A passing build is not proof the page is right. Compiling and passing tests tells you the code is consistent with itself. Only a person looking at the page can tell you it says the right thing.

None of these were disasters, because I had tests and small merges to catch them. That is the argument for the workflow above: it is not there to make the agent better, it is there to make its mistakes cheap.

I have eight years of engineering behind me, and for most of that time I treated execution as the hard part. Knowing how to build the thing, and having the stamina to build it, was the scarce resource. Nobody asked whether I should build it, because the building itself was the filter.

That has flipped for me. Execution is no longer the hard part. These days the hard parts are:

Judgment. Which problem is worth solving, and which one to skip. The JSON API is the perfect example. I could have built ten more things like it in the same two days.

Taste. Knowing when something is good enough, when copy sounds like a person and when it sounds like a template, when a page feels right. An agent will produce competent output forever. Competent is the problem.

Distribution. Shipping a rebuilt site does not mean anyone reads it. When everyone can build quickly, the people who get found are the ones who thought about where their audience is. A big part of this rebuild was making sure search engines and AI tools could read the site properly, which is why llms.txt and the keyword work got real attention. I looked at whether that file actually helps in does llms.txt work for AI visibility.

The honest caveat is that this does not make engineering skill irrelevant. It is the opposite. I could only trust the output because I know what good looks like. I could write useful constraints because I understood what could break. I could review a diff quickly because I have read thousands of them. Agentic coding rewards experience, because the job moves from typing to directing and verifying, and both of those need judgment you have to earn some other way.

If you are earlier in your career, that is worth thinking about carefully. The skills that matter most are the ones the tool cannot give you: reading code critically, understanding systems, and developing opinions about what to build.

Can Claude Code rebuild a whole website? Yes. The rebuild described here is evidence. But "can" is not "should unsupervised." It rebuilt the structure quickly and also broke indexed URLs and built features that I deleted. Treat it as a fast builder that needs constraints and a reviewer.

How good is Claude Code at making websites? Very good at the structure, components, routing and tests, as this Next.js 16 rebuild showed. Weaker at the parts that depend on context it cannot see: which URLs are indexed, what the site is for, what sounds like you. Those are the parts you have to supply.

What is the best workflow in Claude Code? There is no single best one, but the pattern that held up for me was constraints first, tests as the contract, small merges, and a human decision on every audit finding. The checklist is in the workflow section above.

What is the biggest bottleneck in AI coding? It depends on the team. For a lot of teams it is review, as I covered in AI code review is the new bottleneck. For a solo builder like me, it moved one step earlier: deciding what is worth building at all.

How long does it take to rebuild a website with Claude Code? For this project, about two days from the first to the last commit, with a lot of review in between. That is far shorter than it would have taken me alone, but a good chunk of the time was decisions and checks, not generation. The time you save is the typing. The time you still need is the thinking.

Is lines of code a good metric for AI coding? No. It was a weak metric before AI and it is worse now, because generating lines costs almost nothing. Track outcomes: working tests, intact URLs, less surface area, decisions you can explain.

What is the most important Claude Code habit? Writing constraints down where the agent reads them. Most of the failures I hit were the agent doing something reasonable that I had never ruled out.

Do you still need to know how to code? Yes, probably more than before. You are reviewing at speed, so you need to recognize bad code, fragile design and silent regressions quickly.

If I ran this project again, I would change three things.

I would write the URL-preservation test on day one instead of discovering the need for it mid-project. A script that diffs the old sitemap against the new routes would have caught the pagination and hidden-project problem immediately.

I would decide earlier what the site is for. The JSON API existed because I never wrote down the purpose of the site clearly enough to rule it out. A one-paragraph statement of purpose at the top of the instructions file would have saved a day of building.

I would spend even less time on code and more on the two things the tool cannot do for me: choosing what to publish and getting it in front of people.

That was the question at the end of my LinkedIn post, and I mean it as a real one. If you build software, try this: pick your last three projects and write down where the time went. Not the hours on the calendar, the actual friction. Was it typing, debugging, reviewing, waiting, deciding, or promoting?

For most of my career, my answer was typing and debugging. Now it is deciding and distributing. Yours might be different, and the answer should change what you practice.

If you have a product that needs this kind of rebuild, or you want a second opinion on what to build before you build it, tell me what you are working on. I will give you an honest read, and sometimes the honest read is that you should skip the feature.

Sources: DX on lines of code, InfoWorld on AI agents and productivity metrics. Project numbers come from this site's git history and DataForSEO usage log, checked October 23, 2026.

#9865. Germany Busts 'Crime-as-a-Service' Investment Fraud Outfit

Authorities seized more than 100 servers and arrested seven as part of a crackdown on a fraud network spanning more than 50 countries.

You see an online advertisement promising quick returns from trading cryptocurrency, foreign currencies, and stocks. You give the "investment firm" your information, and an operator calls you and convinces you to transfer a small amount of money into a platform. You make early profits quick, so you deposit increasingly large sums of money. But when you attempt to withdraw your earnings, the operator stalls for a while until finally cutting off contact.

This pattern is familiar to victims of investment fraud, a multinational criminal industry that relies on social engineering to convince would-be-investors that they're about to make substantial gains before pulling the rug out from under them.

Europol today shared news of the disruption of one such operation, an investment fraud scheme with potential victims across more than 50 countries and a company allegedly supplying fraudulent trading platforms and leads to criminal groups. According to a press release, Europol and Eurojust supported an international operation involving authorities in Albania, Cyprus, Finland, Germany, Israel, Kosovo, and North Macedonia.

Related:Investors Dish on New Startups & What They'd Back Next

The German Itzehoe Public Prosecutor's Office led the operation, targeting a company suspected of supplying phony trading websites and multiple call centers to criminal groups; investigators estimate losses to exceed 4 million euros.

International authorities searched 17 locations, including a call center in Kosovo, leading to the seizure of 100 servers and the arrests of seven suspects.

The law enforcement action reflects a multiyear investigation that began in 2022, according to Europol, when a German couple reported they could not withdraw money invested through an online trading platform. This led to two previous "action days" by authorities, one in 2022 (involving two arrests and the seizure of evidence) and another in 2025 (involving more arrests and seizures of money and evidence).

"Analysis of the material recovered exposed the suspected infrastructure provider and its links to call centre operators, paving the way for the latest operation," the press release read.

A Eurojust press release provided further detail regarding the extent of the operation. The analysis of evidence seized during the second action day exposed a company based in Cyprus and Israel allegedly offering "crime-as-a-service," supplying criminal groups with fraudulent websites that funnel targets into the central investment scam.

The data of potential victims visiting these websites and expressing interest would be sold as leads to call centers, which contacted the victims to persuade them to invest their money, leading to repeated demands for additional investments. Authorities identified suspected call center-operating clients of this company in Albania, Kosovo, and North Macedonia.

Related:Behind the Scenes of How Operation Blackout Went Down

The fraud operation guaranteed singificant returns for trades in cryptocurrencies, foreign currencies, or stocks, according to Europol. But authorities found that the seemingly legitimate platforms were run by "brokers" that used phony profits and social engineering tactics to convince victims to keep investing. Additionally, investigators also found the operators used affiliate marketing services and deceptive advertisements to lure in potential victims.

Austin Anderson, director of threat intel at cybercrime disruption firm Netcraft, tells Dark Reading that operations like these that target upstream providers can help disrupt investment fraud operations at scale.

"Fraudsters have increasingly specialized in one piece of an attack's supply chain, as seen in this scheme where websites collected personal data that was sold to call centers to ultimately coerce funds from victims," he says. "While this can breed sophistication in each actor's niche, it also introduces fragility when a large dependency like the call center is disrupted. Ultimately, without arrests that remove fraudsters from the market, these operations only temporarily disrupt operations while actors rebuild their infrastructure."

#9864. Introducing Falcon ASR

Arabic WER: 20.92% · Parameters: 1.6B · Emirati WER (TII evaluation): 22.73%

We’re introducing Falcon-ASR, our 1.6 billion parameter speech recognition model for Arabic, with a particular focus on the Emirati dialect. Developed at the Technology Innovation Institute (TII) in Abu Dhabi, it also supports English, French, Spanish and Portuguese.

In our evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved an average word error rate of 20.92% across six Arabic test sets, compared with the best published result of 23.17% in the leaderboard snapshot we used. On our internal Emirati evaluation, it recorded the lowest word and character error rates among the systems we compared.

We also support word-level timestamps for transcriptions, linking each transcribed word to its position in the audio.

Arabic speech varies by region, speaker and setting. A model that handles a formal news broadcast may still struggle with a conversation in Emirati or with speech recorded over a phone line. Dialectal Arabic also has fewer transcribed resources than Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), which makes training and evaluation harder.

We trained Falcon-ASR on Emirati, MSA, other Gulf and Arabic dialects, and English. Our aim is to transcribe the words people use in everyday speech, including dialectal forms and changes between languages.

The Open Universal Arabic ASR Leaderboard, maintained by the ELM Research Center, ranks systems by the equal-weight average WER across six test sets. It also reports character error rate (CER). Lower values are better for both metrics. Our Falcon-ASR evaluation follows this protocol.

WER = Word Error Rate; CER = Character Error Rate. A lower value indicates better performance.

We evaluated Falcon-ASR on the same six benchmarks using the leaderboard’s pinned manifests. Competitor figures are the published leaderboard averages checked on 30 September 2026. Falcon-ASR’s average WER is 2.25 percentage points better than the best published result in that snapshot.

Public evaluation data already includes Emirati: Casablanca has a UAE subset. We complement that coverage with an internal evaluation of additional Emirati and Gulf speech, using held-out recordings and human-validated transcripts to assess transcription accuracy beyond the public UAE subset.

In our internal Emirati evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved 22.73% WER and 10.19% CER:

Falcon-ASR has the lowest WER and CER among the systems compared here. Its WER is 4.07 percentage points below Qwen3-Omni, the next best result. The results show improved transcription accuracy at both the word and character level on this evaluation.

We included background noise, overlapping speech, music, room reverberation and telephony effects, as well as variations in speed and pitch. We applied the same treatment to Emirati recordings, exposing the model to a range of conditions it may encounter in meetings, calls and other everyday recordings.

Falcon-ASR also transcribes English with the same model weights. In our evaluation on the seven public English test sets used by the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard, it achieved a mean WER of 5.74%.

The model also supports French, Spanish and Portuguese. All five languages use the same weights, without requiring a language flag. The output is a transcript in the language spoken.

Falcon-ASR builds on our Falcon3-Audio work. The architecture and training approach for Falcon3-Audio are described in Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data.

Our Hugging Face Demo Space lets you try Falcon-ASR and explore its transcription capabilities. API access and native applications are planned. We invite you to try the Demo with your own recordings.

We thank the team behind the Falcon-Emirati model for their support with Arabic foundation models. Read about their latest work in the Falcon-Emirati blog post.

We also extend our sincere thanks to Mikhail Lubinets for continued support with the compute infrastructure.

نقدّم Falcon-ASR، نموذجنا للتعرف على الكلام العربي بحجم 1.6 مليار معلمة، مع اهتمام خاص باللهجة الإماراتية. طوّرنا النموذج في معهد الابتكار التكنولوجي (TII) في أبوظبي، وهو يدعم أيضًا اللغات الإنجليزية والفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية.

في تقييمنا، حقق Falcon-ASR متوسط معدل خطأ في الكلمات بلغ 20.92% عبر ست مجموعات اختبار باللغة العربية، مقارنةً بأفضل نتيجة منشورة بلغت 23.17% في نسخة لوحة المتصدرين التي استخدمناها. وفي تقييمنا الداخلي للهجة الإماراتية، سجّل النموذج أدنى معدلات خطأ في الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة التي قارناها.

ندعم أيضاً الطوابع الزمنية على مستوى الكلمات في عمليات التفريغ النصي، بحيث ترتبط كل كلمة بموضعها في التسجيل الصوتي.

يختلف الكلام العربي باختلاف المنطقة والمتحدث وظروف التسجيل. فقد ينجح نموذج في تفريغ نشرة إخبارية رسمية، ثم يجد صعوبة في تفريغ محادثة باللهجة الإماراتية أو تسجيل عبر الهاتف. كما أن الموارد الصوتية المفرّغة نصيًا للهجات العربية أقل من تلك المتاحة للعربية الفصحى، مما يزيد صعوبة التدريب والتقييم.

درّبنا Falcon-ASR على اللهجة الإماراتية والعربية الفصحى ولهجات خليجية وعربية أخرى، إلى جانب الإنجليزية. وهدفنا هو تفريغ الكلمات التي يستخدمها الناس في حديثهم اليومي، بما في ذلك الصيغ اللهجية والانتقال بين اللغات.

ترتّب لوحة المتصدرين المفتوحة الشاملة للتعرف على الكلام العربي، التي يديرها مركز ELM للأبحاث، الأنظمة وفق متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات عبر ست مجموعات اختبار، بوزن متساوٍ لكل مجموعة. وتعرض أيضًا معدل خطأ الأحرف (CER). وكلما انخفضت قيمة أي من المقياسين، كان الأداء أفضل. ويتبع تقييمنا للنموذج هذا البروتوكول.

WER هو معدل خطأ الكلمات؛ وCER هو معدل خطأ الأحرف. تشير القيمة الأقل إلى أداء أفضل.

قيّمنا Falcon-ASR على مجموعات الاختبار الست نفسها، باستخدام قوائم العينات المثبّتة في لوحة المتصدرين. وأرقام النماذج المنافسة هي المتوسطات المنشورة في اللوحة، والتي جرى التحقق منها في 30 سبتمبر 2026. وكان متوسط خطأ الكلمات للنموذج أفضل بمقدار 2.25 نقطة مئوية من أفضل نتيجة منشورة في تلك النسخة.

تتوافر بالفعل بيانات عامة لتقييم اللهجة الإماراتية، إذ تضم مجموعة Casablanca قسمًا خاصًا بالإمارات. ونكمّل هذه التغطية بتقييم داخلي لتسجيلات إضافية من الكلام الإماراتي والخليجي، باستخدام تسجيلات مخصّصة للاختبار ونصوص مرجعية خضعت لمراجعة بشرية، لتقييم دقة التفريغ على مواد إضافية إلى جانب البيانات الإماراتية العامة.

حقق Falcon-ASR في تقييمنا الإماراتي الداخلي معدل خطأ كلمات قدره 22.73٪ ومعدل خطأ أحرف قدره 10.19٪:

سجّل Falcon-ASR أقل معدل لخطأ الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة المقارَنة هنا. وكان معدل خطأ الكلمات أقل بمقدار 4.07 نقطة مئوية من Qwen3-Omni، صاحب النتيجة التالية. وتُظهر النتائج تحسنًا في دقة التفريغ على مستوى الكلمات والأحرف في هذا التقييم.

ضمّنا بيانات التدريب ضوضاء خلفية وكلامًا متداخلًا وموسيقى وصدى الصوت وتأثيرات الاتصالات الهاتفية، إلى جانب تغيّرات في سرعة الكلام وحدّة الصوت. وطبّقنا المعالجة نفسها على التسجيلات الإماراتية، لتهيئة النموذج للتعامل مع ظروف مختلفة قد يواجهها في الاجتماعات والمكالمات والتسجيلات اليومية الأخرى.

يفرّغ Falcon-ASR الكلام الإنجليزي باستخدام أوزان النموذج نفسها. وفي تقييمنا على مجموعات الاختبار الإنجليزية العامة السبع المستخدمة في لوحة Hugging Face المفتوحة للتعرف على الكلام، بلغ متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات 5.74٪.

يدعم النموذج أيضًا الفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية. وتستخدم اللغات الخمس أوزانًا واحدة، دون الحاجة إلى تحديد اللغة مسبقًا. ويكون الناتج تفريغًا نصيًا باللغة المنطوقة.

يستند Falcon-ASR إلى أعمالنا في Falcon3-Audio. وتعرض ورقة Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data بنية Falcon3-Audio ونهج تدريبه.

يتيح عرضنا التجريبي على Hugging Face تجربة Falcon-ASR واستكشاف قدراته في تفريغ الكلام. أما الوصول عبر واجهة API والتطبيقات الأصلية فهو مخطّط له. ندعوكم إلى تجربة النموذج باستخدام تسجيلاتكم.

نتوجّه بجزيل الشكر إلى الفريق القائم على تطوير نموذج Falcon-Emirati على دعمهم في مجال النماذج التأسيسية للغة العربية. ويمكن الاطّلاع على أحدث أعمال الفريق من خلال المقال المنشور حول Falcon-Emirati.

كما نتقدّم بخالص الشكر والتقدير إلى Mikhail Lubinets على دعمه المستمر للبنية التحتية الحاسوبية.

#9863. Fresh European Fridge Attacks Put Cold-Chain Security in Focus

Beyond food storage, the same combination of Internet connectivity, remote access, and inadequate security practices can put temperature-controlled infrastructure across other critical sectors at risk.

A second wave of attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems across Europe this week has heightened concerns about the broader "cold chain's" vulnerability to similar attacks, given that supermarkets aren't the only businesses that rely on cold storage.

As in mid-October, an unknown threat actor appears to have gained access to refrigeration controllers at multiple European supermarkets and switched the systems to defrost mode, raising temperatures to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit) and causing food spoilage.

Reporting by the BBC, Reuters, CNBC, and other outlets suggest the latest attacks were smaller in scope compared to the first wave in October that impacted more than 700 retail and grocery stores primarily in France. A smaller number of stores in Belgium, Germany, the Netherlands, Portugal, Poland and Spain were also caught up in the October attacks.

Related:Les supermarchés de l'UE paient d'un firmware de réfrigérateur non mis à jour

BBC reported the new attacks as impacting "dozens of supermarkets" in seven European countries including Belgium, Luxembourg, Estonia, Ireland, Sweden and Finland. Spokespersons from several supermarket chains like France's Carrefour, Belgium's Ahold Delhaize and Colruyt Group, and Sweden's Coop chains confirmed varying but relatively limited impacts from the new attacks.

In a Nov. 2 statement, Carrefour said a cyberattack targeting its refrigeration systems had impacted 15 out of 700 stores in Belgium. In an undated statement, US-based Copeland, which manufactures technologies for regulating commercial refrigeration systems, alluded to a cybersecurity incident affecting refrigeration systems in France, which it said related to a discontinued generation of supervisory controllers.

No individual or group has claimed responsibility for either the first or the second wave of attacks, and the motivation behind it remains a mystery. European authorities are currently investigating the attacks.

Researchers, including those at France's CERT, have linked the hacks so far to Internet-connected refrigeration controllers made by Denmark-based Danfoss, Italy-based Dixell, and Copeland. Organizations using these controllers often connect them to the Internet to enable remote maintenance and support, but in doing so also potentially expose them to unauthorized access and remote attack by threat actors.

Risks include unpatched vulnerabilities in these technologies that attackers can exploit, like three in Danfoss' AK-SM 800A controllers that researchers at Claroty disclosed this August and another two they reported the same month in Copeland controllers. Weak configurations and poor security hygiene are also other major problems.

Related:AI Takes Control of Robotic Arm in 16 Minutes Flat

"Misconfigurations and systemic hygiene failures represent the vast majority of the threat surface," says John Gallagher, vice president at operational technology (OT) and Internet of Things (IoT) security vendor Viakoo. "While unpatched vulnerabilities exist in older firmware, they are rendered dangerous only because basic architectural hygiene was skipped, especially [when] making them Internet-facing."

Common mistakes include widespread use of default passwords, vendor-shared service codes, or static credentials across hundreds of locations makes brute-forcing trivial, Gallagher adds.

The weaknesses are not confined to supermarket refrigeration systems. The same combination of Internet connectivity, remote access, and inadequate security practices can put temperature-controlled infrastructure across other critical sectors at risk, according to security experts.

Sean Tufts, field chief technology officer (CTO) at Claroty, points out that "pharmaceutical storage and distribution, food distribution centers, and industrial facilities all rely on connected operational technology to maintain precise environmental conditions."

Related:EU Grocers Pay a Steep Price for Unpatched Fridge Firmware

The level of exposure will vary depending on how these systems are deployed, connected, and secured. But many organizations that rely on remotely accessible refrigeration or temperature-control equipment face similar challenges around asset visibility, third-party access, and securing legacy systems, Tufts says. "The same types of weaknesses can exist across different industries, even if the equipment and operational requirements differ."

The potential consequences of a compromise, says Tufts, can vary by sector.

"A disruption to pharmaceutical storage could compromise temperature-sensitive medicines, while an incident affecting food distribution could lead to spoilage and supply chain disruptions," he notes. "Industrial environments may face additional operational consequences depending on the materials and processes involved."

The supermarket attacks are a reminder that refrigeration and temperature-control systems are part of essential operations and not just back-of-house equipment, Tufts adds. Organizations should identify these assets and know how they connect to the Internet and third parties.

"Where remote access is necessary, use a VPN, strong authentication, or a centralized secure-access tool with session tracking." Changing default passwords, keeping firmware current, and segmenting are also recommended security practices, he says.

Gallagher says that while it's unclear how the attacks on the commercial refrigeration systems played out, the most straightforward theory is the threat actor likely compiled a target list by scanning the public Internet for specific controller fingerprints, such as those tied to Danfoss, Dixell, and Copeland. They then likely deployed an automated script across that target list to exploit known web vulnerabilities or push default credentials, triggering the defrost mode simultaneously.

Gallagher says the same attacks that worked on commercial refrigeration systems can potentially work across almost any form of OT and IoT systems. That's because these systems often are managed outside of IT, lack automated controls to keep firmware and passwords updated, and have porous network borders. "The growth over the last three years in operational ransomware and in cyberattacks causing physical damage shows that these attacks are on the rise and not specific to any one kind of system."

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#9862. Why Semantic Similarity Can Give AI the Exact Opposite Answer

Jason Lau, founder of SophiArch. 20+ years in software engineering before moving into teaching applied ML, LLM apps, and data science.

Jason Lau, founder of SophiArch. 20+ years in software engineering before moving into teaching applied ML, LLM apps, and data science.

Jason Lau, founder of SophiArch. 20+ years in software engineering before moving into teaching applied ML, LLM apps, and data science.

TL;DR: An embedding's similarity score measures how much two texts share in topic and wording, and a negation is a one-word edit. I wrote 40 invented policy facts and tested six open embedding models. On every model, "Which plan doesn't cover X?" scored closer to "Which plan covers X?" than a plain rewording of the same question did, for 77.5–100% of the items. At a common semantic-cache cut-off (similarity 0.90, RedisVL's default), one model would serve the cached answer to 97.5% of the opposite questions and to 7.5% of the genuine rewordings. In retrieval, models found the "covered" chunk almost every time and the "not covered" chunk between 27.5% and 92.5% of the time. Adding BM25 through rank fusion made five of the six worse. Dropping English stop words, which removes "not", took BM25 to a coin flip. Re-ranking the top ten with a small cross-encoder took every model to 97.5% or better on the negated questions. Run the same test on your own model before you trust a similarity threshold.

A benefits assistant had a semantic cache in front of it, so repeated questions skipped the LLM. On Monday someone asked "Which plan covers dental implants?" and got the right answer: the Gold plan. On Tuesday someone else asked "Which plan doesn't cover dental implants?"

The cache embedded the new question, found Monday's at similarity 0.97, and returned "The Gold plan." That's the opposite of the right answer, delivered in a fraction of a second with no LLM call to blame. Someone asking "What plan pays for dental implants?", which means exactly the same as Monday's question, would have scored 0.85 and missed the cache.

The assistant is invented. The two numbers aren't: they're what all-MiniLM-L6-v2, the most downloaded sentence-similarity model on Hugging Face (about 200 million downloads a month in October 2026), gives for those three questions. The rest of this article is what happened when I ran the same comparison across six models, three tests and 40 facts.

Embedding models are trained to put texts that go together (a question and its answer, a title and its abstract, two captions of one picture) close together. Texts that go together share a topic and, usually, a lot of words. So the model learns a geometry where shared topic and shared wording count for most of the distance, and nothing in training forces a single "not" to move a sentence to the other side of the space.

From the vector's point of view, "Which plan doesn't cover dental implants?" is the original question with one word added. "What plan pays for dental implants?" swaps two words and adds a third. The negation is the smaller edit, so it lands closer.

This isn't new. NevIR (Weller, Lawrie and Van Durme, EACL 2024) built document pairs that differ only by negation and found most retrieval models, including state-of-the-art ones, "performing the same or worse than a random ranking", with cross-encoders doing best. Cao (ECAI 2025) tested general-purpose text embeddings and reported "a significant lack of negation awareness in these models". A June 2026 preprint on agent memory (Yadav, arXiv 2606.26511) reported that cosine similarity separated contradicted facts from duplicates with an AUROC of 0.59, close to chance, and gave the same reason: contradictions came out more similar to the original than duplicates did "because a value-flip is a smaller edit than a genuine rephrasing of the same fact." That result is small (98 labelled pairs, one embedding model), so I wanted to see how far it generalised. An August 2026 audit of similarity thresholds in agent frameworks (Frias, arXiv 2608.10216) is the closest to what follows: a production drift guard "caught 0 of 56 meaning-breaking mutations", including "withhold the study drug" → "administer the study drug", which "came in at cosine 0.9608".

I wrote 40 short policy facts across twelve domains: dental and health plans, home, travel and car insurance, refunds, software tiers and licences, staff benefits, airline fares, warranties, bank accounts, gym memberships and drug formularies. Each fact has three forms:

The contradictions use several kinds of negation on purpose: "does not", "isn't", "excludes", "no", "never", "unpaid", "non-refundable". Each fact also has three questions: one asking which entity covers it, a rewording of that question, and the opposite question ("Which plan doesn't cover dental implants?"). Most opposite questions carry a negation word, but a few flip the meaning without one: "Which tier limits data exports?", "Who gets unpaid parental leave?", and "Which account charges foreign transaction fees?", where it's the original that says "no".

The six models are all open and run locally: all-MiniLM-L6-v2, bge-base-en-v1.5, e5-base-v2, gte-base, mxbai-embed-large-v1 and Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, each with the query and passage prefixes its model card asks for. I didn't test hosted embedding APIs, which is the main reason to run the check below on whatever you use.

For each of the 40 items: how similar is the original question to its rewording, and to its opposite?

The last two columns use 0.90, which is what RedisVL's SemanticCache defaults to (a cosine distance of 0.1). That's RedisVL's threshold applied to these six models, not RedisVL's own default embedding model, which I didn't test. On every model, a cache at that setting answers the opposite question more often than it answers the same question asked differently.

You can't tune your way out of it. Set the threshold low enough to catch 95% of genuine rewordings on each model, and it catches all 40 opposites, on all six. As a separation score, similarity managed an AUROC between 0.01 and 0.25, where 0.5 is chance. A number that low means the score is reliably backwards: higher similarity was evidence that the question meant the opposite.

The same comparison between the fact, its rewording and its contradiction. This is what a deduplication step or a memory store faces when it decides whether a new fact is "the same" as one it already has.

This one is mixed, and it's worth saying so. Three models separate statements well, and mxbai separates them almost perfectly. Three don't: MiniLM, e5 and Qwen3 sit near chance, so "X is not covered" is as likely as a rewording to look like a duplicate of "X is covered". The models that cope with statements still failed the question test. Part of that is my data: the question rewordings change more words than the statement rewordings do, and on every model the rewordings score lower for questions. That's also how people actually ask questions, so I don't think it makes the question result less real. The safe conclusion isn't "embeddings can't do negation". It's that it depends on the model and the text shape, and you can't know which case you're in without measuring.

The cache and deduplication cases compare two texts directly. Retrieval is subtler, because the query and the chunk aren't phrased alike. So I built an index where every item contributes two chunks about different entities: "The Gold plan covers dental implants" and "The Silver plan does not cover dental implants". Then I asked both questions. "Which plan covers dental implants?" should rank Gold's chunk above Silver's, and "Which plan doesn't cover dental implants?" should do the reverse. All 80 chunks sit in the same index, so the other 39 items act as distractors.

Every dense model answered the positive questions well (90–100%). The negated questions are where they split:

Dense top 10, re-ranked: ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2

Dense top 10, re-ranked: bge-reranker-base

Share of the 40 opposite questions ("doesn't", "excludes", "no", "unpaid", "limits" and so on) where the right chunk ranked above its opposite. A coin flip scores 50%.

The MiniLM row is worth a second look. Counting an item as right only when both its questions came out right, the way NevIR scores it, MiniLM got 17.5%. Guessing at random would get 25%.

The standard advice for negation is hybrid retrieval: the "not" is a keyword, so add BM25 and fuse the rankings. I believed that going in, and it's what the outline for this article said.

In this test, BM25 on its own got 77.5% of the negated questions right, which beats two of the dense models and ties a third. Fusing it with them using reciprocal rank fusion (Cormack, Clarke and Büttcher, 2009, k = 60) lowered the score for five of the six. Only MiniLM improved, from 27.5% to 32.5%. The reason is in the wording. The keyword arm only sees the negation when the question and the chunk use the same word. In 25 of the 40 items they did ("excludes" and "excludes", "does not" and "does not"), and BM25 got all 25 right. In the other 15 they didn't ("doesn't" against "not covered", "won't refund" against "non-refundable", "no API access" against "unavailable"), and BM25 got 6 right, which is below a coin flip. There it rewards whichever chunk shares more terms with the question, and that's often the wrong one. Rank fusion gives that vote the same weight as the dense model's.

There's a second trap underneath, and it's a configuration setting. Elasticsearch's english analyzer and its stop token filter both default to the _english_ stop list, which is Lucene's ENGLISH_STOP_WORDS_SET. That list contains "no" and "not". So the keyword that's supposed to rescue you is deleted before it reaches the index. My BM25 is a simple Python one (rank_bm25, lowercase word tokens, no stemming), not Elasticsearch itself, but I gave it the same stop list. With that list applied, it scored exactly 50% on the negated questions, a coin flip, and every hybrid score dropped further. (The standard analyzer keeps stop words by default. Check which one your text fields actually use.)

What worked was the slow, boring stage. A cross-encoder reads the question and the chunk together, so "doesn't" can change its answer in a way that two separately computed vectors can't. Re-ranking each dense model's top ten with ms-marco-MiniLM-L-6-v2, a 22-million-parameter model, took every row to 97.5% on the negated questions. bge-reranker-base took them all to 100%. The dense model you started with stopped mattering here, because the right chunk and its opposite were both in every top ten. The ordering inside it was the problem. That's an easy case: an 80-chunk index where the two rivals share most of their words. In a large index full of near-identical clauses, check that both make it into the candidates you re-rank. This matches NevIR's ranking, and it's why re-ranking gets a whole lesson of its own in SophiArch's Retrieval & RAG Systems course, two lessons after the one on hybrid retrieval: the two stages fix different failures.

The re-rankers aren't perfect, and both made a couple of mistakes in the other direction. bge-reranker-base put "The standard warranty excludes accidental drops" above "The extended warranty covers accidental drops" for "Which warranty covers accidental drops?". ms-marco-MiniLM missed "Which account offers no overdraft?" and "Who refunds return shipping costs?". e5 also missed the overdraft question, and the opposite of the shipping one ("Who doesn't refund return shipping costs?"). That's 2 misses in 80 questions for each re-ranker, against 3 for the best dense model (e5) and 33 for MiniLM. One caution from Frias's audit: swapping in an NLI model as the gate "did no better" there. A re-ranker trained for search relevance and an NLI classifier aren't the same tool, and short policy questions are an easy case. So re-run the triples with the re-ranker in the loop before you rely on it.

This takes a few minutes and needs no labelled data. Write 20 question triples from your own domain: a question, a rewording, and its opposite. Then run:

If the opposite wins most rows, and on every model I tried it did, then no similarity threshold on that model can tell a repeat question from its opposite. Use the same triples for statements if you deduplicate or merge facts.

The facts are invented, short and in English, and there are 40 of them. Real policy text is longer, and a longer chunk dilutes the negation further, so I'd expect statement-level separation to get worse, not better. The retrieval index has 80 chunks, so both rivals always reached the top ten. In a large index, recall into the re-ranker becomes a separate thing to measure. The BM25 numbers come from a simple Python implementation without stemming, not from an Elasticsearch analyzer, so treat them as a direction, not a figure for your cluster. I only tested open models; hosted embedding APIs may do better or worse, which is the point of running the triples yourself. And the rewordings change more words than the negations do. That's deliberate, because it's the comparison a cache faces in production (people reword freely, and a negation is one word), but it means the results describe how real questions differ, not a controlled single-word edit.

None of it means vector search is broken. It means a similarity score answers "are these about the same thing?" and gets used as if it answered "do these mean the same thing?". For dental implants, those are opposite answers.

How to Build Reliable LLM Classifiers With Confidence Thresholds

Jason Lau, founder of SophiArch. 20+ years in software engineering before moving into teaching applied ML, LLM apps, and data science.

#9861. The model that didn't exist, so you made it yourself

Last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1. The official one is a 9B model that needs about 20 GB of memory and thinks for thousands of tokens before writing a single paragraph. On the Hub, I found only compressed copies of that same 9B model. So I described what I wanted to ML Intern, and the next day I had a 0.8B version that runs on a CPU. It returns valid output 99.7% of the time and uses about a quarter of the teacher's tokens. The compute for the whole project, including having the 9B model label 8,797 example requests, came to USD 16.

Over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way. Each one started as a message in HuggingChat with ML-intern switched on, and each one ended as a public model on the Hub with its evaluation in the model card. ML-intern plans the work, asks me for a budget before it spends anything, runs a small test before the real job, then trains, evaluates and publishes on Hugging Face hardware.

The first message is where I spend my effort. My first prompt, for the citrus model shared below, was about 450 words. By my 6th project it was closer to 2,000, because each project taught me something I wanted in the next one. All seven prompts are on GitHub at yvrjsharma/ml-intern-prompts, exactly as I wrote them.

A prompt starts with the idea in one line and why I want it. Then it names the exact pieces: the dataset, the base model, the training script. Anything I have already checked goes under a heading that literally says "Verified facts, do not re-derive", so the agent spends its budget on the work instead of rediscovering what I know. For the camera-angle LoRA that section listed which trainer had just added transparent-image support, and which open GitHub issues made the fallback trainer risky.

Two lines in the prompt are critical. The first asks for a baseline before any training. For example, the citrus prompt says: "Also report the base model's zero-shot score on the same metric before training so we can see the gain." Without it you get a trained model and no idea whether it is better than what you started with. The second is a smoke test with a check attached. For the image LoRAs I asked for 50 training steps, then a check that the saved weights had actually changed, before paying for the full run.

At the end of the prompt, I lay out the expected deliverables and limit the cost. I define what belongs in the model card and include a instruction like: "Cap total spend at USD 12 and ask me before exceeding it." Because ML-intern begins every task with zero dollar budget and needs permission before executing paid jobs, this spending limit stays strictly enforced. When you leave out a budget, the agent suggests a couple of paths depending on project size and asks which one you prefer.

You don't necessarily need all of that on your first attempt. For example, I didn't have the verified-facts section in my citrus brief and ML Intern still produced a model that more than tripled the accuracy of the Qwen3.5-2B model. Let me walk you through 6 things I built with Ml-Intern in just a couple of days.

A general vision model can describe a yellowing citrus leaf. However, telling you whether it is a mite problem or a magnesium deficiency, and the bio and non-bio remedies to treat the plant is very hard. Using Claude, I put together a training dataset merged from three sources hosted by the Project-AgML organization on the Hub. The resulting citrus-disease-vlm-instruct is a dataset containing 3,017 annotated images across 21 distinct pests, illnesses, nutritional gaps, and treatment approaches. ML-intern handled the fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-2B using these examples, making sure to benchmark the foundation model beforehand.

On the 335 test photos, the base model named the right problem 14.9% of the time. After two epochs on one A10G, the fine-tuned model got 52.8%. Compute cost, about USD 1.90.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Citrus Doctor App

Image models know plenty of characters. Huggy, drawn in the flat style of the Hugging Face brand assets, was not one of them. I asked ML-Intern for a LoRA on FLUX.2 klein base 4B, trained on 84 captioned drawings from Chunte/huggy_for_training dataset.

The agent saved a checkpoint every 100 steps and drew the same set of prompts with each one, which made choosing easy. Step 200 was the first where Huggy was fully on-model. From step 500 on, Huggy's style started bleeding into prompts that had nothing to do with Huggy! The trained LoRA also works on the distilled klein model at 4 steps. Compute cost, about USD 7.60.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Huggy Generator App

ML-intern rendered 1,030 scanned household objects from Google Scanned Objects at 24 angles each, 24,722 transparent images, on a CPU job that cost a few cents. It later finalised 461 objects for training and 40 held out for testing, and 1,844 before-and-after training pairs spread evenly over 23 camera instructions.

Training ran 2,000 steps in about 90 minutes on one A100 (~USD 3.75). The whole project took about half a day and 48 jobs, counting the ones that failed on missing packages or wrong paths and had to be resubmitted by ML-Intern. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Viewpoint Orbit App

No dataset existed for this, so my prompt described how to make one. Start from a real photo in Open Images, remove one object with the LaMa inpainting model, and draw a scribble where the object used to be. The untouched photo is the target. ML-intern wrote and tested the pair-building scripts in a CPU sandbox, then ran them as GPU jobs, recording the author and license of every source photo along the way. It built 6,042 training pairs and a 160-pair test set, where 40 of the test pairs come from 23 object classes kept out of training entirely.

Before training, it measured the base model on its own and with the Viggle turbo LoRA, and checked that running edits in batches produced identical images, which made the evaluation cheaper. Training ran 2,000 steps in 1 hour 38 minutes on one A100 (~USD 4), and a comparison of the saved checkpoints on 48 test pairs picked step 500.

Paired with the Viggle turbo LoRA at 6 steps the LoRA performed really well. 67.5% of objects detected where they were drawn, at 4.7 seconds per edit. Objects from the 23 unseen classes landed as reliably as the rest (65.0% versus 64.2%). The project took a little over a day and 59 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 24.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Doodle-in App

Training the 0.8B and 2B students took 12 and 18 minutes on an A10G (USD 0.75 for both). The 0.8B also ships as an 812 MB GGUF file for running on a CPU. The project took about 11 hours and 24 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Pocket rewriter 0.8B Student · 2B Student · Dataset · Pocket Studio App · Compare the teacher-student in Rewriter Arena

It took two runs. The first cached 155,000 training images as latents, baked the guidance into the model, then cut the step count in stages from 16 to 8 to 4, all on A100s. The 4-step student beat the teacher run at the same 4 steps on GenEval and FID, after that ML-intern exported it to ONNX for the browser. This run took about 13 hours and USD 22.

I did a second training run by asking ML-Intern to improve the 4-step student a bit more. It then made 24,000 more image pairs with the teacher at 16 steps and fine-tuned the 4-step student against them for about an hour. GenEval went from 0.509 to 0.536, against the teacher's 0.563 at 50 steps, with just 4 steps (one-fourth the compute). ML-intern re-exported the browser version. The second run took about 8 hours. Total compute cost across both runs, about USD 37.

Check out: Agate 4-step model · Dataset · Run Agate in your browser · Agate 4-step LIVE

These are the GPU and CPU job charges reported for each session.

ML-intern is in HuggingChat. Switch on ML-intern mode and paste a prompt. If you want a starting point, my example prompts are free to copy. Start from a model you wish existed and a dataset you have, or one you can describe. Give it a small budget, ask for a baseline and a smoke test, and read what comes back before you raise the cap.

If you make something with it, share it on X and tag @Gradio and @HuggingFace. We would love to see the models you make that nobody else would think to build for you.

#9859. Phishing-Resistant Isn't Enough; Yubico Takes Aim at Identity-Verification Gap

News, news analysis, and commentary on the latest trends in cybersecurity technology.

The new YubiID service bridges identity verification with credential enrollment and recovery across existing identity platforms, closing a phishing-resistant authentication gap. Plus: post-quantum YubiKey beta.

Yubico wants to help employers verify a person’s identity before enrolling login credentials — and again when the employee needs to regain access after losing a key or mobile device.

On Tuesday, the maker of YubiKey authentication devices unveiled YubiID, a subscription service entering limited early access that links identity verification with credential enrollment and account recovery. Announced at Yubico's inaugural YubiNation user conference in San Francisco this week, the service integrates with major identity providers, including Microsoft Entra, Okta, and Ping, and supports enrolling credentials on YubiKeys and mobile phones. This extends Yubico's reach to organizations that have decided against deploying hardware keys.

The launch addresses a growing recognition that protecting a login to be phishing-resistant is no longer enough. It does not establish that the right person received the credential, or that someone requesting a replacement is the legitimate owner. Yubico field CTO Derek Hanson described that shift at the FIDO Alliance's Authenticate conference last month, saying the help desk "has moved from an operational control to an actual security control in most enterprises."

Related:Cyera's Oasis Security Buy Is All About AI Agent Control

Yubico is working with a group of unnamed "large organizations" as design partners and hopes to make YubiID generally available in the first half of 2027, CEO Jerrod Chong tells Dark Reading. The company has not revealed pricing.

According to Chong, the problem YubiID addresses used to be an afterthought: confirming that a key reaches the right person and that someone reporting it as lost is indeed that person. The new service provides a baseline identity-verification capability, but customers can also use their own verification process or rely on other providers. Planned integrations with Clear, Nametag, and HYPR will allow organizations to combine providers whose coverage differs by region.

For most enterprises, this is a familiar scenario: employees prove their identities to HR in one part of the office, then collect their login credentials from IT in another part of the office. Connecting these steps reduces opportunities for impersonation because identity verification is required for both initial enrollment and enrollment of replacement credentials.

"Recovery is such a weak spot for credential management," Andrew Shikiar, executive director and CEO of the FIDO Alliance, tells Dark Reading. Digital identity credentials provide enterprises with a way to reestablish a user's identity during recovery without relying on knowledge-based secrets, Shikiar says. Solving the recovery challenge involves more than just technology; it also requires policy, regulatory alignment, user behavior change, and business process design.

Related:USA Fencing Lunges Into the Hidden Identity Challenge in Amateur Sports

For organizations already investing in Okta, Ping, or Microsoft Entra, YubiID coordinates verification and enrollment; it does not replace those identity platforms. Yubico has built connectors to enroll credentials from those providers and also supports homegrown identity systems.

"We're not being an IDP," Chong says. "I think that there are more opportunities for collaboration than competition."

The practical benefit is tighter coordination. An organization can connect its chosen verification process to enrollment in the identity systems employees already use, rather than managing those steps as disconnected workflows. That becomes especially relevant for enterprises running multiple identity providers, where the employee's immediate need is simply to receive working credentials, regardless of which platform manages the account.

For a company onboarding 10,000 temporary workers ahead of the holiday season, YubiID can support both administrator-assisted, in-person enrollment and remote enrollment and verification, giving the company multiple ways to connect identity checks to access setup. The benefit, Chong says, is as much operational as security-related — fewer disconnected steps between verifying a worker and getting that person authenticated — though he did not provide figures on potential time savings or reductions in help-desk work. Interest is strongest among organizations with large, distributed or seasonal workforces, including transportation, retail, healthcare, consulting, and global services companies.

Related:Flaws in Passkey Implementation Show Old Attacks Still Work

Yubico is entering a market where identity providers and verification specialists already offer overlapping onboarding and recovery capabilities. Microsoft Entra's verified account recovery became generally available in May, using identity verification to help users regain access and register authentication methods without relying on a conventional manual help-desk process. Nametag and HYPR—both planned YubiID integration partners—also sell workforce verification and recovery capabilities. Beyond Identity already connects Nametag's identity checks to passkey enrollment and recovery, while 1Kosmos combines identity verification with passwordless authentication.

Chong maintains YubiID's differentiator is connecting verification and enrollment across platforms, rather than tying the workflow to a single identity provider. Yubico also brings its hardware business into those relationships: it makes the devices where many customers' authentication credentials reside. Chong connects that experience with the challenge of distributing keys, verifying recipients, and enrolling replacements across a global workforce.

Hardware is not required. Support for credentials on mobile devices could appeal to customers who find hardware key distribution too difficult. Those customers haven't necessarily rejected the keys' security benefits; rather, the logistics are "sometimes quite challenging," Chong says.

Federal agencies could also use employees' existing PIV credentials to establish their identities when enrolling FIDO credentials on YubiKeys or mobile authenticators, Chong says, while noting that those workflows are future potential capabilities and not fully available at launch.

Separately, Yubico announced a public beta program for a post-quantum-ready YubiKey. The beta YubiKey will support NIST-standardized post-quantum algorithms, but Yubico did not specify which ones. Yubico has tested early implementations with Chrome and Firefox, with early keys sent to federal labs and hyperscalers. Yubico expects to submit the key for FIPS validation within about a year, depending on beta testing and customer feedback, although completion is not guaranteed.

Despite being "crypto-agile," Chong confirms the beta devices cannot receive firmware upgrades, meaning organizations would later need to replace those keys if different algorithms are required. "Doing firmware upgrades safely across the web is not trivial," he says.

A June executive order directs agencies to transition high-value assets and high-impact systems to post-quantum cryptography for key establishment by the end of 2030 and digital signatures by the end of 2031. Organizations evaluating the beta keys will need to test both the new cryptography and the process for replacing and enrolling devices.

Yubico ultimately envisions providing verifiable proof that a person authorized a specific AI agent action, but Chong confirms that agent-authorization capabilities are not part of this launch. While the combination of Yubico's backend services, applications, and hardware keys forms the foundation for additional use cases, for now the YubiID service focuses on verifying people, enrolling credentials, and handling recovery.

"In a simple way to look at it, we're offering an end-to-end solution rather than just a YubiKey solution," Chong says.

#9858. Run fast, private agents on-device with LFM2.5-24B-A2B

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages:

We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters.

*All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters.

For your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads.

These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.

Edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300.

Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

Install the latest version of transformers (compatible with transformers>=5.0.0):

Serve LFM2.5-24B-A2B locally behind any OpenAI-compatible backend, then point your agent harness at it. For example, with Hermes Agent:

The port depends on your serving backend: llama.cpp and MLX use 8080, vLLM uses 8000, SGLang uses 30000, and LM Studio uses 1234. See the model card for OpenClaw and Pi configs, and our guide for the full setup. Check out our release blog for video examples.

#9856. Philippine Migrant Worker Data Likely Leaked in 69GB Government Breach

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

An unknown operator appears to have exfiltrated SQL Server backups from the Philippine Overseas Employment Administration in under a half hour.

An unknown threat actor managed to gain access to sensitive databases belonging to the Philippine Overseas Employment Administration, exfiltrating nearly 69GB of information on workers, contracts, and financial records, according to an analysis of a staging server used in the breach.

Over 24 minutes, the attacker copied 27 backup databases with information on overseas-employment case management, including accreditation, contracts, and cashier and LandBank records, according to threat intelligence firm Hunt.io's Oct. 28 analysis of the logs found on a Singaporean staging server used by the attacker. The cyberattackers used privileged escalation tools, namely GodPotato and SeImpersonate, and the Impacket network library for Python to move the data, but the trail stopped at the staging server, says Esteban Borges, head of research for Hunt.io.

The server had been later accessed, but by who is not clear, Borges says. While Hunt.io has not yet discovered the data as advertised for sale, the information may have been detected and removed, but that seems unlikely, he says.

Related:State Bank of India Suffers a Customer PII Data Leak

"I won't claim the backups stopped on the staging server," he says, so it's "still a breach, since the data was copied out of the agency’s control and the log shows the transfer completing."

This is not the first time that cybersecurity firms have found evidence that Philippine government data had been stolen. In August, Hunt.io discovered another threat actor's workspace hosting a number of tools and, in that case, 1.2GB of data stolen from a Philippine nuclear regulatory agency and a maritime shipbuilding contractor. A year ago, Philippine police arrested the mayor of a small town after discovering she was a Chinese national posing as a Filipina citizen and operating a cyber-scam center.

Whether the current incident involved China or cybercriminal groups is not clear. While Hunt.io did find some Chinese language fragments in the parts of the code, that code belonged to a third-party software library; thus, Hunt.io did not attribute the hack. The company did say, however, that both cybercriminals and nation-state adversaries would find value in the personally identifiable information (PII).

"That kind of migrant-worker PII, plus contract and payment data, is useful for fraud and identity theft, so it has commercial value," Borges says. "It's also a detailed map of a diaspora population, which can interest a state actor."

The latest insight into attacks on the Philippine government came after Hunt.io researchers discovered an open directory on a server hosted on the Singaporean address space of a Helsinki-based firm UpCloud Ltd., the analysis stated. The open directory contained tools and logs files for the attack, including a rebranded version of the GodPotato privilege escalation library, a PowerShell stager to unpack tools in memory, and the full Impacket Python environment.

Related:Russian Influence Operation Widely Targets Latin America

While Hunt.io considered the incident a confirmed compromise, the lack of runtime telemetry meant that Borges could not answer where the attacker moved the data.

"[W]e still can’t answer ... how they got in, whether the payload ran, and where the data went," he says.

However, the tools and the attacker's process indicated an operator with some strong ability, but who also made some simple mistakes, Borges says.

"The payload engineering is competent, [but] the operational security is poor — they left the staging server and its logs wide open," he says. "[It was] someone who can build the tool properly but was careless about keeping their own server quiet. I wouldn't call that top-tier or amateur."

The impact of the breach may boil down to the identity of the attacker and what they do with the stolen data. While Hunt.io notified the CERT Philippines (CERT-PH) and the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW), the company declined to provide any more details of the national responses to the leak.

Related:Venezuelan Cartel's Malware Honcho Nabbed for ATM Jackpotting

However, Borges did say that, so far, the information has not appeared for sale on the Dark Web.

"We haven't seen the backups surface for sale or in a leak," he says. "We never opened the backups themselves."

Governments in the region need to scan their own networks and lock down their attack surface area, he says. Workers with too many privileges allow attackers with tools such as SeImpersonate to gain more access to assets on the network. Hunt.io also found that the migrant-worker portal exposed a number of risky ports, including SMB on 445 and WinRM on 5985 and 47001.

Rob is an award-winning, veteran technology journalist of more than 30 years, reporting on global cybersecurity issues, the latest offensive and defensive technologies, malware incidents, cyber conflict, and AI's impact on software and cybersecurity.

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients.
