#9845. Normalizing a Wide Well and Pipeline Telemetry Table Without Re-Ingesting History

Tiger Data, the creators of TimescaleDB, develops the open-source time-series database built on PostgreSQL.

Tiger Data, the creators of TimescaleDB, develops the open-source time-series database built on PostgreSQL.

Tiger Data, the creators of TimescaleDB, develops the open-source time-series database built on PostgreSQL.

An oilfield SCADA migration guide: reshape a wide sensor table into a narrow hypertable plus a metadata table, in place, with your dashboards still running.

Every new instrument the field commissions turns into a schema change for you. A casing-pressure transmitter goes on a pad, a flow computer lands on a gathering line, and your wide telemetry table gets another indexed column on top of years of readings. You already know the shape is wrong. What has kept you from fixing it is the cost of the fix: reshaping a table that size looks like re-ingesting all of that history, and the dashboards on top of it cannot go dark while you do.

This guide walks through that migration: moving a wide time-series table to a narrow schema in place, with history intact and dashboards still running. It leaves out the harder case of tags whose descriptors change over time, and it picks up where Time-Series Cardinality leaves off, so it does not re-argue the shape.

If you control both the ingest and the queries, there is a gentler route: run a second ingest into the new table alongside the old one, then move queries over one at a time. That breaks the migration into small, separately reversible steps, and it is worth taking when you can. This guide covers the common case where you can't, because the ingest can't be duplicated or the queries aren't yours to rewrite. If you are on Tiger Cloud and would rather not run it yourself, the Enterprise plan includes a migration team that will help design a migration plan around your own tables.

What you get at the end is a table that stops fighting you. Readings land in a narrow hypertable of (recorded_at, tag_id, value), so the next instrument the field adds becomes one row in a metadata table instead of a column across years of history. Every descriptor the wide table repeated on each reading now lives once, on the tag. And the dashboards you cannot take down keep working, because the old table name and the old columns survive as a view over the new shape. On a hundred million generated readings, the whole sequence took under seven minutes of machine time on our hardware, against a clean dataset with no live ingest competing for the disk; most of that was the reshape in Step 2.

Three things need to be true before you schedule it:

This is a typical wide origin table. Tables shaped like this rarely come from a commercial historian such as PI, which keeps tag metadata apart from the readings and does not store them in SQL at all. They come from in-house ingest, where a project starts with a few wells and a hand-written INSERT, then keeps growing as pads and instruments are added. Map your own columns onto it; the names below are the ones every later step uses.

The DDL is shown in the current table-option form. Yours was probably created with create_hypertable(), and that changes nothing below. If your origin is a plain Postgres table rather than a hypertable, the migration gets easier in exactly two places: Step 3 gets CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY back, and the rename in Step 4 is an ordinary Postgres rename. Everything else is identical.

Create the destination before you touch the origin. Two tables: the metadata table owns the descriptors, and the narrow hypertable owns the facts.

The shape itself is the standard one, and TigerData's metadata table best practices cover the reasoning; the cardinality piece measured the benefits. Three choices inside that DDL decide whether the narrow shape pays off.

Keep tag_id a narrow BIGINT surrogate. The text tag path goes in tag_name once, on the metadata row. A fat TEXT key repeated on every fact row forfeits most of the win.

Enforce referential integrity at the ingest layer. A foreign key from the facts to tag_metadata adds a per-row check on a high-ingest path, which is why the DDL above declares none. If you want the constraint anyway, the supported direction is a hypertable referencing a regular table, which is the direction drawn here.

Segment by tag_id. Compression segmented by the tag is where the narrow schema's advantage widens most, and a source identifier is the usual segmentby candidate.

One consequence of creating the table this way: columnstore is on by default, so TimescaleDB creates a columnstore policy automatically, set to convert any chunk older than one chunk interval on a daily schedule. Every historical slice you are about to load is older than that, so the policy would start converting chunks while Step 2 is still writing next to them. The docs' own guidance for backfilling while converting is to pause the policy until the load is done, because conversion contends for locks with any concurrent write to the same chunk. Pause it now and re-enable it once the verification checks pass.

Two things are deliberately absent from the DDL. There is no index on the narrow table yet; tsdb.create_default_indexes = false keeps TimescaleDB from adding one, and Step 3 builds the composite index after the load. And there is one value DOUBLE PRECISION column, which assumes every tag is a float. Industrial tags are not uniformly float. If yours carry booleans, state codes, or strings, the appendix at the end shows the typed-column variant of this schema and the three places it changes the steps. Make that call before you reshape.

The whole migration rests on one assumption about your data: that a tag's descriptors are functionally dependent on the tag, so a given tag is always on the same device, at the same site, on the same line, reporting the same unit. The original post closes by asking you to check one property of your data before you plan anything. This is that check. Its answer decides whether the migration is an afternoon or a project. One scan, and it took about a minute against a hundred million rows.

An empty result is the clean case: every tag has carried exactly one descriptor set across its whole history, the backfill in Step 1 falls straight out of the data, and the rest of this guide is for you.

Rows mean some tags changed descriptors over their lifetime. On a pad this is routine. A workover moves a transmitter from one well to another, an instrument swap changes the device behind a tag path, or an RTU firmware upgrade bumps firmware_ver on every tag it serves. Those tags need availability windows, which is what the ts_start and ts_end columns in the metadata table exist for: one metadata row per descriptor set, bounded in time, with ts_last_seen tracking which row is current. That path makes the reshape join in Step 2 time-dependent and materially slower, and it is a longer migration, not just a different INSERT. This guide does not walk it; a follow-up will. If Step 0 returns rows, stop here and scope that migration instead of forcing this one.

One scan of the wide table, one row per tag. The text tag path lands in tag_name, and the surrogate is generated.

The guard is NOT EXISTS rather than ON CONFLICT ... DO NOTHING, and the difference matters. Both make the backfill safe to re-run, which Step 2 depends on. Only NOT EXISTS leaves Step 0's safety net armed: a tag that somehow carries two descriptor sets still trips the UNIQUE constraint on tag_name loudly, where ON CONFLICT would swallow it in silence and keep whichever set it saw first.

The pattern is a control table plus one transaction per time slice, where each transaction writes both the facts and its own completion marker. One unbounded INSERT ... SELECT over a multi-terabyte hypertable is the wrong instinct at this size, because a backfill this large cannot afford one long transaction: it holds a lock for hours, generates write-ahead log faster than replicas can consume it, and cannot resume if it dies at 90 percent.

A control table, rather than a unique constraint on (tag_id, recorded_at), records completions because that constraint would be expensive at this scale and may not even hold in field telemetry. A week is a reasonable slice width for a table this size; pick whatever keeps one transaction to minutes on your hardware.

The primary key on slice_start covers both ways a slice can be run twice. Retry a slice that already completed and the control-row insert fails on the key, taking the facts written in the same transaction down with it: nothing duplicated, one wasted slice of work. Kill a slice mid-run, as we did in the drill, and the transaction rolls back whole, no control row is written, and the retry starts from a clean slice.

The inner join silently drops any tag missing from tag_metadata, with no error and no warning, and a tag that first appears after Step 1's backfill is exactly such a tag. That is what the registration freeze in the prerequisites is for. If you cannot hold the freeze, re-run Step 1 before each slice; the NOT EXISTS guard makes that free.

How you drive the loop is the other trap. Ask the control table which windows are missing, and never track a MAX(slice_end) high-water mark, which steps straight over holes left by parallel slices or a crashed run.

Feed that list to whatever runs your slices, in parallel if you like, and the loop is done when it returns nothing. Stop one slice short of the present, though. Ingest is still landing in the wide table until the swap in Step 4, so the slice that contains now is incomplete by construction. Run it last, after the cutover, with sensor_readings_old as the source, because by then that table receives no writes and the slice is final. Never re-run a completed slice without first deleting its rows and its control row, or every fact in the window lands twice.

Build the indexes after the bulk load, not before. The load runs materially faster without an index to maintain, and the resulting B-tree is denser. The live-table reflex, CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY, is not supported on hypertables. The substitute is a one-line table option that builds the index one chunk per transaction.

One transaction per chunk means inserts into other chunks keep running while the index builds. If your read path has time-only scans with no tag predicate, add a plain (recorded_at DESC) index in the same step, since the DDL disabled the default one.

This only goes wrong if the build is interrupted, by a cancel, a crash, or an error partway through. Then the root index is marked invalid, with some chunks indexed and some not. It keeps working and still applies to new chunks; only the chunks the build missed go without it. To guarantee full coverage, find it, drop it, and rebuild:

Then ANALYZE both sensor_readings_narrow and tag_metadata. The join the compatibility view is about to put on the read path is exactly the plan that needs fresh statistics, and the planner has not seen a row of either table yet.

A rename is cheap in Postgres because tables are identified by OID rather than name, so ALTER TABLE ... RENAME TO is a metadata operation whatever the table's size, and hypertables rename the same way. Renaming alone is still not a non-breaking cutover. The rename preserves the table's name, not its shape. The narrow table has three columns where the old one had eight, so every query selecting site or line fails the moment the swap commits. A view restores the old shape under the old name, and the dashboards never learn the table moved.

The lock_timeout is not optional. The rename takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE. If one long-running read is in flight, the rename queues behind it, every later reader queues behind the rename, and a metadata operation turns into an outage. In a live two-session test, a three-second lock_timeout fired on schedule against a single held-open read instead of queueing behind it. Set it short and expect to retry during a quiet minute. The CREATE VIEW sits inside the same transaction on purpose: between the rename committing and the view existing there is no sensor_readings at all, and one short transaction closes that gap.

The view is a join on the read path, and the cardinality piece measured what that join costs against querying the narrow table directly: about two percent on the rollups and below measurement noise on the sub-millisecond queries. The view is read-path only, so repoint your ingest at sensor_readings_narrow explicitly rather than through an INSTEAD OF trigger. In practice that is the ingest service writing (recorded_at, tag_id, value) with the surrogate resolved from tag_metadata, as soon as the swap commits. Without the view, normalizing would mean rewriting every dashboard query on cutover day; with it, the rewrite becomes incremental. Repoint your hottest queries at the narrow table when it suits you. The rewrite happens on your schedule, not on cutover day's.

Dependent objects do not follow a rename. Continuous aggregates, retention and compression policies, triggers, and grants all stay bound to the renamed-away table. In our drill a real continuous aggregate kept aggregating sensor_readings_old, and nothing reported it: the rollup simply stopped seeing new rows the moment ingest moved to the narrow table. This is the class of failure most likely to cost you real data.

Inventory every dependent object before the swap, while the table still has its original name.

Then re-point each one after the swap. A continuous aggregate cannot be re-targeted, so recreate it against sensor_readings_narrow (joined to tag_metadata if it groups by a descriptor, which continuous aggregates support from TimescaleDB 2.10; note that only changes to the hypertable are tracked, so an edit to a metadata row does not reach the aggregate until you refresh it by hand), add its refresh policy back, and drop the old one once the new one has caught up. Triggers get recreated on the narrow table. Grants on the old table become grants on the view, since that is what the old readers now hit.

Treat retention policies as the dangerous ones, and re-create them last. A policy added to the narrow table judges every chunk you just moved on its first run, measured from now(), and any chunk older than drop_after goes immediately. In our drill a re-created 365-day policy over history whose newest rows were already older than a year deleted every chunk within seconds. Before you add the policy back, compare its window against the oldest chunk the narrow table now holds, and decide on purpose whether that history is meant to survive. If it is, the policy waits until you have moved or archived it. The old table's own retention policy is the mirror problem: it followed sensor_readings_old into retirement and keeps dropping chunks from the fallback you are counting on. Pause it with the same alter_job call right after the swap.

Keep the old table until old and new agree on the overlap. Ingest is writing to the narrow table, the view is serving reads from it, and sensor_readings_old is still there untouched. Hold that reconciliation window open until the checks below pass.

The cheap check is per-slice row counts, using the counts the control table already recorded.

An empty result means every slice moved as many rows as the wide table held for that window. A row means either the inner join dropped a tag in that slice or ingest was still landing in that window when the slice ran; the failure table below has the move.

The stronger check is a per-day checksum over a sample window on both sides: row count and first and last timestamp compared exactly, and the sum of every value compared with a relative tolerance. The tolerance is doing real work. Two full scans sum a hundred million doubles in a different physical order, and an exact comparison of the sums fails on floating-point rounding with no row out of place. In our validation run a seven-day checksum came back with zero mismatches.

Only when both checks pass, and your dashboards have run a normal cycle against the view, drop sensor_readings_old. That is also the moment to re-enable the columnstore job you paused in the schema step, with the same alter_job call and scheduled => true. Until you drop the old table, the cutover is a reversible rename.

If a step fails before then, find your row.

Step 1 trips the UNIQUE constraint on tag_name

You are in the lifecycle case from Step 0. Stop and re-scope; do not weaken the constraint.

Crash, kill, or timeout inside the transaction

Re-run the slice. The transaction rolled back whole and the primary key on slice_start makes a blind retry safe.

A tag was registered after the backfill and the inner join dropped it, or ingest was still landing in the window when the slice ran

Re-run Step 1, delete that slice's rows and its control row, and run the slice again from sensor_readings_old.

The loop was driven from a high-water mark

Ask migration_slices which windows are missing and run those.

pg_index WHERE indisvalid IS FALSE finds it. Drop it and rebuild.

Retry during a quiet minute. Do not remove the lock_timeout.

The view does not expose a column that query selects

An aggregate or policy still reads the old table

A narrow hypertable, a metadata table with one row per tag, dashboards that never noticed the swap, and an old table you can still fall back to until you choose not to. Before you book the window, rehearse it. Run Step 0 tonight. Then copy one week of your wide table into a scratch schema, run Steps 1 through 4 against it with the same freeze in place, and kill a slice mid-run on purpose so you see the rollback happen on your own hardware. And if you would rather not own the columnstore and retention policies you just re-created by hand, Tiger Cloud manages the hypertable, compression, and policies. If the rehearsal leaves you wanting a second pair of eyes before the real window, TigerData's support plans put PostgreSQL and TimescaleDB experts on the other end of the ticket.

The float-only schema keeps every step above readable, and plenty of telemetry tables really are all measurements. When yours also carry pump run states, valve positions, alarm codes, or a text mode label, the standard fix is what TigerData calls the medium table layout: one nullable value column per data type instead of one value column for everything. A new tag still costs one metadata row; only a new data type costs a column.

The float column keeps the name value, so the Step 4 view still serves the old value column unchanged for every measurement tag. The CHECK enforces exactly one value per row and needs no lookup, so unlike a foreign key it stays cheap on the ingest path. The rest of the migration changes in three places:

RAG Complexity Is a Bet Against the Model

Tiger Data, the creators of TimescaleDB, develops the open-source time-series database built on PostgreSQL.

#9844. Canva Review 2022: Details, Pricing & Features


Are you looking for a new graphic design tool? Would you like to read a detailed review of Canva? As it's one of the tools I love using. I am also writing my first ebook using canva and publish it soon on my site you can download it is free.  Let's start the review.

Canva has a web version and also a mobile app

What is Canva?

Canva is a free graphic design web application that allows you to create invitations, business cards, flyers, lesson plans, banners, and more using professionally designed templates. You can upload your own photos from your computer or from Google Drive, and add them to Canva's templates using a simple drag-and-drop interface. It's like having a basic version of Photoshop that doesn't require Graphic designing knowledge to use. It’s best for nongraphic designers.

Who is Canva best suited for?

Canva is a great tool for small business owners, online entrepreneurs, and marketers who don’t have the time and want to edit quickly.

To create sophisticated graphics, a tool such as Photoshop can is ideal. To use it, you’ll need to learn its hundreds of features, get familiar with the software, and it’s best to have a good background in design, too.

Also running the latest version of Photoshop you need a high-end computer.

So here  Canva takes place, with Canva you can do all that with drag-and-drop feature. It’s also easier to use and free. Also an even-more-affordable paid version is available for $12.95 per month.

Free vs Pro vs Enterprise Pricing plan

The product is available in three plans: Free, Pro ($12.99/month per user or  $119.99/year for up to 5 people), and Enterprise ($30 per user per month, minimum 25 people).

Free plan Features

  • 250,000+ free templates
  • 100+ design types (social media posts, presentations, letters, and more)
  • Hundreds of thousands of free photos and graphics
  • Invite members to your team
  • Collaborate and comment in real-time
  • 5GB of cloud storage
  • Try Canva Pro for free for 30 days

Pro Plan Features 

  • Everything Free, has plus:
  • 100+ million premium and  stock photos, videos, audio, and graphics
  • 610,000+ premium and free templates with new designs daily
  • Access to Background Remover and Magic Resize
  •  Create a library of your brand or campaign's colors, logos, and fonts with up to 100 Brand Kits
  • Remove image backgrounds instantly with background remover
  • Resize designs infinitely with Magic Resize
  • Save designs as templates for your team to use
  • 100GB of cloud storage
  • Schedule social media content to 8 platforms

Enterprise Plan Features

  • Everything Pro has plus:
  • Establish your brand's visual identity with logos, colors and fonts across multiple Brand Kits
  • Control your team's access to apps, graphics, logos, colors and fonts with brand controls
  • Built-in workflows to get approval on your designs
  • Set which elements your team can edit and stay on brand with template locking
  • Unlimited Storage
  • Log in with single-sign on (SSO) and have access to 24/7 Enterprise-level support.

How to Use Canva?

To get started on Canva, you will need to create an account by providing your email address, Google, Facebook or Apple credentials. You will then choose your account type between student, teacher, small business, large company, non-profit, or personal. Based on your choice of account type, templates will be recommended to you.

You can sign up for a free trial of Canva Pro, or you can start with the free version to get a sense of whether it’s the right graphic design tool for your needs.

Canva Sign Up

Designing with Canva



When you sign up for an account, Canva will suggest different post types to choose from. Based on the type of account you set up  you'll be able to see templates categorized by the following categories: social media posts, documents, presentations, marketing, events, ads, launch your business, build your online brand, etc.

 Start by choosing a template for your post or searching for something more specific. Search by social network name to see a list of post types on each network.

Templates



Next, you can choose a template. Choose from hundreds of templates that are ready to go, with customizable photos, text, and other elements.

You can start your design by choosing from a variety of ready-made templates, searching for a template matching your needs, or working with a blank template.


 Canva has a lot to choose from, so start with a specific search.if you want to create business card just search for it and you will see alot of templates to choose from

Elements

Inside the Canva designer, the Elements tab gives you access to lines and shapes, graphics, photos, videos, audio, charts, photo frames, and photo grids.The search box on the Elements tab lets you search everything on Canva.


To begin with, Canva has a large library of elements to choose from. To find them, be specific in your search query. You may also want to search in the following tabs to see various elements separately:

Photos

The Photos tab lets you search for and choose from millions of professional stock photos for your templates.

You can replace the photos in our templates to create a new look. This can also make the template more suited to your industry.

You can find photos on other stock photography sites like pexel, pixabay and many more or simply upload your own photos.


When you choose an image, Canva’s photo editing features let you adjust the photo’s settings (brightness, contrast, saturation, etc.), crop, or animate it.

 When you subscribe to Canva Pro, you get access to a number of premium features, including the Background Remover. This feature allows you to remove the background from any stock photo in  library or any image you upload.

Text

The Text tab lets you add headings, normal text, and graphical text to your design.

When you click on  text, you'll see options to adjust the font, font size, color, format, spacing, and text effects (like shadows). 

Canva Pro subscribers can choose from a large library of fonts on the Brand Kit or the Styles tab. Enterprise-level controls ensure that visual content remains on-brand, no matter how many people are working on it.

Audio

Create an animated image or video by adding audio to capture user’s attention in social news feeds.

If you want to use audio from another stock site or your own audio tracks, you can upload them in the Uploads tab or from the more option.

Video

Want to create your own videos? Choose from thousands of stock video clips. You’ll find videos that range upto 2 minutes

You can upload your own videos as well as videos from other stock sites in the Uploads tab. 

Once you have chosen a video, you can use the editing features in Canva to trim the video, flip it, and adjust its transparency.

Backgrounds

On the Background tab, you’ll find free stock photos to serve as backgrounds on your designs. Change out the background on a template to give it a more personal touch.

Styles


The Styles tab lets you quickly change the look and feel of your template with just a click. And if you have a Canva Pro subscription, you can upload your brand’s custom colors and fonts to ensure designs stay on brand.

Logos

If you have a Canva Pro subscription, you’ll have a Logos tab. Here, you can upload variations of your brand logo to use throughout your designs.

With Canva, you can also create your own logos. Note that you cannot trademark a logo with stock content in it.

Publishing with Canva

With Canva, free users can download and share designs to multiple platforms including Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack and Tumblr.

Canva Pro subscribers can create multiple post formats from one design. For example, you can start by designing an Instagram post, and Canva's Magic Resizer can resize it for other networks, Stories, Reels, and other formats.

Canva Pro subscribers can also use Canva’s Content Planner to post content on eight different accounts on Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, LinkedIn, Pinterest, Slack, and Tumblr.

Canva Team

Canva Pro allows you to work with your team on visual content. Designs can be created inside Canva, and then sent to your team members for approval. Everyone can make comments, edits, revisions, and keep track via the version history.

Canva Print

When it comes to printing your designs, Canva has you covered. With an extensive selection of printing options, they can turn your designs into anything from banners and wall art to mugs and t-shirts. 

Canva Print is perfect for any business seeking to make a lasting impression. Create inspiring designs people will want to wear, keep, and share. Hand out custom business cards that leave a lasting impression on customers' minds.

Canva Apps

The Canva app is available on the Apple App Store and Google Play. The Canva app has earned a 4.9 out of five star rating from over 946.3K Apple users and a 4.5 out of five star rating from over 6,996,708 Google users.

In addition to mobile apps, you can use Canva’s integration with other Internet services to add images and text from sources like Google Maps, Emojis, photos from Google Drive and Dropbox, YouTube videos, Flickr photos, Bitmojis, and other popular visual content elements.

Canva Pros and Cons

Pros:

  • A user-friendly interface
  • Canva is a great tool for people who want to create professional graphics but don’t have graphic design skills.
  • Hundreds of templates, so you'll never have to start from scratch.
  • Wide variety of templates to fit multiple uses
  • Branding kits to keep your team consistent with the brand colors and fonts
  • Creating visual content on the go
  • You can find royalty free images, audio, and video without having to subscribe to another service.

Cons:

  • Some professional templates are available for Pro user only
  • Advanced photo editing features like blurring or erasing a specific area are missing.
  • Some elements that fall outside of a design are tricky to retrieve.
  • Features (like Canva presentations) could use some improvement.
  • If you are a regular user of Adobe products, you might find Canva's features limited.
  • Prefers to work with vectors. Especially logos.
  • Expensive enterprise pricing

Conclusion

In general, Canva is an excellent tool for those who need simple images for projects. If you are a graphic designer with experience, you will find Canva’s platform lacking in customization and advanced features – particularly vectors. But if you have little design experience, you will find Canva easier to use than advanced graphic design tools like Adobe Photoshop or Illustrator for most projects. If you have any queries let me know in the comments section.

#9843. TorchNeuron: running HF models on AWS Trainium is easier than ever

TorchNeuron provides a new native backend for PyTorch on AWS Trainium. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels natively support it, making it easier than ever to run models on Trainium and to share them on the HF hub.

TorchNeuron is a PyTorch plugin that brings a new backend for Trainium enabling support for eager mode, torch.compile and native distributed APIs like FSDP and TP. Read the Pytorch blog to learn more about TorchNeuron.

Starting Oct. 20, 2026, TorchNeuron will be available as a public beta. Researchers and developers will be able to install it with pip install torch-neuronx.

To date, the Hugging Face experience on AWS Trainium and Inferentia — AI chips designed respectively for cost-effective training and inference at scale — has been delivered through optimum-neuron. This library relies on the torch-neuronx package, which is based on PyTorch XLA. It was the natural choice at the time, but it meant thinking like a compiler: lazy tensors instead of eager execution, static shapes only, a recompilation for every graph break. Optimum Neuron existed to hide that complexity, and maintained custom code (modeling classes, trainers, etc) to do so.

TorchNeuron changes this. It integrates directly into PyTorch and exposes neuron as a native device, with eager execution, PyTorch's own distributed primitives (DTensor, FSDP2) and torch.compile.

For the Hugging Face libraries, Trainium becomes a device like any other: Transformers, Diffusers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL run on it directly, with the same classes and scripts you would use on any other accelerator. From now on, we recommend that Neuron users use these libraries directly instead of going through Optimum Neuron.

Text generation is now natively supported in Transformers for a wide range of models. With TorchNeuron, 89% of the top 100 most-used text-generation model architectures are supported out of the box, compared to 46% with Optimum Neuron v0.4.5. You just need to pass the device_map=neuron argument in your code and your model will be moved to the Neuron devices.

The following is an example of text-generation with tensor parallelism, which will enable to fully benefit from your Neuron instance. Note that it uses a static cache for generation as this is strongly recommended with Neuron to prevent frequent recompilations.

Now that Neuron is a native PyTorch device, training on Trainium uses the same Hugging Face libraries as any other accelerator: Transformers, Accelerate, PEFT and TRL. You no longer need a dedicated trainer or a Neuron-specific fork of the model code. A standard TRL fine-tuning script runs on a Trainium instance with only a few Neuron-specific settings.

Here is a supervised fine-tuning script built on TRL's SFTTrainer. If you have fine-tuned a model with TRL on GPUs before, it should look familiar.

Parallelism is handled natively by Transformers. You put a DistributedConfig with the tensor-parallel (TP) and FSDP sizes in model_init_kwargs, SFTTrainer passes it to from_pretrained, and the model is sharded as its weights are loaded. The Trainer sees that the model is already distributed and does not wrap it again. You don't need an --fsdp flag or an Accelerate FSDP config.

Nothing in the script is tied to Trainium: the same code runs on any hardware. A few things are worth knowing when you run it on Trainium:

The command below launches training with torchrun, which starts one process per NeuronCore. TP_SIZE and FSDP_SIZE set the parallelism layout, and their product is the number of processes: here 4 x 8 = 32, matching --nproc_per_node. The 32 processes form a 4 x 8 grid. Tensor parallelism splits each layer across the 4 cores of a TP group, and FSDP shards the parameters, gradients and optimizer state across the 8 TP groups.

We ran it on 8 Trainium2 chips (32 NeuronCores), which is half a trn2.48xlarge instance.

Training runs to completion, and trainer.save_model writes a standard Transformers checkpoint. Nothing in it is tied to Neuron: you can push it to the Hugging Face Hub as is and load it on any other hardware.

Many pipelines from the Diffusers library are compatible with TorchNeuron in eager and compiled mode. FLUX.1-dev, FLUX.2, Qwen-Image, Qwen-Image-2.1 and H3 are also compatible with tensor parallelism to make the most of your Neuron devices. The following is an example showing how you can use TP:

You can run this piece of code with: NEURON_LOGICAL_NC_CONFIG=2 torchrun --nproc_per_node=8 run.py.

More and more pipleines will be compatible with TP. If a pipeline you like is not, you can also add support for it following this guide.

Make sure to check out the kernels from the Neuron team as more and more Neuron kernels will become available on the Hub to speed up your models. Neuron kernels can be written using the Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI), which gives lower control to optimize operations. This way, users can run their own custom operations and share them on the hub.

You can use for example this kernel to speed up your vision transformers with up to a x2.4 speedup on Trainium!

Special thanks to the AWS team for their work on TorchNeuron and for their reactivity to our feedback to make the HF integration as good as possible.

Hi, we now have a space where you can chek if a model is supported: https://huggingface.co/spaces/aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support

#9842. MPS in PyTorch 2.15

If you run models on your Mac or use MPS as your primary acceleration tool for computing, there's plenty to look forward to in PyTorch 2.15! FP8 arrives on MPS, language-model decoding gets faster paths through linear layers and softmax and new Metal kernels tackle some surprisingly expensive parts of audio, video and training workloads.

A quick word about who we are: we're the PyTorch team at Hugging Face. We contribute across PyTorch, and one of our focus areas is the MPS backend, where the goal is to make your Mac a first-class place to run and train PyTorch models. At the start of 2026, running even small models on MPS often meant working around unsupported operations, performance cliffs and unexpected memory growth. So we run real models from the Hugging Face Hub across language, image and video, find where MPS falls short and fix it upstream in PyTorch, more and more often by replacing MPSGraph with dedicated Metal kernels. Much of this post is the result of that work, done together with the PyTorch maintainers and community contributors.

If you run models on a Mac with transformers, diffusers or tools like ComfyUI, here's what 2.15 changes in practice:

You'll need an Apple silicon Mac with macOS 15 or later and Python 3.11 or later (see the 2.15 compatibility matrix). If your OS is too old or no Metal GPU is available, the MPS availability check now tells you why.

To try the release candidate in a separate environment:

FP8 gives you another way to save memory on your Mac. PyTorch 2.15 adds torch.float8_e4m3fn tensors on MPS: one byte per value, half the storage of FP16 or BF16.

You can multiply these tensors with F.scaled_mm, which supports both tensorwise and rowwise scaling. Here's a small example with one scale per tensor:

Every LLM has a prefill phase and a decode phase. During decode, each new token goes through the model as a single row, so the big matrix multiplications turn into matrix-vector products. PyTorch 2.15 speeds up both kinds of layers that dominate this step: dense linear layers and mixture-of-experts layers.

MPS has had GEMV kernels for torch.mm since 2.14, but F.linear still went through MPSGraph. PyTorch 2.15 connects them to F.linear, so the common [1, 1, hidden_size] decoding input uses them directly, with eligible bias additions fused in. Across 96 BF16 layer shapes from real models, that's a 1.23× geometric-mean speedup. The biggest wins land on small projections, such as the gates in MoE models, where the old path left most of the memory bandwidth unused. Large layers and LM heads were already close to bandwidth-bound, so they stay near 1×.

A mixture-of-experts layer sends different numbers of tokens to each expert. Grouped matmul handles those uneven groups in a single operation, and 2.15 gives MPS a native implementation.

In 2.14, grouped matmul copied the group offsets to the CPU and looped over the groups. The new Metal kernels read the offsets directly on the GPU, using Metal Performance Primitives where available and a separate Metal path elsewhere. Small groups, the common case during decoding, get their own kernel as well.

For example, 64 tokens can be split into groups of 16, 32, and 16:

The decoding kernel shows up directly in token throughput. On an M3 Ultra with torch.compile, MoE models generate about 1.3× more tokens per second:

Working with complex tensors gets easier. complex64 LU factorization, LU solve and triangular solve now run on MPS, which also unlocks the operations and gradients built on them, such as complex determinants. Here's a small system solved directly on the GPU:

Small matrices get fast kernels too. For camera geometry and image transformations, batches of FP32 matrices up to 4 × 4 are inverted in a single Metal kernel that combines factorization and solving. Larger problems get attention as well: QR uses blocked updates, and triangular solves turn much of their work into efficient matrix multiplication.

Gated DeltaNet workloads get a dedicated fast path for batches of 16 × 16, 32 × 32 and 64 × 64 FP32 triangular systems with at least eight right-hand sides.

SVD is also more robust at numerical extremes. It now correctly handles very small singular values, very large or very small input magnitudes and basis completion with full_matrices=True, which in turn makes pseudoinverse and least-squares results more reliable.

Audio models, video decoders and training loops have their own expensive operations. This release gives several of them new paths through Metal:

Token sampling gets faster in 2.15 as well. softmax and log_softmax now run on dedicated Metal kernels, and large vocabularies benefit the most: an FP32 softmax over a [1, 128256] row of logits drops from 57 µs to 7 µs, about 8× faster than the MPSGraph version. The speedup holds across other common vocabulary sizes:

One of the most striking results in this release comes from the constant-padding change. The VAE decode in Wan-AI/Wan2.2-TI2V-5B-Diffusers makes 8,764 padding calls over a full 28-tile decode. With padding on Metal, peak driver memory drops from about 270 GiB to 8 GiB:

You can now pick which MPS stream runs your work, directly from Python. torch.mps.Stream and the torch.mps.stream context manager provide the interface, and Tensor.record_stream lets the allocator track a tensor's use on another stream.

Here's a small example that sends work to a separate stream and synchronizes before reading the result:

Several more operations now run on MPS: torch.frexp, torch.logspace, torch.take and Tensor.put_, torch.heaviside, torch.special.laguerre_polynomial_l and unsigned-integer comparisons. logspace doesn't yet support integer or boolean outputs with more than one element.

Attention gets a correctness fix too: the MPS math implementation of scaled dot-product attention now handles batch and head broadcasting correctly.

Work on 2.16 is already well underway. Some of the changes below have landed on main and are available in the nightlies; others are still in review, so details may change before the release.

Once a model's decode path no longer contains any MPSGraph ops, the GPU only starts on a token after the CPU has finished encoding all of its kernels. PyTorch 2.16 commits the command buffer every 16 kernels, so the GPU gets to work while the CPU is still encoding the rest. For compiled BF16 decoding at a 2048-token context:

Scaled dot-product attention is dropping MPSGraph completely: every shape will run on Metal kernels, with dedicated vector kernels for decoding and Metal Performance Primitives for half-precision prefill on newer macOS versions. The shapes that used to fall back to MPSGraph benefit the most. On an M5 Pro, decoding with grouped-query attention (32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head dim 80, 4K context) drops from 465 µs to 65 µs, and a 4K × 4K prefill with head dim 40 goes from 42 ms to 6 ms.

The move away from MPSGraph continues. Batch norm forward and backward are in progress, while MSE loss (up to 12× faster on small inputs), std_mean and var_mean (up to 4× faster) and bincount have already landed. bincount is the most dramatic: when most values fall into a single bin, counting 4 million integers used to take 6.8 seconds and now takes half a millisecond.

Bundled shaders will build for Metal 3.1 by default, with Metal 4 versions compiled only for the kernels that need them. That shrinks libtorch_cpu.dylib by about 25%, from 384 MiB to 287 MiB, and lays the groundwork for Metal 4.1 shaders with faster matmuls and native FP8 matrix multiplication.

PyTorch 2.15 brings FP8 to the Mac, faster LLM decoding for dense and MoE models, more linear algebra on the GPU and a long list of operations moved from MPSGraph to dedicated Metal kernels. Give the release candidate a try!

A big thank you to Nikita Shulga, Kurt Mohler and Aaron Gokaslan for reviewing much of this work, and to everyone who contributed to MPS in this release.

#9841. How to Turn Engineering Productivity Gains Into Measurable Revenue

VP of Engineering @ Mews. SW Product Builder. See more at https://www.kamenistak.com/mentoring

VP of Engineering @ Mews. SW Product Builder. See more at https://www.kamenistak.com/mentoring

VP of Engineering @ Mews. SW Product Builder. See more at https://www.kamenistak.com/mentoring

A VP of Engineering wrote a small code change himself, his first in two years. Three hours of work took a day to build and a week to ship. That one task became the benchmark for the platform team business case below, with the capacity splits, the 90/10 ownership rule and the payback table his exec team saw.

"We shipped more features this year than last year. I didn't see the revenue." That was the head of product's answer when Tomáš, a VP of Engineering, promised his exec team three times the throughput. A platform team business case is the ask that survives that answer: one quarter of roadmap capacity, shown coming back within three, in money.

Tomáš (not his real name) runs engineering at a B2B SaaS company. His platform teams spend 60% of their time keeping production up, 2% making their components open to other teams and 38% building features. The product teams can't move without them, so every cross-team initiative waits in someone's queue.

His deck was good. Dependencies drawn as spaghetti, autonomous teams, a 3x target. Every number on it was a percentage.

One slide was missing, and I told him so. There wasn't a single dollar in the deck. Stripe's Developer Coefficient found developers spend 17.3 hours of a 41.1-hour week on maintenance, bad code and technical debt. Your exec team already pays that bill, so show them the invoice.

Ask ChatGPT how to get a platform team funded and it tells you to "stop selling it as an engineering improvement and start selling it as a business investment". Right, and not enough. An investment without a date is a wish.

So say the date. "Give me half of Q1. You'll have it back by the end of the year, and from then on we run faster." You're not scratching at the door for platform time, you're a VP selling an investment.

A percentage invites a negotiation about the percentage. A payback date invites a decision, and the decision belongs to the people in the room. That's where you want it.

The bill is big enough to carry it. CIOs told McKinsey that 10 to 20% of the technology budget meant for new products gets diverted to tech debt.

Tomáš got lucky. His CEO had his own "the train is leaving without us" moment the weekend before the offsite and was ready to break the roadmap. But a mandate doesn't come from one hour of talking, and the payback slide is what you keep coming back with. At Mews and at the companies I've advised since, I've watched that fight take half a year to a year before people get it: you're not selling a slower roadmap; you're speeding up the company.

You can't sell a payback date on a guess about today. The first slide shows where the time goes now, and the numbers have to come from the teams, not from you.

Split every team's time into roadmap work, platform investment, reactive production work (incidents, on-call, hotfixes), customer escalations and help for other teams. The first two are planned, the last three mostly aren't. The unplanned share is your headline number: it's how much room your teams really have for the roadmap.

Each team lead splits their team's person-days into the five buckets. Fifteen minutes, ±10% is enough. Run it for two weeks as a pilot, then switch to a rolling six weeks, because one big incident skews two weeks completely.

Next to every bucket, write which division asked for the work. Now capacity becomes a budget you can hand out: "Your division has 400 person-days this quarter, you decide what goes in." A new request becomes a trade, and the fight over priorities moves to the people who own the priorities.

Person-days times the fully loaded cost of a day. That's the number a CFO reads. If you've never priced an engineering decision for an executive, I wrote up the smaller version of this in how to talk to executives.

Here is what Tomáš's measurement and target looked like. These are one real company's numbers, anonymised. The product-team target is a target, not a measurement.

Changes in the platform (via contribution)

Look at the bottom row. The product teams already spend 62% on features.

What holds them back is the 35% they spend looking back at production and the queue they stand in for the platform. More feature capacity is a side effect of removing that. If you want an outside read on where your teams' time goes before you build this slide, that's what an engineering productivity audit is for.

Tomáš's priority order for platform teams is production first, opening the components second, features last. 30% production is the desired share, not a cap: when production burns, production wins.

The platform-team flip Tomáš asked for. Today's 2% on opening components isn't drawn.

Why features last? Ten autonomous teams that all need the same five people in the shared core aren't ten parallel streams. They run fast for a few weeks, then they wait on reviews, questions and dependencies again.

The queue only moved. DORA's research calls this "downstream disorder": gains in coding speed get swallowed by bottlenecks in testing, security review and beyond.

The 90/10 rule: 90% of changes flow through open components.

Product teams change the platform when they need to. Platform teams change product code when production needs it, for example when something falls over or can't keep up on performance. Both sides have to be fine with someone else in their code. Years of strong ownership at Tomáš's company grew red tape around every component, and he wants 90% of it gone.

No capability "because it might come in handy in three years". Build what a team needs now. The platform follows where the product teams go, it doesn't run ahead of them.

Platform teams get measured by how much faster the product teams ship, not by what they built. That's the Team Topologies idea of a platform team in practice: an internal product that exists to speed up the stream-aligned teams. If you want the role itself explained, here's the platform engineer role.

The counter-voice deserves a fair hearing. The 2024 DORA report found a 6% gain in team productivity with a dedicated platform team, and an 8% drop in throughput among those using a platform. A platform done badly slows you down, which is exactly why you measure it by the other teams' speed and prove it on one task first.

This is the slide Tomáš didn't have. Three numbers make it.

Person-days moved off the roadmap times the loaded day cost. That's your investment, in money.

The roadmap output you lose in the investment quarter against what you gain after it, quarter by quarter, until the running balance turns positive. Expect the teams to slow down, or nearly stop, for about two months while they adopt new tools and a new way of working. Say it out loud on the slide: slow down to get faster later.

Don't guess the speed-up. Take it from the pilot (next section): whatever the benchmark task shows at the first read is your Q2 number, and you don't extrapolate further than the pilot proved.

Your CPO should know how much revenue you generate every quarter and how much of it is attributed to new functionality. That's your price per quarter of roadmap. Put the result on the slide as a hypothesis, and still put the number there. That's when people stop debating whether to allow it.

Here's the shape, with numbers made up for this post (illustrative, not Tomáš's). Output is in "today's quarters", where 1.0 is a quarter like the current one, and $3M a quarter of revenue comes from new functionality.

Extra revenue vs today, if adoption holds

One quarter in, three to get it back: by the end of Q4 you're 0.7 quarters ahead, about $2.1M. If year two holds the Q4 speed, that's 0.6 extra quarters of output each quarter, about $7.2M a year.

Read the last column header again. "If adoption holds" is the head of product's objection, written onto your own slide, and it's why the next section exists.

Reliability and security work gets a revenue number too. Jade Rubick's ValueSum scores a delivered item so that 100 points means adding 100% ARR over one year, multiplied by the probability of success. His reliability example, step by step:

A third of customers at risk of churn from this instability

They skew large, so it's really about 45% of revenue

Real churn risk per customer about 20%: 45 × 20%

Rubick also gives you the argument for a standing platform share instead of a fight per project: "a certain percentage of every engineering organization should be focused on things that make the organization more efficient over time", because that work "will typically get shortchanged" if you only optimise for value delivered.

The head of product was right. That we speed up the machine doesn't mean we'll deliver the right things at that speed. Pendo's feature adoption report found that 80% of features in the average software product are rarely or never used.

So the business case needs a second owner. I told Tomáš what we did at Mews, where I grew engineering from 8 to 80 teams as VP of Engineering. My KPI, the one I was known for: every quarter I delivered at least 80% of the roadmap. If I didn't deliver, they could fire me.

I tracked it as roadmap contribution: what percentage of my teams' time goes on the roadmap as opposed to off it. Two teams working off the roadmap for whatever reason put the whole quarter at risk. I taught my leaders the rule I lived by: if you don't bring me the roadmap, I have a problem too.

My product peer had another KPI. "Thank you, Marian, for building me a fast machine. But I have to throw things into the machine." His job was to feed my roadmap with things that matter, measured as product adoption, and we set it up on purpose so we'd be twins in a pair.

A faster machine sells nothing on its own. Somebody has to own what goes into it.

Every initiative was locked in a quarter and had a custom field in Jira with its adoption grade. I'll admit it, we graded by hand, there was no automated metric:

It earns back what it cost: people, licences, infrastructure

Too early to grade, allowed for one quarter at most

Timing is part of a good product decision, so nothing stays ungraded longer than a quarter.

I had 80% roadmap delivery. The product leader next to me had 65% product adoption, meaning high or ultra-high. Waiting doesn't count, because waiting doesn't generate money.

And honestly, we yelled at each other. "I'm holding a fast roadmap for you, and you're throwing junk into it? Then my people are unhappy and somebody leaves."

Sometimes I said a thing didn't belong on the roadmap. Sometimes he wanted to label something a success and I said, that's probably not a success. But now you have valid discussions, about value.

Rubick lands in the same place from the other side. He recommends re-scoring every feature three or six months after delivery and keeping both the predicted and the retroactive score. Two more rules from that work I'd copy: product or division leaders score the value, not engineering, and you don't use the score to rate individuals or teams.

Tomáš couldn't get an adoption KPI agreed at the top yet, so his version of the twin sits one level down: every autonomous area gets a product manager and an engineering manager who own one business outcome together. The pair should exist on every level, team, director, VP, CTO and CPO. If you're an engineering director setting this up below the VP, your product counterpart is your twin.

Tomáš wrote a small code change himself, his first in two years. It should have taken three hours. Reviews, pipelines and information he couldn't find about how the change would hit customers turned it into a day of development, and gating turned the rollout into a week.

For the pilot he set one target. By the first read, 60% of the friction points on that task's path get better. Each one is small, an hour here, half an hour there, fifteen minutes somewhere else.

If your teams work with AI agents, the friction list includes what the agent can't do: see a slow endpoint before a customer does, know the product history, run a dev instance, observe the deployment.

Tomáš started with a team that had a light roadmap, so the pilot wouldn't kill the plan. You need a reference before you need a transformation.

A small tooling group builds what the pilot team can't build itself: feature flags, faster pipelines, whatever the friction list asks for. After the pilot, the SWAT becomes a regular team with more people.

Tomáš cut his candidate outcome areas for autonomous teams from 18 to 5. Each area needs a strong engineering leader and a strong product leader, and five pairs is what he has. The existing leaders own fewer, broader areas, with no new leadership layer.

Here's the deck I'd want Tomáš to walk in with. Each slide answers one question an exec will ask anyway.

Capacity split, unplanned share, in money, by requesting division

The shared components every team waits on

Target split per team type, the 90/10 rule, reported every sprint

What do we give up, and when does it come back?

Cost of the quarter, running balance, revenue if adoption holds

Benchmark task, pilot team, date of the first read

Delivery KPI, adoption KPI, named owners, grading scale

I put the outline, a capacity sheet and a payback sheet into a free kit: download the platform business case kit (16 KB zip: Markdown, Word and three CSV sheets, no email needed).

Bring a proposal, not only a photo. A snapshot alone invites "why so much on support?" and then someone else decides. Let your directors collect the data; your job is to interpret it and propose one change.

Report the contract against reality every sprint. Every quarter my 100% was split into three agreed boxes, product, tech and everything else, and I checked them each sprint. When the delta grows, the right call is sometimes paradoxical: stop the technical work for two sprints and do product work, to get the balance back.

And the hard part comes after the yes. Not everyone will make the switch, either because they don't take ownership or because they can't work in a pair and are big egos. A few of them will have to leave.

Tomáš walked out with agreement to start the pilot. Its first read is still ahead, so I can't show you his benchmark numbers yet; when it reads out, I'll add them here. What will your exec team say when you ask for one quarter and promise three back? If you want to build that slide together before you present it, that's what my CTO mentoring is for.

From Corporate Job to Solopreneurship — Insights From Running My Own Mentorship Business For a Year

VP of Engineering @ Mews. SW Product Builder. See more at https://www.kamenistak.com/mentoring

#9840. AnyLanguageModel 1.0: One Year of Local Models on Apple Platforms

Last November, we introduced AnyLanguageModel on this blog: a drop-in replacement for Apple's Foundation Models framework that lets you choose the model and provider your app uses. We heard from app developers who were curious about local models but weren't always sure how to get started. They also wanted to avoid the added complexity of supporting multiple inference providers. AnyLanguageModel grew out of that feedback.

Local and hosted inference each have their strengths, and both have a role in building this new generation of intelligent apps. A shared API makes it easier to choose the right model for each task.

A year and dozens of releases later, AnyLanguageModel 1.0 is out, along with swift-huggingface 1.0 and swift-xet 1.0.

The core idea of AnyLanguageModel remains the same: use the Foundation Models API with the model that fits your app. To get started, change your import statement:

The same session code then works with the system model, with open-weight models through llama.cpp, MLX, and Core ML, and with the hosted providers below.

Over the past year, we've added several major features:

On OS 27, AnyLanguageModel also works with any model that conforms to Foundation Models' LanguageModel protocol, including Core AI models.

Alongside AnyLanguageModel, we've built out swift-huggingface and swift-xet to bring accelerated model downloads from the Hub to Swift apps.

Support for hosted models expanded this year, too. AnyLanguageModel now supports:

With Inference Providers, you can use open-weight models that are too big to run on the device with the same session code:

Hosted providers get the same features as local models: guided generation, tool calling with streaming, and token usage on responses.

Reasoning is now part of the transcript too. When you switch providers, reasoning blocks are automatically omitted from requests if the new provider can't replay them.

API keys come from a closure instead of a string, so your app can fetch short-lived tokens from your own server. The README explains when to let people bring their own keys and when to route requests through a proxy.

AnyLanguageModel also runs on Linux, so the same code can work on a server.

While we've made local models easier to use, the models themselves have become more capable, making the small ones a good place to start. Here are some of the most downloaded models on the Hub right now:

The first two fit on an iPhone, and Qwen3.8 27B runs on a Mac with 32 GB of memory or more. Selecting the MLX model takes one line:

And if you have four maxed-out Mac Studios handy, GLM-5.3 from Z.ai takes about 1.5 TB in BF16. For the rest of us, it's available through Inference Providers.

If you're upgrading an existing app, see the migration guidance in the AnyLanguageModel, swift-huggingface, and swift-xet release notes for help updating your code.

Community feedback and contributions have shaped several of our major features. Thank you to everyone who contributed for helping make AnyLanguageModel more useful to app developers.

Language models have proven to be a powerful tool for building intelligence into products. They're also one of many kinds of models developers can put to work. We're excited to bring the same approach to more capabilities: familiar Swift APIs with a choice of models running on the device. Coming soon: models that decide, and models that listen.

#9839. Data Broker Radaris Loses Domains in Privacy Fight

The radaris.com website, prior to the domain transfer to Atlas.

Less than a month after Atlas sued Radaris, KrebsOnSecurity published a deep dive into the Radaris co-founders — Igor and Dmitry Lubarsky (also spelled Lybarsky) — Russian-born brothers living in Massachusetts who operate a dizzying array of people-search companies as well as a number of Russian language dating services and affiliate programs.

Attorneys for the Lubarsky brothers threatened to sue for defamation if the story wasn’t removed and an apology issued. Their attorney asserted that our reporting was wildly inaccurate, and that the true owners of the company were Ukrainians living in Ukraine.

The Lubarsky brothers Dmitry or “Dan” (left) and Gary/Igor.

KrebsOnSecurity doubled down and showed how the Lubarsky brothers built and operated Radaris and other data broker companies using a fictitious CEO’s name. Our follow-up story noted that Radaris’s attorney — a lawyer with the Boston Law Group named Val Gurvits — admitted his clients had invented the CEO pseudonym “Gary Norden,” and that Radaris also had issued multiple press releases over the years that quoted the fake CEO while seeking money from potential investors.

Attorneys for Radaris waited until the last minute to appear in court and contest what was all but certain to be a default judgment in favor of the plaintiffs, and then told the court that Atlas had failed to serve the real owners and operators of Radaris and several of its sister data broker companies.

Atlas re-filed the lawsuit in June 2025, this time dramatically expanding the number of Radaris family data brokers accused of violating Daniel’s Law. Matt Adkisson, president and CEO of Atlas, said Radaris turned to a tried-and-true playbook: Delaying in court until the last possible minute, and playing shell games with Radaris’s true country of origin and the individuals listed as owners and operators of these sites.

Adkisson said when the defendants updated their terms of service to state that Radaris was suddenly managed by a company in the Marshall Islands, Atlas hired an investigator in that country and soon learned the brand new entity that Radaris claimed was managing the company didn’t even exist yet.

Mr. Gurvits stepped forward as Radaris’s attorney in a class action lawsuit the company temporarily lost in 2017 because it never contested the claim in court. When the plaintiffs told the judge they couldn’t collect on the $7.5 million default judgment, the court ordered the domain registry Verisign to transfer the radaris.com domain name to the plaintiffs.

Mr. Gurvits appealed that verdict, arguing the lawsuit hadn’t named the actual owners of the Radaris domain name — a Cyprus company called Bitseller Expert Limited — and thus taking the domain away would be a violation of their due process rights.

The judge in the 2017 case ruled in Radaris’ favor — halting the domain transfer — and told the plaintiffs they could refile their complaint. Soon after, the operator of Radaris changed from Bitseller to Andtop Company, an entity formed (PDF) in the Marshall Islands in Oct. 2020. The plaintiffs never re-filed their lawsuit.

A mind map of various entities tied to Radaris and the company’s co-founders. Click to enlarge.

“That seemed to be their modus operandi,” said Raj Parikh, a partner at PEM Law in New Jersey who handles most of the Daniel’s Law litigation for Atlas. “In the past, they won by attrition. Plaintiffs’ attorneys tired of the procedural games and just gave up. That strategy worked for a decade, and it probably would have worked in this case too, since any financial recovery from foreign actors will be difficult. But we were acutely aware of the threat this website posed to law enforcement officers and other public officials in New Jersey, and decided early on to commit whatever time and resources were necessary to remove that threat.”

On August 26, the judge in the New Jersey case found the defendants were given multiple chances to appear and defend the claims against them but had failed to do so. Mr. Gurvits declined to comment on the case, saying it had been assigned to another attorney, a Mr. Victor Worms. In response to questions, Mr. Worms asserted the New Jersey court transferred Radaris.com to Atlas as part of a default judgment against Radaris.com, which is not a legal entity.

“We have made a motion to vacate that default judgment on the grounds that it is void since a non-entity has no legal capacity to sue or be sued,” Worms replied. “We also intend to pursue all appropriate appeals because we believe the transfer of Radaris.com amounts to a forfeiture in violation of various constitutional principles.”

While radaris.com still comes up prominently in results when searching online for U.S. residents by name, the domain no longer sells detailed personal dossiers on millions of Americans. Its homepage now displays a notice from Atlas, as well as links to our previous reporting on Radaris.

Atlas told KrebsOnSecurity that it has obtained more than 10,000 emails and documents in the course of litigation, and that those messages confirm our previous reporting on the owners and operators of Radaris and its myriad companies.

Atlas said the emails clearly establish that the nominal legal vehicles — Radaris America, Inc.; Bitseller Expert Limited; Digital Orbit Corp; Core Solutions Group Inc; Lucky Solutions Inc; Virtura Corp; Veripages Inc.; Nuform Solutions Inc.; Growth Data Advisors Inc.; Property Experts, Inc — are all administered by the same three or four people from the same mailboxes, share one bank or payment card set, and are all managed from one virtual office address.

“The corpus establishes, with documentary evidence generated independently by banks, payment processors, hosting providers, registrars, software-as-a-service vendors and the operators’ own systems, that radaris.com and at least twenty-five other people-search websites are one operation run by a small Boston-area group whose administrative, financial and technical functions sit on the difive.com mail domain and its successors (centerex.com, scienteco.com, eprofit.com, realmo.com, pub360.com),” reads a summary shared by Atlas.

Atlas said the emails show Radaris.com earns approximately $42,000 a month, while Veripages.com earns around $45,000 monthly via its partnership with the Lifetime Value Company, a marketing and advertising firm whose brands include PeopleLooker, PeopleSmart, NumberGuru, and Bumper, a car history site.

According to Atlas, the emails also showed the Radaris family of websites earns as much as $25,000 each month from their partnership with Onerep, a company that claims to help people remove their information from people-search sites. In March 2024, KrebsOnSecurity revealed how the Belarusian founder of Onerep had launched and operated dozens of people-search sites over the years and was continuing to operate one of them (Nuwber), effectively spreading the disease and selling the cure.

The domain radaris.com now redirects to this notice from Atlas about the court-ordered domain transfer.

All told, the New Jersey court has so far transferred 14 domain names from the Radaris family of companies to Atlas. Radaris.com now redirects to a notice of the court-ordered domain transfer.

The Radaris family of companies is still potentially facing fines of $1,000 per alleged violation of Daniel’s Law. For the time being, however, Daniel’s Law is facing a constitutional challenge from virtually all of the 150 other consumer data broker firms being sued by Atlas.

The data broker industry responded by having at least 70 of the Atlas lawsuits moved to federal court, challenging the New Jersey statute as overly broad and a violation of the First Amendment. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit has not yet issued a decision on the constitutional challenge, but either way the case is widely expected to be appealed all the way to the U.S. Supreme Court.

Meanwhile, at least 14 other states have now passed laws modeled after the New Jersey statute, with more states considering similar measures. However, West Virginia’s Daniel’s Law was ruled facially unconstitutional under the First Amendment by a federal district court in August 2025.

“These days at the federal level, add in the intense amount of lobbying against these laws from social media companies, big tech, cryptocurrency firms, and now AI proponents in the mix who claim that limiting their data scraping is somehow going to collapse the whole U.S. economy under Chinese rule,” he said.

At least 25 states have passed or implemented laws requiring age verification for residents seeking to access adult content online, but there is no federal law that limits how the companies that are scanning everyone’s drivers license can use, share or keep the data provided. Had such restrictions been enshrined in law, we may have avoided the recent breach at IDScan.net, which exposed the drivers license information on more than 153 million Americans when the records were briefly turned into a point-and-click identity theft service on the dark web.

#9838. Hugging Face ❤️ TorchTPU: TPUs, Natively

If you ever tried to run PyTorch on a TPU, you probably ported your code to torch_xla, or you ended up having to learn JAX. With TorchTPU, a native PyTorch backend, TPU is now just another device. It opens up native support of TPU in the Hugging Face ecosystem. Transformers, Diffusers and Kernels run natively on TPU. Pick a model from the Hub, send it to "tpu", and you're done.

TPU stands for Tensor Processing Unit. TPUs are Google's own AI accelerators. They are chips built for one job: the matrix math that neural networks spend most of their time on. Google has been designing them for about ten years, and uses them to train and serve its own models, including Gemini.

TPUs are available on Google Cloud, from a single chip up to pods of thousands of chips. They shine when you need a lot of compute, for training or for serving at scale.

The catch has always been software. The TPU stack grew up around TensorFlow and JAX, and PyTorch users had to work harder to get in.

Until now, running PyTorch on TPUs meant going through PyTorch/XLA (torch_xla). It worked, but it had its quirks. Tensors were lazy (the tensors, not you), so your code didn't always run when you thought it did. Small changes could trigger graph recompilations, and debugging was hard to reason about.

To make life easier, we built Optimum TPU. It gave Hugging Face models inference and training support on TPUs. Now that TorchTPU brings native support, Optimum TPU is not required anymore to run Hugging Face models with Transformers and Diffusers.

TorchTPU adds TPU as a new backend to PyTorch. You write regular PyTorch code. It comes with Pallas kernels tuned for TPUs, support for distributed training, and a torch.compile integration for when you want more speed. Installing it on a TPU VM takes one command:

The extra index gives you the CPU build of torch. Without it, pip pulls the much bigger CUDA build, which you don't need on a TPU.

Transformers v5 was built around one idea: be the source of truth for model definitions, so they can run anywhere. "Anywhere" now includes TPUs. To load a model on a TPU, pass device_map="tpu". That's it.

The model runs in eager mode by default. You can also use torch.compile for better performance, or run it in a distributed setup.

TPU is now a first-class device in Diffusers. For prototyping or debugging, eager mode only needs pipe.to("tpu"). For deployment, compiled mode adds one compile call. Your pipelines and code stay the same, and there's no TPU fork to maintain.

The first call compiles, and every call after that with the same image size reuses the graph.

Models too big for one chip? Pass a TensorParallelConfig to from_pretrained and the transformer is sharded across chips as it loads, so the full model never has to fit in one place. Many popular pipelines support it out of the box, and the ones that don't are just a tp_plan away. The Diffusers TPU guide has the full recipe.

Here are some examples run on a Cloud TPU v6e-4:

TP=4 (each model split across four chips) · bf16 · batch 1

The Kernels Hub has ready-to-use TPU kernels. Load one with the Kernels library and give your model a speed boost.

TPU kernels are written in Pallas, which gives you low-level control over the hardware. You can also bring in kernels from the Tokamax library. Here is a ragged-dot kernel from Tokamax plugged into a Mixture-of-Experts model:

The bigger the batch, the bigger the win. At batch size 64, decoding is 21.5× faster on Qwen3-30B-A3B and 12.8× faster on Gemma 4 26B-A4B.

Decode throughput on a TPU v6e-8, Hub kernel vs. the default implementation.

We're continuously improving TPU support in transformers by running the library test suite. We are working to add a nightly CI on TPU and make the results available in the (transformers dashboard)[https://huggingface.co/spaces/transformers-community/transformers-ci-dashboard].

The Transformers CI dashboard, with TPU results next to other accelerators. Work in progress!

It's not all green yet, and we're fine with that. Of the tests that run on TPU, 96.5% pass. Every failure we find becomes a small repro script and an issue on the TorchTPU repo. So far we have reported 34 issues, and 19 are already fixed. Running on TPU also caught a few bugs in Transformers itself, like in StaticCache and the Qwen3 tensor-parallel plans. We fixed those upstream.

If something breaks on TPU, we want to find out before you do.

TPUs are no longer a side quest for PyTorch users. Install TorchTPU, grab a model from the Hub, and send it to "tpu".

We can't wait to see what you build 🤗. If you hit a problem, open an issue and tell us about it.

Once upon a time there was a young woman. Her name is Alice. Every morning Alice gets up, sits down at her desk and starts writing a beautiful story. She writes one story a day. Alice types all her stories on this beautiful old-fashioned typewriter. Whenever she's done writing, she pulls the paper out of the machine and puts her lovely new story on her desk. #9836. Kalshi's $40 Billion Valuation Signals Growing Investor Confidence in Prediction Markets

Co-Founder & Research Director at Prediction Frontier | Market Intelligence specialist covering prediction markets.

Co-Founder & Research Director at Prediction Frontier | Market Intelligence specialist covering prediction markets.

Co-Founder & Research Director at Prediction Frontier | Market Intelligence specialist covering prediction markets.

Kalshi raised another $1 billion this week at a $40 billion valuation, up from $22 billion in May.

The company’s latest Series G funding round, co-led by Sequoia Capital and Wellington Management, brings its valuation to eight times the $5 billion reported in October 2025.

Kalshi also disclosed that its non-sports businesses now generate over $1 billion in annualised revenue. Its institutional business is also growing, with approximately 500 entities trading on the exchange in September.

The valuation comes amid ongoing regulatory disputes, suggesting investors are increasingly confident in Kalshi's long-term prospects. Whether that confidence reflects expectations of favourable regulatory outcomes or a broader conviction that prediction markets are here to stay remains an open question.

Trading activity provides some context for the latest valuations.

Prediction Frontier’s Markets dashboard, using Dune data through October 25, shows $115.8 billion in notional volume, up 61.5% against the preceding 30-day period. Transactions reached 610.8 million, an increase of 37%.

The figures suggest trading activity is growing faster than participation. Existing traders may be generating more volume, although the aggregate data alone cannot establish how much of the increase comes from more frequent trading.

It is a distinction worth tracking as the industry continues setting volume records.

Another interesting development this week is the NBA naming Kalshi and Polymarket its preferred prediction-market exchanges this week, granting both platforms access to official league data, intellectual property and marketing rights.

The agreements also introduce restrictions on permissible markets, prohibit league and team personnel from trading NBA event contracts, and require information sharing around suspicious activity.

Separately, the NBA signed a memorandum of understanding with the CFTC on integrity oversight.

Beyond the commercial agreements, the interesting development is the league's role in determining which markets can be offered. The NBA retains approval rights over permissible contracts, giving it direct influence over market design.

This raises a question about how responsibility should be divided between sports leagues, exchanges and regulators.

Whether this arrangement becomes a wider model for sports prediction markets will depend partly on how effectively the restrictions and monitoring obligations work in practice.

Regulatory approaches remain fragmented outside the US. Gibraltar has established a dedicated framework for prediction markets, while Britain, Germany and the wider EU apply different legal classifications and restrictions.

Prediction Frontier’s latest analysis, Prediction Market Regulation in Europe: Can Gibraltar Offer a Model?, examines whether Gibraltar's approach can offer a workable framework for operator authorisation, contract approval and participant protection.

The discussion comes ahead of Prediction Markets Summit Europe, taking place on 9–10 November at Sunborn Gibraltar, organised by Eventus International.
